$$ \boxed{A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;1}=-\frac{i}{3}\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}}{(4\pi)^{2}}\frac{1}{\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n1}\rangle}\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<i_{3}<i_{4}\leq n}\langle{i_{1}i_{2}}\rangle[i_{2}i_{3}]\langle{i_{3}i_{4}}\rangle[i_{4}i_{1}].} $$

Note that the expression is rational and does not depend on the reference spinor $|\alpha\rangle$ , as promised.

The full amplitude can be written as a sum of single-trace partial amplitudes and double-trace partial amplitudes via

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{\text{1-loop}}(1,\ldots,n)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}/\mathbb{Z}_{n}}N_{c}\tr(T^{\sigma(1)} \ldots T^{\sigma(n)} )A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;1}(\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(n)) \displaystyle+\sum_{j=2}^{\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor+1}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}/\mathbb{Z}_{j-1}\times\mathbb{Z}_{n-j+1}}\tr(T^{\sigma(1) } \ldots T^{\sigma(j-1)})\tr(T^{\sigma(j)} \ldots T^{\sigma(n)})A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;j}(\sigma(1)\ldots\sigma(n)). $$

We review one-loop color ordering in more detail in appendix C. The point we want to make here is that the double-trace partial amplitudes are uniquely determined by the single-trace partial amplitudes via

$$ A_{n;j}^{\text{1-loop}}(1,2,\ldots,j\!-\!1;j,\ldots,n)=(-1)^{j-1}\sum_{\sigma\in\text{COP}\{\alpha\}\{\beta\}}A_{n;1}^{\text{1-loop}}(\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(n)) $$

where “ $\text{COP}\{\alpha\}\{\beta\}$ ” is a certain set of color-ordered-permutation we again define in appendix C. From the above formula and (208), one can check the following closed-form expression for the double-trace terms of the one-loop-all-plus amplitude holds: [132, 133]

$$ A_{n;j}^{\text{1-loop}}=-2i\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}}{(4\pi)^{2}}\frac{(p_{1,j-1}^{2})^{2}}{(\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{j-1,1}\rangle)(\langle{j,j+1}\rangle\ldots\langle{nj}\rangle)}. $$

### 11.2 SDG double-off-shell current calculation

Let us look at the analogous calculation for gravity. The authors BDPR [50] presented an expression for the double-off-shell SDG current in appendix B of their paper without proof. The 4-dimensional double-off-shell current satisfies the recursion relation

$$ (\ell+p_{N})^{2}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(\ell\,;\,N)=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\cup B=N\\
A\cap B=\emptyset,B\neq\emptyset\end{subarray}}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{A})p_{B}|\alpha}\rangle^{2}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(\ell\,;\,A)\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B) $$

and, with our conventions, is determined by the base case

$$ \mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(\ell)=\frac{i}{\ell^{2}}. $$

The closed-form expression is given by

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(\ell\,;\,N)= \displaystyle\frac{(\kappa/2)^{n}(-i)}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n\!-\!1,n}\rangle\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,j})j|\alpha}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2}}\right)\left(\sum_{m=1}^{n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,m})m|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,m-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,m})^{2}}\right) \displaystyle+\mathcal{P}(1,2,\ldots,n). $$

Here $\mathcal{P}(1,2,\ldots,n)$ is a sum over all permutations of the elements $1,2,\ldots,n$ . If one takes $\ell^{2}\to 0$ on-shell, amputates the $\ell$ propagator and accounts for the overall polarization factors, the double-off-shell current becomes equal to the single-off-shell current:

$$ \lim_{\ell^{2}\to 0}(\tfrac{\ell^{2}}{i})\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(\ell;1,\ldots,n)=\langle{\alpha\ell}\rangle^{4}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(\ell,1,\ldots,n)\Big\rvert_{\ell^{2}=0}. $$

The $4-2\epsilon$ -dimensional double-off-shell current is defined by going one stage up in the recursion relation, continuing all the denominators to $4-2\epsilon$ dimensions while keeping the numerators in $4$ dimensions:

$$ \mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(L\,;\,N)\equiv\frac{-\kappa/2}{(L+p_{N})^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\cup B=N\\
A\cap B=\emptyset,B\neq\emptyset\end{subarray}}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{A})p_{B}|\alpha}\rangle^{2}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(\ell\,;\,A)\Big\rvert_{\ell\,\mapsto L}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B). $$

BDPR provide an expression for this current as well. It is

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(L\,;\,N) \displaystyle=\frac{(\kappa/2)^{n}(-i)}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n\!-\!1,n}\rangle\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,j})j|\alpha}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2}}\right) \displaystyle\times\sum_{m=1}^{n}\frac{1}{(L+p_{1,m-1})^{2}(L+p_{1,m})^{2}}\left[\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,m})m|\alpha}\rangle-\frac{\mu^{2}}{(L+p_{1,n})^{2}}\langle{\alpha|p_{m,n}m|\alpha}\rangle\right] \displaystyle+\mathcal{P}(1,2,\ldots,n). $$

In their paper, they claim that they numerically checked the 4-dimensional current up to $n=8$ , and checked the $\mu^{2}$ -correction up to $n=3$ . We have numerically checked the full current, including the $\mu^{2}$ -correction, up to $n=10$ by generating random values for all the momenta and $\mu^{2}$ .

The formula (217) of course does not look like the tree formula for the single-off-shell current. There is almost certainly a nicer formula for $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(L;N)$ which generalizes the tree formula in some direct way. It would be interesting to find this expression.

Armed with the formula for the double-off-shell current, we can use it to compute an all-multiplicity expression for the one-loop-all-plus gravity amplitudes. This computation was sketched in words in [50] and we are told the authors performed the computation for $n=4,5$ , but here we carry it out to all $n$ . Note we cannot simply glue the two off-shell legs together due to an issue with overcounting. For instance, the configurations with $r$ trees coming off the central loop will be overcounted by a factor of $r$ because said trees can be cycled around the loop. To fix this issue, we have to glue a single-off-shell current containing one particular particle, say particle 1, to the double-off-shell vertex. The configuration is analogous to what we used in the Yang-Mills case in figure 29. Here, we sum over all the non-empty subsets $A$ and $B$ such that $A\cup B=N$ and $1\in B$ . We then attach the single-off-shell current $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B)$ to the double-off-shell current $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(L;A)$ :

$$ \mathcal{M}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{+},\ldots,n^{+})=\frac{i\kappa}{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\cup B=N\\
A\cap B=\emptyset\\
1\in B,A\neq\emptyset\end{subarray}}\int\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{B}|\alpha}\rangle^{2}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(L;A)\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B). $$

(An overall factor of 2 for the orientations of the $(+-)$ propagators is cancelled by a $1/2$ for graph-reflection symmetry after the currents are glued.) Using this expression, it is easy to introduce Feynman parameters and do the loop integrals exactly as we did in SDYM. The 4-dimensional “bubble” piece can immediately be seen to vanish due to the numerator structure. Only the $\mu^{2}$ -corrected triangle piece remains, and any term with an $\langle\alpha|\ell^{\prime}\ldots$ after the Feynman parameter shift vanishes. Only a simple scalar triangle integral in $6-2\epsilon$ dimensions remains which we already computed in (205). The final result is

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{+},\ldots,n^{+})=\frac{-i\kappa/2}{(4\pi)^{2}} \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\cup B=N\\
A\cap B=\emptyset\\
1\in B,A\neq\emptyset\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{all possible}\\
\text{permutations}\\
\text{of }A\text{ in }\mathcal{P}(A)\end{subarray}}\sum_{m=1}^{|A|}\int_{[0,1]^{3}}d^{3}u\,\delta(1\!-\!u_{1}\!-\!u_{2}\!-\!u_{3}) \displaystyle\times\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B)\langle{\alpha|(u_{1}p_{A}+u_{2}p_{a_{1},a_{m-1}}+u_{3}p_{a_{1},a_{m}})p_{B}|\alpha}\rangle^{2} \displaystyle\times\frac{(\kappa/2)^{|A|}}{\langle{\alpha a_{1}}\rangle\langle{a_{1}a_{2}}\rangle\ldots\langle{a_{|A|-1}a_{|A|}}\rangle\langle{\alpha a_{|A|}}\rangle}\langle{\alpha|p_{a_{m}a_{|A|}}a_{m}|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle\times\prod_{j=1}^{|A|}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(-u_{1}p_{A}-u_{2}p_{a_{1},a_{m-1}}-u_{3}p_{a_{1},a_{m}}+p_{a_{1},a_{j}})a_{j}|\alpha}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha a_{j}}\rangle^{2}}. $$

Note that we have not performed the trivial integrals over Feynman parameters. They are given by $\int_{[0,1]^{3}}d^{3}u\delta(1\!-\!u_{1}\!-\!u_{2}\!-\!u_{3})u_{1}^{n_{1}}u_{2}^{n_{2}}u_{3}^{n_{3}}=n_{1}!n_{2}!n_{3}!/(2+n_{1}+n_{2}+n_{3})!$ , but we haven’t executed this above because it would make the formula more complicated.

Admittedly, the above formula is a bit less than inspiring, but it is at least a closed form expression for the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes that can be derived using Feynman diagrammatics.

An interesting point is that the above expression can easily be transformed into an expression for the one-loop-one-minus amplitudes if one replaces the all-plus current $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B)$ with the one-minus current we could denote by $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1^{-},(B-\{1\})^{+})$ :

$$ \mathcal{M}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{-},2^{+},\ldots,n^{+})=\eqref{1141}\big\rvert_{\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B)\,\mapsto\,\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1^{-},(B-\{1\})^{+})}. $$

An all-multiplicity solution for the one-minus current was recently found by Hasuwannakit and Krasnov [93], which means that there does now exist an all multiplicity expression for the one-loop-one-minus gravity amplitudes.

## 12 Unitarity cuts in $D$ dimensions

In this section we will give a cursory overview of the unitarity method for computing one-loop-all-plus amplitudes [134, 131, 135]. In particular, we compute the 4-pt one-loop-all-plus SDYM amplitude with this method.

It is well known that unitarity (the optical theorem) implies that the discontinuities of a one-loop amplitude are given by the on-shell cuts of the amplitude. Furthermore, as discussed in section 9.1, all the cuts of the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes are zero, meaning the amplitudes are rational. So, given that the cuts are zero, how could we possibly use cuts to compute these amplitudes? The answer is that, while all of the 4-dimensional cuts are zero, the $D=4-2\epsilon$ dimensional cuts are not zero! Strictly speaking, however, it does not make sense to talk about $4-2\epsilon$ dimensional cuts using standard unitarity theorems. This method should more precisely be thought of as a way to construct simplified ansatze for Feynman integrands. In its modern incarnation, one typically performs four cuts, specifying the four components of the loop momentum, and turns any loop into a sum of boxes, triangles, and bubbles. This is of course even more remote from actual unitarity and is therefore referred to as “generalized unitarity.” For a description of the modern method, see for instance the work of Badger [136, 110]. See also for instance the discussion in [72]. Here however we will stick to the old-fashioned method based on two-particle cuts.

The method essentially boils down to constructing Feynman integrals which have all the correct cuts in all possible channels by gluing simplified on-shell tree amplitudes together. This is especially simple when all particles are massless, although see for instance [131] on the massive case.

*Figure 30: The two cuts of the planar 4-pt SDYM amplitude.*

For a 4-pt massless planar color-ordered amplitude, the only non-zero cuts occur in the $s_{12}$ and $s_{23}$ channels. Let’s focus first on the $s_{12}$ , where we cut through the loop momenta $L$ and $L+p_{1}+p_{2}$ . We denote the 4-dimensional part of these $4-2\epsilon$ dimensional momenta as $\ell$ and $\ell+p_{1}+p_{2}$ . On this cut, we have the on-shell condition

$$ L^{2}=0,\hskip 14.22636pt(L+p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}=0. $$

This is equivalent to saying the 4-dimensional parts of the loop momenta have a mass $\mu^{2}$ :

$$ \ell^{2}=\mu^{2},\hskip 28.45274pt(\ell+p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}=\mu^{2}. $$

Now let us define the tree-amplitude $A^{\rm tree}(L,1^{+},2^{+},-L-p_{1}-p_{2})$ which satisfies the above on-shell condition. For simplicity, we imagine the $L$ and $-L-p_{1}-p_{2}$ legs to be “scalars” with no associated polarization factors. The two diagrams that contribute to this amplitude are drawn in figure 31.

*Figure 31: The two diagrams that contribute to $A^{\rm tree}(L,1^{+},2^{+},-L\!-\!p_{1}\!-\!p_{2})$*

Summing up the two diagrams, we get the following expression:

$$ \displaystyle A^{\rm tree}(L,1^{+},2^{+},-L\!-\!p_{1}\!-\!p_{1}) \displaystyle=\frac{i(\sqrt{2}g)^{2}}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{2}}\left(\frac{\langle{\alpha|\ell 1|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|(\ell+1)2|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{1})^{2}}+\frac{\langle{\alpha|12|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|\ell(1+2)|\alpha}\rangle}{\langle{12}\rangle[12]}\right). $$

This expression can be simplified using the following identity (proven in appendix F.3)

$$ \displaystyle\langle{\alpha|\ell 1|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|(\ell+1)2|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle=\frac{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle}{\langle{12}\rangle}\Big((\ell+p_{1})^{2}\langle{\alpha|\ell(1+2)|\alpha}\rangle-(\ell+p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}\langle{\alpha|\ell 1|\alpha}\rangle-\ell^{2}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+1)2|\alpha}\rangle\Big). $$

Using the cut condition (222) and the above identity, the tree amplitude simplifies to

$$ A^{\rm tree}(L,1^{+},2^{+},-L\!-\!p_{1}\!-\!p_{1})=i(\sqrt{2}g)^{2}\frac{\mu^{2}}{(L+p_{1})^{2}}\frac{[12]}{\langle{12}\rangle}. $$

Note that this amplitude is proportional to $\mu^{2}$ , which implies that it is zero in exactly 4-dimensions, as expected. Crucially, the above formula is also exact in general dimension $D$ , i.e. for all possible values of $\epsilon$ not necessarily small. The use of the exact tree amplitude in general $D$ is required in order for this method to produce the correct result.

For the 4-particle amplitude, the expression is simply a sum of the two cuts.

$$ \displaystyle A_{4;1}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{+},2^{+},3^{+},4^{+}) \displaystyle=\int\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}\frac{i}{L^{2}}\frac{i}{(L+p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}}A^{\rm tree}(L,1^{+},2^{+},-L\!-\!p_{1}\!-\!p_{2})A^{\rm tree}(L\!-\!p_{3}\!-\!p_{4},3^{+},4^{+},-L) \displaystyle+\int\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}\frac{i}{L^{2}}\frac{i}{(L+p_{2}+p_{3})^{2}}A^{\rm tree}(L,2^{+},3^{+},-L\!-\!p_{2}\!-\!p_{3})A^{\rm tree}(L\!-\!p_{4}\!-\!p_{1},4^{+},1^{+},-L). $$

(A factor of 2 for the two polarizations of particles which can run across the cut is cancelled by an identical particle phase space factor of 1/2.)

For more than 4 particles, however, the amplitude is not simply a sum over cuts as shown above. This is, of course, because the tree-amplitudes themselves generically contain multi-particle propagators which will affect the values of other cuts. In general the difficulty comes in engineering expressions that agree on all cuts. Nowadays this is often done using computer software such as BlackHat [137].

In any case, for 4 particles the expression becomes

$$ \displaystyle A_{4;1}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{+},2^{+},3^{+},4^{+}) \displaystyle=\frac{[12]}{\langle{12}\rangle}\frac{[34]}{\langle{34}\rangle}(\sqrt{2}g)^{4}\int\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}\frac{\mu^{4}}{L^{2}(L+p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}(L+p_{1})^{2}(L-p_{4})^{2}} \displaystyle+\frac{[23]}{\langle{23}\rangle}\frac{[41]}{\langle{41}\rangle}(\sqrt{2}g)^{4}\int\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}\frac{\mu^{4}}{L^{2}(L+p_{2}+p_{3})^{2}(L+p_{2})^{2}(L-p_{1})^{2}}. $$

The integrals are easy to evaluate and give

$$ A_{4;1}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{+},2^{+},3^{+},4^{+})=\frac{-i(\sqrt{2}g)^{4}}{6(4\pi)^{2}}\left(\frac{[12]}{\langle{12}\rangle}\frac{[34]}{\langle{34}\rangle}+\frac{[23]}{\langle{23}\rangle}\frac{[41]}{\langle{41}\rangle}\right) $$

which is the correct expression.

## 13 One-loop-all-plus gravity expression of Bern, Dixon, Perelstein, Rozowsky

In this section we write down the nice closed-form expression for one-loop-all-plus SDG amplitudes, due to BDPR [50, 51], and explain where it comes from. We do not provide a proof of this formula because, at the time of writing this note, none exists. We expect the situation will be rectified in the near future.

Without further ado, the BDPR formula is

$$ \mathcal{M}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{+},...,n^{+})=-\frac{i}{(4\pi)^{2}960}\left(-\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)^{n}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq a<b\leq n\\
A,B\end{subarray}}h(a,A,b)h(b,B,a)\tr^{3}[aAbB]. $$

We have checked numerically that the above expression matches equation (219) up to $n=9$ on the support of momentum conservation. In this formula, $A$ and $B$ are indistinguishable sets such that $A\cup B\cup\{a,b\}=\{1...n\}$ , $A\cap B=\emptyset$ , $a,b\notin A,B$ . We also have the definition

$$ \tr[aAbB]\equiv\langle a|p_{A}|b]\langle b|p_{B}|a]+\langle b|p_{A}|a]\langle a|p_{B}|b] $$

and define the “half-soft function” by

$$ h(a,\{1,2,...,n\},b)\equiv\frac{[12]}{\langle{12}\rangle}\frac{\langle a|p_{1,2}|3]\langle a|p_{1,3}|4]...\langle a|p_{1,n-1}|n]}{\langle{23}\rangle\langle{34}\rangle...\langle{n-1,n}\rangle\langle{a1}\rangle\langle{a2}\rangle\langle{a3}\rangle...\langle{an}\rangle\langle{1b}\rangle\langle{nb}\rangle}+\mathcal{P}(2,\!3,...,n) $$

where $p_{1,m}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_{i}$ and $\mathcal{P}(2,3,\ldots,n)$ represents a sum over all permutations of the denoted elements.

There are other nicer-looking presentations of the half-soft function [107]. These other presentations are equal to (231) identically, without the use of momentum conservation.77 7 To prove that the expression (231) is equal to these other expressions, all one has to do is show that all the expressions satisfy the same Berends-Giele recursion relation (236). Luckily for us, formula (231) was proven to satisfy it in appendix C.2 of [50].

If one defines the $n\times n$ matrix $\Psi$ via

$$ \Psi=\begin{cases}-\dfrac{[ij]}{\langle{ij}\rangle}\langle{ai}\rangle\langle{bi}\rangle\langle{aj}\rangle\langle{bj}\rangle&i\neq j\\
\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k=1\\
k\neq i\end{subarray}}^{n}\dfrac{[ik]}{\langle{ik}\rangle}\langle{ai}\rangle\langle{bi}\rangle\langle{ak}\rangle\langle{bk}\rangle&i=j\end{cases} $$

then the half soft function turns out to be equal to

$$ h(a,\{1,2,\ldots,n\},b)=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\langle{ai}\rangle^{2}\langle{bi}\rangle^{2}}\right)|\Psi|^{i}_{i} $$

where $|\Psi|^{i}_{i}$ is the determinant of the minor of $\Psi$ where the row and column $i$ has been removed. The determinant is independent of $i$ . Note that none of the $i$ ’s are equal to $a$ or $b$ . This equation was given in [95].

Using the matrix tree theorem, the half-soft function can also be rewritten [107] as the tree sum

$$ h(a,\{1,2,\ldots,n\},b)=\left(\prod_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\langle{ak}\rangle^{2}\langle{bk}\rangle^{2}}\right)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{trees with }\\
n\text{ nodes}\end{subarray}}\prod_{\text{edges }(ij)}\frac{[ij]}{\langle{ij}\rangle}\langle{ai}\rangle\langle{bi}\rangle\langle{aj}\rangle\langle{bj}\rangle. $$

The “trees” in the above formula are graphically the same trees that we saw for the all-plus current in figure 12. Having said that, the rules for the edges are different, as they depend on $|a\rangle$ and $|b\rangle$ instead of $|\alpha\rangle$ . However, if we set $|a\rangle=|b\rangle=|\alpha\rangle$ , then the half-soft function is in fact equal to the all-plus current via

$$ \mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,2,\ldots,n)=\left(-\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)^{n-1}h(\alpha,\{1,2,\ldots,n\},\alpha). $$

As one might expect from the above relation, the half-soft function also satisfies a slightly more general form of the Berends-Giele recursion relation that $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}$ satisfies, namely [98]

$$ p_{N}^{2}h(a,N,b)=\sum_{A,B|A\cup B=N}\langle{a|p_{A}p_{B}|a}\rangle\langle{b|p_{A}p_{B}|b}\rangle h(a,A,b)h(a,B,b) $$

where here $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $a,b\notin N$ . As a final relation, if we imagine that all of the momenta now sum to zero, the half-soft function is equal, up to a factor, to the NSVW formula for the tree-level gravity MHV amplitude [97]

$$ \mathcal{M}^{\rm tree}(1^{-},2^{-},3^{+},\ldots,n^{+})=i(-\kappa/2)^{n-2}\langle{12}\rangle^{6}h(1,\{3,\ldots,n\},2)\Big|_{p_{1}+\ldots+p_{n}=0}. $$

Why the all-plus currents and the MHV amplitudes are so closely related is actually not so clear, although it is reasonable enough given that both expressions have similar soft and collinear properties.

Now that we have written down the BDPR formula (229), as well as some properties of the half-soft function, you may be wondering how the authors actually came up with this formula. The all- $n$ expression (229) originated from a guess that comes from a few different lines of reasoning.

Firstly, it was conjectured in [138] and then checked up to $n=6$ that the following relationship between one-loop-all-plus amplitudes in pure Yang-Mills in $D$ dimensions and one-loop MHV amplitudes in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM in $D+4$ dimensions holds:

$$ \displaystyle A_{n;1}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{+},\ldots,n^{+}) \displaystyle=-2\epsilon(1-\epsilon)(4\pi)^{2}\left[\frac{A_{n;1}^{\mathcal{N}=4,\text{1-loop}}(1^{-},2^{-},3^{+},\ldots,n^{+})}{\langle{12}\rangle^{4}}\Bigg|_{D\to D+4}\right] \displaystyle=2\frac{A_{n;1}^{\mathcal{N}=4,\text{1-loop}}(1^{-},2^{-},3^{+},\ldots,n^{+})[\mu^{4}]}{\langle{12}\rangle^{4}}. $$

This was recently revisited and proven in [139, 140].

To reiterate, on the LHS we have the one-loop-all-plus amplitude in pure Yang-Mills theory in $4-2\epsilon$ dimensions, while on the RHS have the one-loop $\mathcal{N}=4$ MHV amplitudes in $8-2\epsilon$ dimensions, for all $\epsilon$ . In particular, the MHV amplitudes in $D=8-2\epsilon$ dimensions have a $1/\epsilon$ divergence that is cancelled out by the factor of $\epsilon$ , making the expression finite. The RHS is equivalent to inserting a factor of $\mu^{4}$ in all of the Feynman integrals that appear in the $D=4-2\epsilon$ dimensional amplitudes.

*Figure 32: Box integrals with two on-shell legs are the only integrals that contribute to the $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM one-loop MHV amplitudes. Image is figure 1 of [50].*

Due to the fact that the supersymmetric amplitudes are 4-dimensional cut constructible, it was also known that the $D=4-2\epsilon$ , $\mathcal{N}=4$ MHV amplitudes can be expressed as a sum over scalar box integrals where two legs are on-shell, [141, 142]

$$ \displaystyle A_{n;1}^{\mathcal{N}=4,\text{1-loop}}(1^{-},2^{-},3^{+},\ldots,n^{+})=\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}}{4}\frac{\langle{12}\rangle^{4}}{\langle{12}\rangle\langle{23}\rangle\ldots\langle{n1}\rangle}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a,b\\
\text{cyclic}\end{subarray}}\,\tr[aK_{1}bK_{2}]\,\mathcal{I}_{4}^{aK_{1}bK_{2}}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon) $$

where $\mathcal{I}_{4}^{aK_{1}bK_{2}}$ is the scalar box integral with two on-shell legs $a$ and $b$ , depicted in figure 32, and we sum over all cyclic orderings where $\{a\}\cup K_{1}\cup\{b\}\cup K_{2}=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ . (The $\mathcal{N}=8$ supergravity one-loop MHV amplitudes similarly depend on the same type of box integrals.)

Based on the Yang-Mills formula (238), it was then conjectured that a similar formula should hold for gravity between pure Einstein gravity one-loop-all-plus amplitudes in $D=4-2\epsilon$ dimensions and $\mathcal{N}=8$ supergravity one-loop MHV amplitudes in $D=12-2\epsilon$ dimensions, namely

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{+},\ldots,n^{+}) \displaystyle=-2\epsilon(1-\epsilon)(2-\epsilon)(3-\epsilon)(4\pi)^{4}\left[\frac{\mathcal{M}^{\mathcal{N}=4,\text{1-loop}}(1^{-},2^{-},3^{+},\ldots,n^{+})}{\langle{12}\rangle^{8}}\Bigg|_{D\to D+8}\right] \displaystyle=2\frac{\mathcal{M}^{\mathcal{N}=4,\text{1-loop}}(1^{-},2^{-},3^{+},\ldots,n^{+})[\mu^{8}]}{\langle{12}\rangle^{8}}. $$

Looking at the above formulae, we can begin to see how one might come up with (229), as the structure of the box integrals from figure 32 looks very similar to the structure of (229). Although certainly a bit of black magic has occurred.

BDPR also showed that (229) satisfies a number of consistency conditions. It was checked to have the correct soft limit and collinear limits. To be more precise, it was showed to satisfy the correct “double-scaled holomorphic collinear limit” where $[ij]\to 0$ , $\langle{ij}\rangle\to 0$ , $[ij]/\langle{ij}\rangle\to\infty$ . (See our discussion in section 9.3). A later work by Ball, Narayan, Salzer, and Strominger [113] confirmed that it also has the correct pure holomorphic collinear limits $\langle{ij}\rangle\to 0$ as well, as written in (164). This check required the use of the quite non-trivial identity

$$ \sum_{b\neq a}\langle{ba}\rangle\sum_{A,B}h(a,A,b)h(a,B,b)\langle b|p_{A}|a]\langle a|p_{B}|b]^{3}=0 $$

where the sum is over $b$ , $A$ , $B$ , such that $A\cup B\cup\{a,b\}=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ , $A\cap B=\emptyset$ , $a,b\notin A,B$ and $(A,B)$ is not distinct from $(B,A)$ . Note that this identity only holds on the support of momentum conservation. This identity was checked to hold for $n\leq 13$ in [143] and proven for all $n$ by Rao and Feng [144].

Via direct computation, BDPR showed that their the formula (229) matched the correct amplitudes at $n=4,5,6$ on the support of momentum conservation. Their computation of the ‘correct amplitudes’ used the $D=4-2\epsilon$ -dimensional unitarity cuts technique we reviewed in the last section. In order to obtain the $D$ dimensional gravitational tree amplitudes, the authors employed a dimensionally-analytically-continued form of the the KLT relations, double-copying the analogous gauge theory amplitudes. They also used supersymmetry to replace the graviton running around the loop with a complex scalar, simplifying the numerator structure of the problem. Note that this provides the same computational advantage as working with the lightcone scalar, which we do in this note. (In their appendix B, they also used the double-off-shell current method to match the amplitudes at $n=4,5$ , which we straightforwardly extended to all- $n$ in (219).)

Let us now highlight another result from [50]. Now that they had computed the $n=4,5,6$ gravity amplitudes on the LHS of (238), they in principle knew the $n=4,5,6$ $\mathcal{N}=8$ MHV amplitudes on the RHS as well. Using these expressions, they then conjectured the following formula for the $\mathcal{N}=8$ amplitudes in $D=4-2\epsilon$ (see their equation (6.18)):

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{\mathcal{N}=8,\text{1-loop}}(1^{-},2^{-},3^{+},\ldots,n^{+}) \displaystyle=\frac{(-\kappa/2)^{n}}{8}\langle{12}\rangle^{8}\sum_{1\leq a<b\leq n,A,B}h(a,A,b)h(b,B,a)\tr^{2}[aAbB]\,\mathcal{I}^{aAbB}_{4}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon). $$

This closely resembles (229), and it seems like it should be a straightforward matter to compare them via (240), but strangely the connection is not as simple as it seems. This is because dimension shifting the box integrals in the above equation by $\mu^{8}$ does not give the extra trace term $\tr[aMbN]$ as one would expect, so the true relationship is much more complicated.

We also mention that in section 4.2 of [50] the authors provided a KLT “proof” of (240) using (238). Essentially, if one cuts both sides of (238), the gauge theory cuts on the LHS must be equal to the $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM cuts multiplied by $\mu^{4}$ on the RHS. One can then use the KLT relations to double copy both sides and get (240).

## 14 Classical self-dual solutions and $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ / $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ symmetry

### 14.1 SDG and $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$

Classical SDYM and SDG are integrable theories, implying their solution spaces are acted on by infinite-dimensional Lie-algebras. These Lie algebras are $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ for SDYM and $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ for SDG. In this section we will discuss how these symmetries act perturbatively on the space of solutions. Note this section is a summary of the paper [109], although here we work in momentum space instead of the “Mellin space” more common in celestial holography papers. (The full paper also finds that a subset of $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ transformations are pure spacetime diffeomorphisms, and discusses the action of the ‘recursion operator,’ but we won’t be reviewing those stories here.)

Let us begin our discussion by defining the notion of a “perturbiner expansion.” A perturbiner expansion is a solution to an equation of motion which is built perturbatively out of plane waves. For economy of notation, we denote these plane waves as $\phi_{i}$ via

$$ \phi_{i}\equiv\epsilon_{i}e^{ip_{i}\cdot x}. $$

These are positive-helicity gravitons. Here, $p_{i}$ is an on-shell momentum with $p_{i}^{2}=0$ , and $\epsilon_{i}$ is an infinitesimal parameter. Each plane wave has its own infinitesimal parameter. These parameters are defined such that each one squares to zero

$$ (\epsilon_{i})^{2}=0 $$

but the product of distinct $\epsilon_{i}$ ’s is non-zero,

$$ \epsilon_{i}\,\epsilon_{i^{\prime}}\neq 0,\hskip 28.45274pt\text{ if }i\neq i^{\prime}. $$

We are now interested in perturbatively generating solutions to the SDG equation of motion

$$ \Box\,\phi-\frac{\kappa}{2}\{\partial_{u}\phi,\partial_{w}\phi\}=0. $$

We notate the perturbiner expansions as

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi_{i}+\ldots $$

The perturbiner expansion $\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n})$ is defined as the classical solution defined via the following procedure. Start with a sum of free plane waves multiplied by infinitesimal parameters, and, by recursively plugging the solution into the equation of motion (246), solve for all the higher order terms in the $\epsilon_{i}$ ’s. Note that a term of order $k$ in the $\epsilon_{i}$ ’s will have $\kappa^{k-1}$ powers of the coupling. Note also that the perturbiner expansion will terminate at a term with all $n$ infinitesimal parameters, $\epsilon_{1}\epsilon_{2}\ldots\epsilon_{n}$ .

Based on this definition, it is straightforward to see that a perturbiner expansion is essentially the exact same thing as a Berends-Giele current with one off-shell leg. We have provided a review of this connection in appendix H for the uninitiated. But the upshot is that, because we already have a closed-form expression for the all-plus Berends-Giele current in SDG (134), we also have a closed-form expression for the full perturbiner expansion. If we notationally separate out the perturbiner expansion into the individual terms which only depend certain seed functions via

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}\,(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n})=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\}\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}\end{subarray}}\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(k)}(\phi_{i_{1}},\ldots,\phi_{i_{k}}), $$

where here we are summing over all subsets $\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\}$ of seed functions, then the expression for the perturbiner expansion is given by

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(k)}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{k})=\left(\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)^{k-1}\sum_{\rm{trees}}\left(\prod_{\text{edges }(ij)}\frac{D^{ij}}{z_{ij}}\right)\left(\prod_{a=1}^{k}\phi_{a}\right). $$

In the above expression for $\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(k)}$ , we sum over trees (like in figure 12) with $k$ nodes.

The symbol $D^{ij}$ is defined as

$$ D^{ij}\equiv\partial_{u}^{(i)}\partial^{(j)}_{w}-\partial_{w}^{(i)}\partial^{(j)}_{u} $$

where $\partial_{\mu}^{(i)}$ is a differential symbol that only acts on the seed function $\phi_{i}$ , but not $\phi_{i^{\prime}}$ for $i\neq i^{\prime}$ :

$$ \partial_{\mu}^{(i)}\phi_{i}\equiv\partial_{\mu}\phi_{i},\hskip 28.45274pt\partial_{\mu}^{(i)}\phi_{i^{\prime}}\equiv 0\hskip 14.22636pt\text{ for }i\neq i^{\prime}. $$

For example

$$ \partial_{\mu}^{(1)}(\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\phi_{3})=(\partial_{\mu}\phi_{1})\phi_{2}\phi_{3}, $$

and

$$ D^{12}(\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\phi_{3})=\{\phi_{1},\phi_{2}\}\phi_{3}. $$

Recall the Poisson bracket is defined using the two lightcone coordinates $u$ and $w$ via

$$ \{f,g\}=\partialderivative{f}{u}\partialderivative{g}{w}-\partialderivative{f}{w}\partialderivative{g}{u}. $$

Equation (249) could have also been written as a sum over cubic Feynman diagrams, but the sum over “trees” makes the holomorphic collinear limits manifest.

As a consequence of the integrability of SDG, the above perturbiner expansion satisfies an extra recursive formula based on collinear limits. This is the same recursive formula we noted that the Berends-Giele current satisfied in (151). It is

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(n)}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n})=\frac{\kappa}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(n-1)}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\frac{1}{z_{in}}\{\phi_{i},\phi_{n}\},\ldots,\phi_{n-1}). $$

The above formula is what we call the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ Ward identity. It is a manifestly 2-dimensional formula that generates classical solutions to the 4-dimensional theory. In fact, from the above formula, we can almost instantaneously read-off the fact that the theory is acted on by the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ Lie algebra. In order to explain this, let us first define what the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ Lie algebra is. It is the “loop algebra” of the $\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ algebra, where the $\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ is simply the algebra of functions on the 2d plane under the Poisson bracket. Here, we use $(u,w)$ as the coordinates of the plane, and $\{\cdot,\cdot\}$ is given by (254).

Let us parameterize the generators of the $\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ Lie algebra in a suggestive way, via 2-dimensional plane-waves. Let us treat the two components of the anti-holomorphic spinor $|\tilde{\lambda}]$ , denoted $\tilde{\lambda}_{\dot{A}}$ with $\dot{A}=\dot{1},\dot{2}$ , to be the two components of momentum in the 2d $(u,w)$ plane. (Actually, it turns out that these two components really will be two components of the physical momenta of a particle in lightcone coordinates, with $\tilde{\lambda}_{i,\dot{A}}=(-\omega_{i}{\bar{z}}_{i},\omega_{i})=(p_{i,w},p_{i,u})$ , but we’ll get to that momentarily.)

So, we define the plane-wave generators of the $\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ algebra as

$$ \mathbf{T}_{|\tilde{\lambda}]}\equiv e^{i(\tilde{\lambda}_{\dot{2}}u+\tilde{\lambda}_{\dot{1}}w)}\in\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}. $$

The $\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ commutator of two such generators within the Poisson bracket can easily be calculated to be

$$ \{\mathbf{T}_{|1]},\mathbf{T}_{|2]}\}=-[12]\,\mathbf{T}_{|1]+|2]} $$

where we recall the notation

$$ [12]=-\varepsilon^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\tilde{\lambda}_{1,\dot{A}}\tilde{\lambda}_{2,\dot{B}}\equiv-\tilde{\lambda}_{1,\dot{1}}\tilde{\lambda}_{2,\dot{2}}+\tilde{\lambda}_{1,\dot{2}}\tilde{\lambda}_{2,\dot{1}}. $$

Let us now “loopify” the $\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ algebra to get the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ algebra. To loopify a Lie algebra, we simply append an integer index to the generators that add under the commutator. (We also add 1 to the index in our conventions). So, the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ generators are denoted

$$ \mathbf{T}_{|\tilde{\lambda}],n^{\prime}}\in\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}\hskip 28.45274pt\text{for }n^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z} $$

and the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ commutation relation is defined to be

$$ [\mathbf{T}_{|1],n_{1}},\mathbf{T}_{|2],n_{2}}]\equiv-[12]\,\mathbf{T}_{|1]+|2],n_{1}+n_{2}+1}. $$

Notice that the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ generators are labelled by three degrees of freedom: two components of $|\tilde{\lambda}]$ and one integer $n^{\prime}$ . This is the same as the three-degrees of freedom for the on-shell momentum of a positive-helicity graviton. In fact, every $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ generator should be thought of as being equivalent to a positive-helicity graviton, as we’ll explain shortly.

First, let us introduce a convenient set of conventions to discuss on-shell momenta $p=|\lambda\rangle[\tilde{\lambda}|$ in lightcone coordinates. We shall now set the spinor variables $|\lambda\rangle$ , $|\tilde{\lambda}]$ and reference spinor $|\alpha\rangle$ to be

$$ \lambda_{i}^{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\
z_{i}\end{pmatrix},\hskip 14.22636pt\tilde{\lambda}_{i}^{\dot{A}}=\begin{pmatrix}\omega_{i}\\
\omega_{i}{\bar{z}}_{i}\end{pmatrix},\hskip 14.22636pt\alpha^{A}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\
1\end{pmatrix}. $$

With these definitions, we have the relations

$$ \langle{ij}\rangle=z_{ij},\hskip 28.45274pt\langle{\alpha i}\rangle=1,\hskip 28.45274pt[12]=\omega_{1}\omega_{2}{\bar{z}}_{12}, $$

where $z_{ij}=z_{i}-z_{j}$ . The massless momenta are parameterized by $(\omega,z,{\bar{z}})$ via

$$ p^{\mu}_{i}=(p^{0}_{i},p^{1}_{i},p^{2}_{i},p^{3}_{i})=\frac{\omega_{i}}{2}(1+z{\bar{z}}_{i},z_{i}+{\bar{z}}_{i},-i(z_{i}-{\bar{z}}_{i}),1-z_{i}{\bar{z}}_{i}). $$

*Figure 33: The action of $\mathbf{T}_{|\tilde{\lambda}],n^{\prime}}$ on the spacetime. Add in one extra graviton seed function $\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}],z}$ to the perturbiner expansion and integrate it in a contour around all pre-existing seed functions, weighted by $1/z^{n^{\prime}+1}$ .*

Notice that $|\tilde{\lambda}]$ depends only on $(\omega,{\bar{z}})$ . Therefore, we can actually think of our massless momenta $p$ as being parameterized by $(|\tilde{\lambda}],z)$ , which we can denote as $p_{|\tilde{\lambda}],z}$ . Note that we are not treating our holomorphic and anti-holomorphic spinors on equal footing.

With these parameterizations, we shall now explain how we can use the recursive formula (255) to read off the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ action on classical solutions. We define the linear change that comes from “adding in” one more graviton seed function into the spacetime using a vertical line:

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n}|\phi_{n+1})\equiv\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n},\phi_{n+1})-\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n}). $$

We now write the action of $\mathbf{T}_{|\tilde{\lambda}],n^{\prime}}$ on the spacetime, which we’ll denote as $\delta_{|\tilde{\lambda}],n^{\prime}}$ , as

$$ \delta_{|\tilde{\lambda}],n^{\prime}}\cdot\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n})\equiv\oint_{C}\frac{dz}{2\pi i}\frac{1}{z^{n^{\prime}+1}}\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n}|\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}],z}), $$

where $C$ is a contour that surrounds $z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}$ . See figure 33.

To reiterate, an $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ transformation simply “adds in” one extra positive-helicity graviton into the spacetime. The momentum of this graviton is $p_{|\tilde{\lambda}],z}$ , where the position $z$ is integrated in a loop around all the pre-existing gravitons, and the integral is weighted by $1/z^{n^{\prime}+1}$ .

Now, why does (265) satisfy the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ commutation relation (260)? The proof follows the natural “contour deformation” argument that one encounters in introductory discussions of 2d CFTs.

If one wants to compute the action of two sequential $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ transformations, i.e. $\delta_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{2}],n_{2}}\cdot\delta_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{1}],n_{1}}$ , on a spacetime, one needs to choose a bigger contour for the second transformation that encloses the first contour as well as the previous seed functions and the origin. Let us say that the contour $C^{\prime}$ is the bigger contour enclosing $C$ . Then one has

$$ \displaystyle[\delta_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{2}],n_{2}},\delta_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{1}],n_{1}}]\cdot\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi i)^{2}}\left(\oint_{C}\frac{dz_{1}}{z_{1}^{n_{1}+1}}\oint_{C^{\prime}}\frac{dz_{2}}{z_{2}^{n_{2}+1}}-\oint_{C^{\prime}}\frac{dz_{1}}{z_{1}^{n_{1}+1}}\oint_{C}\frac{dz_{2}}{z_{2}^{n_{2}+1}}\right)\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n},\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{1}],z_{1}},\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{2}],z_{2}}). $$

(In second line of the above equation, only terms in the perturbiner expansion which contain both $\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{1}],z_{1}}$ and $\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{2}],z_{2}}$ won’t be projected out by the contour integrals. Terms which have neither are trivially killed by the difference of contour integrals because they don’t depend on $z_{1}$ or $z_{2}$ , and terms with only one of $\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{1}],z_{1}}$ or $\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{2}],z_{2}}$ are also killed by the difference of integrals, because if a term only depends on either $z_{1}$ or $z_{2}$ then the contours $C$ and $C^{\prime}$ can be moved past each other and are interchangeable.)

*Figure 34: Figure 2.4 from Polchinski Vol. 1 [145] where he presents the 2d CFT contour deformation argument to derive the Lie algebra commutation relation from OPEs. The proof also works in the SDG context here!*

Deforming the contours in (266) in exactly the same way that they are in chapter 2 of Polchinksi Vol. 1 [145], copied in figure 34, we can read off that the commutator is defined by the $z_{12}\to 0$ residue

$$ [\delta_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{1}],n_{1}},\delta_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{2}],n_{2}}]\cdot\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n})=\oint\frac{dz}{2\pi i}\mathop{\mathrm{Res}}_{z_{2}\to z_{1}}\frac{1}{z^{n_{1}+1}}\frac{1}{z^{n_{2}+1}}\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n},\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{1}],z_{1}},\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{2}],z_{2}}). $$

The pole in $z_{12}$ can then be instantly read off from (255) and is

$$ \mathop{\mathrm{Res}}_{z_{2}\to z_{1}}\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n},\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{1}],z_{1}},\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{2}],z_{2}})=\frac{1}{z_{12}}\frac{\kappa}{2}\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{n}|\{\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{1}],z},\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{2}],z}\}) $$

but plugging the plane wave seed functions with the same $z$ into the $u$ , $w$ commutator,88 8 A helpful formula to check this equation is $p_{i}\cdot x=\omega_{i}(u+z_{i}{\bar{z}}_{i}{\bar{u}}-{\bar{z}}_{i}w-z_{i}{\bar{w}})$ .

$$ \{\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{1}],z},\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{2}],z}\}=-[12]\phi_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{1}]+|\tilde{\lambda}_{2}],z} $$

which follows from $p_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{1}],z}+p_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{2}],z}=p_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{1}]+|\tilde{\lambda}_{2}],z}$ , we see that they satisfy the $\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ Poisson bracket relation! Plugging the above formula into (267), we now have

$$ [\delta_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{1}],n_{1}},\delta_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{2}],n_{2}}]=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\delta_{|\tilde{\lambda}_{1}]+|\tilde{\lambda}_{2}],n_{1}+n_{2}+1} $$

which is now the loopified $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ (260) commutation relation, up to the coupling constant $\kappa/2$ . So we see that our action of adding positive-helicity gravitons into self-dual spacetimes, defined via (265), satisfies the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ commutation relation.

It may seem strange that a non-abelian Lie algebra can arise from our operation defined by adding positive-helicity gravitons into the spacetime, given that perturbiner expansions are permutation invariant among the seed functions. The reason that the order of operations matters is that the loop must get sequentially larger with each subsequent action of the Lie algebra.

We conclude this subsection by saying that there is another basis of generators one can use for the $\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ algebra. One can define the basis of polynomial functions

$$ \mathbf{T}^{p}_{m}\equiv\frac{1}{2}u^{p+m-1}w^{p-m-1},\hskip 28.45274pt\{\mathbf{T}^{p}_{m},\mathbf{T}^{q}_{n}\}=\left(m(q-1)-n(p-1)\right)\mathbf{T}^{p+q-2}_{m+n}, $$

and these are the more natural generators from a celestial perspective. They correspond directly to the Mellin-transformed soft modes [109]. Furthermore, the generators which correspond to positive-power monomials, i.e. $p+m-1\geq 0$ and $p-m-1\geq 0$ , are said to live in the wedge subalgebra $\mathfrakalt{w}_{\wedge}\subset\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ .

We also mention that the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ algebra is deformed in the presence of a cosmological constant [146, 147], and can also be studied on various other non-trivial backgrounds as well. See for instance [148, 149, 150, 151, 152, 153, 154].

### 14.2 SDYM and $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$

Let us see how the analogous story works in SDYM. The seed functions are now defined as

$$ \Phi_{i}\equiv\epsilon_{i}T^{a_{i}}e^{ip_{i}\cdot x} $$

where $T^{a}\in\mathfrak{g}$ are color generators. The SDYM perturbiner expansion

$$ \raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{n})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Phi_{i}+\ldots $$

is defined to solve the equation of motion

$$ \Box\,\Phi+i\sqrt{2}g[\partial_{u}\Phi,\partial_{w}\Phi]=0. $$

Let us separate out the terms in the perturbiner expansion which depend only on subsets of seed functions via

$$ \raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}\,(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{n})=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\}\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}\end{subarray}}\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(k)}(\Phi_{i_{1}},\ldots,\Phi_{i_{k}}). $$

Recycling the expression for the SDYM Berends-Giele current (125), we can instantly write down the formula

$$ \raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(k)}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{k})=(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{k-1}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{k}}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}\frac{1}{z_{\sigma(i)\sigma(i+1)}}\right)\Phi_{\sigma(1)}\Phi_{\sigma(2)}\ldots\Phi_{\sigma(k)}. $$

Here $S_{k}$ is the permutation group of $k$ elements and we sum over all possible color orderings.

This perturbiner expansion satisfies a version of the collinear-limits based recursive formula (147), namely

$$ \raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(n)}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{n})=-i\sqrt{2}g\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(n-1)}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\frac{1}{z_{in}}[\Phi_{i},\Phi_{n}],\ldots,\Phi_{n-1}). $$

This is an $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ Ward identity. Namely, if we define the following action $\delta^{a}_{|\tilde{\lambda}],n^{\prime}}$ of adding a positive-helicity gluon to the gauge field via

$$ \delta^{a}_{|\tilde{\lambda}],n^{\prime}}\cdot\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{n})\equiv\oint_{C}\frac{dz}{2\pi i}\frac{1}{z^{n^{\prime}+1}}\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{n}|\Phi^{a}_{|\tilde{\lambda}],z}) $$

then using the same logic as the last section, we can derive the commutation relation

$$ [\delta^{a}_{|1],n_{1}},\delta^{b}_{|2],n_{2}}]=\sqrt{2}gf^{abc}\,\delta^{c}_{|1]+|2],n_{1}+n_{2}+1}. $$

This is in fact nothing more than the commutation relation of the Lie algebra $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ , which is the loop algebra of a Lie algebra we’ll call $\mathfrak{s}$ . (Many works refer to $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ as “ $S$ ”, but we prefer this naming convention as it is parallel with $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ .) We will now define $\mathfrak{s}$ and $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ in turn.

Elements of $\mathfrak{s}$ are functions from $(u,w)$ to $\mathfrak{g}$ , where the commutator is the usual $\mathfrak{g}$ commutator. It can be spanned by a basis of plane wave generators

$$ \mathbf{T}^{a}_{|\tilde{\lambda}]}\equiv T^{a}e^{i(\tilde{\lambda}_{\dot{2}}u+\tilde{\lambda}_{\dot{1}}w)}\in\mathfrak{s}. $$

The $\mathfrak{s}$ commutation relation is then

$$ [\mathbf{T}^{a}_{|1]},\mathbf{T}^{b}_{|2]}]=if^{abc}\mathbf{T}^{c}_{|1]+|2]}. $$

To loopify the Lie algebra, we append an integer onto the generators

$$ \mathbf{T}^{a}_{|\tilde{\lambda}],n^{\prime}}\in\text{L}\mathfrak{s}\hskip 28.45274pt\text{for }n^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z} $$

and define the $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ commutation relation to be

$$ [\mathbf{T}^{a}_{|1],n_{1}},\mathbf{T}^{b}_{|2],n_{2}}]\equiv if^{abc}\mathbf{T}^{c}_{|1]+|2],n_{1}+n_{2}+1}. $$

This is exactly (279) up to a factor of the coupling $-i\sqrt{2}g$ .

### 14.3 $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ and $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ beyond tree-level-self-dual

The integrability of classical SDG and SDYM implies these theories have infinite dimensional $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ and $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ symmetries, but it also means that the tree-level amplitudes all vanish. So while there is a beautiful story for generating classical solutions using the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ / $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ algebras, the amplitudes associated with these solutions are zero! The sad fact is that the knife of integrability cuts both ways.

One could then ask, is there a way to see how these symmetries manifest beyond the self-dual sector? The answer, which originates from the celestial holography program, is yes. Simply put, the symmetry lives on in the holomorphic collinear limits of non-self-dual amplitudes.

*Figure 35: Holomorphic collinear limit outside of self-dual sector.*

Say, for instance, we have a tree-level amplitude containing two external massless gravitons with momenta

$$ p_{1}=|1\rangle[1|,\hskip 28.45274ptp_{2}=|2\rangle[2|. $$

Say $p_{1}$ is positive-helicity while $p_{2}$ could either have either helicity. If we take the holomorphic collinear limit

$$ |1\rangle\to|2\rangle $$

then the sum of momenta $P=p_{1}+p_{2}$ becomes

$$ P\to|2\rangle([1|+[2|). $$

We can see that the kinematic addition of the square brackets is exactly the same structure we saw in the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ commutation relation (260). In this limit the amplitude factorizes as

$$ \lim_{|1\rangle\to|2\rangle}\mathcal{M}^{\rm tree}(1^{+},2^{\pm},\ldots)=\text{Split}^{1^{+}2^{\pm}}_{{\rm G},P^{\mp}}\,\mathcal{M}^{\rm tree}(P^{\pm},\ldots). $$

In section 9.3 we computed the $+$ $+$ $-$ and $+$ $-$ $+$ gravitational splitting functions from the lightcone 3-pt vertex. (The $+$ $+$ $+$ splitting function is zero, and one can also compute that the $+$ $-$ $-$ splitting function vanishes when $\langle{12}\rangle\to 0$ .) They are

$$ \displaystyle\text{Split}^{1^{+}2^{+}}_{{\rm G},P^{-}} \displaystyle=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\frac{[12]}{\langle{12}\rangle}\frac{\langle{\alpha P}\rangle^{4}}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{2}}=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\frac{[12]}{z_{12}}\,, \displaystyle\text{Split}^{1^{+}2^{-}}_{{\rm G},P^{+}} \displaystyle=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\frac{[12]}{\langle{12}\rangle}\frac{\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{6}}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha P}\rangle^{2}}=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\frac{[12]}{z_{12}}\,. $$

For the second equalities we plugged in the spinor parameterizations (261).

Equation (287) is interesting because it is a statement which holds beyond the self-dual sector, as all the other particles in the amplitude need not be gravitons of a particular helicity. What’s more, they need not be gravitons at all. One is for instance allowed to couple Einstein gravity to any fields with minimal coupling [155] and the tree-level splitting function will remain uncorrected. (The analogous statement holds for gauge theory, where in this context minimal coupling means one simply promotes derivatives to covariant derivatives.) Therefore, equation (287) is exciting because it is quite general. See also [156] where the set of EFTs which preserve the Jacobi identity are explored, which put certain constraints on the couplings.

The relationship between (288) to the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ algebra is immediate. It clearly takes the form of a level-0 OPE of a 2d current with a $\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ color Lie-algebra, hence the putative 2d theory has an $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ symmetry. If we formally define the “operators” $G^{\pm}_{|i]}(z_{i})$ to signify inserting positive-helicity gravitons in an S-matrix, then we have the OPE

$$ \lim_{z_{12}\to 0}G^{+}_{|1]}(z_{1})G^{\pm}_{|2]}(z_{2})=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\frac{[12]}{z_{12}}G^{\pm}_{|1]+|2]}(z_{2}). $$

In terms of operator notation, it is as if $G^{+}$ is a 2d conserved current of $\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ symmetry and $G^{-}$ is a charged matter operator that transforms in the adjoint representation.

These equations also of course have gauge theory analogs. If we take the holomorphic collinear limit of two gluons

$$ \lim_{|1\rangle\to|2\rangle}\mathcal{A}^{\rm tree}(1^{a+},2^{b\pm},\ldots)=\text{Split}^{1^{a+}2^{b\pm}}_{{\rm YM},P^{c\mp}}\,\mathcal{A}^{\rm tree}(P^{c\pm},\ldots), $$

from (160) and (162) we have

$$ \displaystyle\text{Split}^{1^{a+}2^{b+}}_{{\rm YM},P^{c-}} \displaystyle=\sqrt{2}gf^{abc}\frac{1}{\langle{12}\rangle}\frac{\langle{\alpha P}\rangle^{2}}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle}=\sqrt{2}g\frac{f^{abc}}{z_{12}}, \displaystyle\text{Split}^{1^{a+}2^{b-}}_{{\rm YM},P^{c+}} \displaystyle=\sqrt{2}gf^{abc}\frac{1}{\langle{12}\rangle}\frac{\langle{\alpha P}\rangle^{2}}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle}=\sqrt{2}g\frac{f^{abc}}{z_{12}}. $$

If we define $O^{a\pm}_{|\tilde{\lambda}]}(z)$ to denote the operator which inserts a gluon into the S-matrix, then

$$ \lim_{z_{12}\to 0}O^{a+}_{|1]}(z_{1})O^{b\pm}_{|2]}(z_{2})=\sqrt{2}g\frac{f^{abc}}{z_{12}}O^{c\pm}_{|1]+|2]}(z_{2}) $$

which is the $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ equivalent of our gravitational $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ formula (289).

In this note, we have seen that the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ and $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ OPEs generate all-plus off-shell currents and classical solutions in the self-dual sector. The amplitudes corresponding to these objects are of course zero. But what about beyond the self-dual sector?

The first class of amplitudes outside of the self-dual sector are the tree-level MHV amplitudes. Let us now denote the full amplitude expressions, with the momentum conserving delta function, as $\mathcal{A}$ , while we denote a “stripped” amplitude, without the delta function, as $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ .

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{\rm tree}(1^{a_{1}-},2^{a_{2}-},3^{a_{3}+},\ldots,n^{a_{n}+}) \displaystyle=(2\pi)^{4}\delta^{(4)}(p_{1}+\ldots+p_{n})\overline{\mathcal{A}}^{\rm tree}(1^{a_{1}-},2^{a_{2}-},3^{a_{3}+},\ldots,n^{a_{n}+}) $$

(Note that we are utilizing the “barred = stripped amplitude” notation for this section alone. In the majority of this note we by default dropped the delta function $(2\pi)^{4}\delta(\ldots)$ from our amplitude expressions, as is often conventional, for brevity.)

The stripped amplitude is of course not a unique expression, as it is only defined up to the addition of terms that vanish on the support of momentum conservation. Nevertheless, there are often natural representatives one often uses, as in the case of MHV amplitudes.

Our choice of the stripped amplitude representative will of course be the famous Parke-Taylor formula, for which the color-ordered partial amplitude is

$$ \overline{A}^{\rm tree}(1^{+},\ldots i^{-}\ldots j^{-}\ldots n^{+})=i(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n-2}\frac{\langle{ij}\rangle^{4}}{\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n1}\rangle}. $$

Note that this formula has no multiparticle singularities like $\frac{1}{P^{2}}$ associated to internal propagators going on-shell. This is because one side of such a channel would always be either a tree-level-all-plus or one-minus amplitude, which vanishes.

This stripped amplitude then satisfies a recursive “ $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ Ward identity” which is

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\mathcal{A}}^{\rm tree}(1^{-a_{1}},2^{-a_{1}},\ldots,n^{+a_{n}}) \displaystyle=\sqrt{2}g\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{f^{a_{n}a_{i}c}}{\langle{ni}\rangle}\frac{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\overline{\mathcal{A}}^{\rm tree}(1^{-a_{1}},\ldots,i^{c},\ldots,(n\!-\!1)^{+a_{n-1}}). $$

Note that we sum over all particles $1$ through $n\!-\!1$ , including the two negative-helicity particles $1$ and $2$ . The equation (295) is not coming from a momentum-conserving BCFW shift, but rather is based on the meromorphicity of the Parke-Taylor formula.

This recursive formula is related to the soft theorem, as well as the WZW interpretation of the Parke-Taylor formula by Nair [157] and Witten’s twistor string [158]. See also [159, 160, 161, 162]. More recently, it appeared in the work of Costello and Paquette [28] to compute amplitudes from self-dual chiral algebras, which we will mention again later in section 15.3. In that work, the “stripping” of the delta function can be seen as an artifact of their procedure for computing amplitudes, where one first computes a form factor for an operator placed in the spacetime and then integrates over the position of the operator, giving the delta function at the end.

In a recent paper by Guevara, Himwich, and the author [38], an analogous recursive formula was found for gravitational MHV stripped amplitudes. Defining the stripped amplitude as

$$ \mathcal{M}^{\rm tree}(1^{-},2^{-},3^{+},\ldots,n^{+})=(2\pi)^{4}\delta^{(4)}(p_{1}+\ldots+p_{n})\overline{\mathcal{M}}^{\rm tree}(1^{-},2^{-},3^{+},\ldots,n^{+}) $$

we will take our representative for $\overline{\mathcal{M}}$ to be one due to Hodges [105]. Defining the $n\times n$ matrix $\Psi$ by

$$ \Psi_{ij}=\begin{cases}-\frac{[ij]}{\langle ij\rangle}\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2}&i\neq j\\
\sum^{k=n}_{k=1,k\neq i}\frac{[ik]}{\langle ik\rangle}\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2}&i=j\end{cases}, $$

it turns out the graviton MHV amplitude can be written as

$$ \overline{\mathcal{M}}^{\rm tree}(1^{-},2^{-},3^{+},\ldots,n^{+})=i(-\kappa/2)^{n-2}\frac{\langle{12}\rangle^{8}}{\langle{12}\rangle^{2}\langle{23}\rangle^{2}\langle{31}\rangle^{2}}\left(\prod_{a=4}^{n}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha a}\rangle^{4}}\right)|\Psi|^{123}_{123}, $$

where $|\Psi|^{123}_{123}$ denotes the determinant of the $(n-3)\times(n-3)$ minor of $\Psi$ with rows and columns $1,2,3$ removed. Using the matrix tree-theorem [95] this formula can also be expressed as a sum over “rooted forests,” where nodes $1$ , $2$ , and $3$ are the roots for three disconnected trees. An example is drawn in figure 36a.

*Figure 36: (a): A forest of three trees that contributes to Hodges’ MHV formula $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{n}^{\rm tree}$ for $n=18$ . (b): Another graviton MHV formula ${\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{n}^{\rm tree}}^{\prime}$ , here for $n=12$ , is a sum of $\xi,\chi$ -trees. The special $\xi$ and $\chi$ edges lie on the unique path which connects node 1 to node 2.*

Denoting a rooted forest in the set of all such rooted forests $F\in\mathcal{F}^{n}_{123}$ , we may write

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\mathcal{M}}^{\rm tree}_{n} \displaystyle=i(-\kappa/2)^{n-2}\frac{\langle{12}\rangle^{8}}{\langle{12}\rangle^{2}\langle{23}\rangle^{2}\langle{31}\rangle^{2}}\left(\prod_{a=4}^{n}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha a}\rangle^{4}}\right)\sum_{F\in\mathcal{F}_{123}^{n}}\left(\prod_{\text{edges }(ij)}\frac{[ij]}{\langle ij\rangle}\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2}\right). $$

In [38], it was shown that this formula satisfies the recursive $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ Ward identity, which in the conventions of this note reads

$$ \overline{\mathcal{M}}^{\rm tree}_{n}=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{[ni]}{\langle ni\rangle}\frac{\langle\alpha i\rangle^{2}}{\langle\alpha n\rangle^{2}}\overline{\mathcal{M}}^{\rm tree}(\,\ket{1},|1],\,\cdots,|i\rangle,|i]{+}\frac{\langle\alpha n\rangle}{\langle\alpha i\rangle}|n],\,\cdots,\ket{n{-}1},|n{-}1]\,) $$

for $n>3$ . Once again, we sum over all particles $1$ through $n\!-\!1$ , including the two negative-helicity particles. Note that this recursive formula the same type of formula that generates the self-dual Berends-Giele currents/classical solutions, which is how it was found. It is superficially similar to, although not equal to, BCFW “inverse-soft” recursion formula [105, 106, 107, 108, 98, 94]. They differ because the BCFW formula uses the NSVW form of the amplitude where only the positive-helicity gravitons have associated nodes, and the negative helicity graviton spinors $|1\rangle$ and $|2\rangle$ define the rules of the edges. As a result only the positive gravitons are summed over in that formula, but not the two negative gravitons.

There is also however another representative for the stripped MHV amplitudes that also satisfies the exact same recursive formula. Let us denote it ${\overline{\mathcal{M}}^{\rm tree}_{n}}^{\prime}$ , which is unequal to $\overline{\mathcal{M}}^{\rm tree}_{n}$ off the support of momentum conservation, but equal to it on the support of momentum conservation. The formula, which originates from [61], is

$$ {\overline{\mathcal{M}}^{\rm tree}_{n}}^{\prime}=-i(-\kappa/2)^{n-2}\frac{\langle{12}\rangle^{4}\langle{1\alpha}\rangle^{2}\langle{2\alpha}\rangle^{2}}{[\xi 1][\chi 2]}\left(\prod_{a=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha a}\rangle^{4}}\right)\sum_{\xi,\chi\text{-trees}}\prod_{\text{edges }(ij)}\frac{[ij]^{\prime}}{\langle{ij}\rangle}\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2}. $$

Here, we do not sum over rooted forests but rather a different kind of tree we’ll call a $\xi,\chi$ -tree. We’ve drawn one such tree in figure 36b.

If $1$ and $2$ are the two negative-helicity particles, then a $\xi,\chi$ tree is a tree with $n$ nodes for which the nodes $1$ and $2$ obey a special rule. Node 1 and node 2 each have one special edge we’ll call the $\xi$ edge and $\chi$ edge, respectively. The $\xi$ edge is the unique edge connected to 1 that lies on the unique path from 1 to 2. Likewise, the $\chi$ edge lies on the path from 2 to 1.

Here, $|\xi]$ and $|\chi]$ are arbitrary anti-holomorphic reference spinors. The notation $[ij]^{\prime}$ in (301) means the following: if neither $i$ nor $j$ is 1 or 2, then $[ij]^{\prime}=[ij]$ . Otherwise, if $i$ is $1$ (or $2$ ), then one is to replace $|1]\to|\xi]$ (or $|2]\to|\chi]$ ) if $j$ lies on the path to 2 (or 1). In other words,

$$ \displaystyle{}^{\prime} \displaystyle=\begin{cases}[\xi j]&\text{ if }j\text{ is on path from $1$ to $2$}\\
[1j]&\text{ otherwise}\end{cases} \displaystyle[2j]^{\prime} \displaystyle=\begin{cases}[\chi j]&\text{ if }i\text{ is on path from $1$ to $2$}\\
[2j]&\text{ otherwise}\end{cases}. $$

In the extra-special case that nodes 1 and 2 are neighbors, one would have $[12]^{\prime}=[\xi\chi]$ , although we mention that the sum over all such $\xi,\chi$ -trees where 1 and 2 are neighbors is actually zero on the support of momentum conservation due to a matrix identity.

In any case, ${\overline{\mathcal{M}}^{\rm tree}_{n}}^{\prime}$ also satisfies the recursive $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ Ward identity (300) that Hodges formula ${\overline{\mathcal{M}}^{\rm tree}_{n}}$ does, again only for $n>3$ .99 9 Strangely, if we try to use the recursion to go from $n=2$ to $n=3$ , we run into a problem. The only $n=2$ diagram has nodes 1 and 2 as neighbors, which has the $[\xi\chi]$ edge. Under the recursive Ward identity, this base case will only generate all the diagrams where 1 and 2 remain next to each other, but as mentioned in the text these diagrams sum to zero. So we generate only exactly the wrong diagrams. It seems as though this formula could also have some chiral algebra interpretation, given that it was computed in the perturbiner framework in [61] by computing the expectation value of the operator $\Sigma^{AB}\wedge\Gamma^{AC}\wedge\Gamma^{B}_{\;\;C}$ in the spacetime. The reference spinors $|\xi]$ and $|\chi]$ are used to set a gauge to write down the spin connection $\Gamma_{AB}$ . The full amplitude can then be generated from the Ward identity given the 3-pt seed $\frac{\langle{12}\rangle^{4}}{[\xi 1][\chi 2]}\frac{[\xi 3]}{\langle{13}\rangle}\frac{[3\chi]}{\langle{32}\rangle}$ . (This seed actually generates all trees where $1$ and $2$ are not neighbors, but as we said the trees where they are neighbors sum to zero anyway.)

One natural question is, can these algebras be used to compute amplitudes beyond the MHV sector? In a certain sense this has already been done, once again by Costello/Paquette [28]. By computing the position integrals of the expectation value of the appropriate number of operators $\tr(B^2)$ , which deform SDYM to YM, one can use the $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ OPEs of the self-dual sector to compute any tree-level amplitude in pure YM theory if one can do the integrals. While this isn’t exactly the set up one would call “holography,” it is certainly closely related.

In any case, in this particular note we have seen that “ $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ / $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ Ward Identities” generate all the self-dual classical solutions/Berends-Giele currents, as well as tree-level stripped MHV amplitudes in both gauge theory and gravity. A natural question we should ask is, could a similar statement be true for the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes?

On the face of it, this seems quite plausible. These amplitudes are rational, and their only singularities are the holomorphic collinear ones. Furthermore, the splitting functions of these amplitudes are not loop corrected, as we showed in section 9.3, so they remain the “pure” $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}/\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ OPEs we see at tree-level. These properties are quite tantalizing. Could we describe quantum self-dual gravity as the dual to some 2-dimensional boundary theory with an exact $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ symmetry?

The most basic question one could ask is, can one-loop-all-plus stripped amplitudes in gauge theory or gravity be “generated” by an $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ / $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ Ward Identity? It’s possible, but difficult to know for sure. This would require one to identify a “good” stripped amplitude representative which will satisfy the recursive formula, and there’s no guarantee that such a representative exists. For those who are wondering, the BDPR formula (229) for the gravity one-loop-all-plus amplitudes does not satisfy the recursive Ward-identity formula. This is because it only satisfies the correct splitting relation (164) on the support of momentum conservation, through the use of the identity (241), and therefore we can’t treat the particle variable $|n\rangle$ as an unconstrained variable on $\mathbb{C}P^{1}$ and invoke the residue theorem. It could be the case that some other formula would have nicer properties. (Likewise, the canonical formula for the one-loop-all-plus gauge theory amplitudes (208) also requires the use of momentum conservation to see that it has the correct holomorphic collinear limits. Maybe there is some other formula which does not need momentum conservation for this, although at this time we do not know.) This should be contrasted with, say, the Parke-Taylor formula which manifestly has all the correct holomorphic collinear limits without the use of momentum conservation. Hodges’ formula is a bit of a special case, because it has all the correct holomorphic collinear limits without the use of momentum conservation except between the three particles 1,2,3, i.e., for the limits $\langle{12}\rangle\to 0$ , $\langle{23}\rangle\to 0$ , or $\langle{13}\rangle\to 0$ . This is enough, however, for the recursive formula (300) to hold for $n>3$ .

Even if there doesn’t exist a nice “Ward identity” for the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes, however, there could still be other ways that $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ OPE’s could uniquely fix these amplitudes. An interesting idea in this direction comes from the study of celestial KZ-type null state conditions, which could potentially constrain the MHV and one-loop-all-plus amplitudes uniquely [163, 164, 165].

## 15 On the “anomaly interpretation” of one-loop-all-plus amplitudes

In 1995, it was suggested by Bardeen that the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes in SDYM were somehow an “anomaly” to the symmetries of classical integrability [166]. There have been a number of works which attempted to realize this idea explicitly in different ways, some of which we’ve collected in this section.

### 15.1 CSW/MHV rules

One idea in a work from Brandhuber, Spence, and Travaglini [127] is based on the CSW/MHV rules [167, 168] for computing YM amplitudes. While it is known that these rules for Yang-Mills theory fail to produce the rational terms in loop amplitudes, and hence cannot compute the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes, these authors showed that if one performs a certain holomorphic change of variables of the lightcone MHV Lagrangian [169], the action will pick up a Jacobian that allows one to compute the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes. It does not appear that this scheme possesses a computational advantage over standard Feynman diagrammatrics. In a later work with Zoubos [122], they also showed the amplitudes are captured by adding a certain bubble counterterm to the MHV Lagrangian. In fact this bubble counterterm alone computes the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes, which was apparently first observed by Bern at 4-pts [124]. This relies on the planarity of SDYM amplitudes in particular. The idea was revisited by Chattopadhyay and Krasnov in [170, 126] where a new all-multiplicity expression for the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes was conjectured based on it. A satisfactory understanding of how MHV rules can be used to compute general loop amplitudes remains a topic of interest. See for instance [171, 172].

A twistor space investigation of similar ideas was conducted by Boels [173]. In particular, in equation (4.17) of his paper, a generating function for the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes, apparently due to Mason, is motivated and written down without proof. See also [159]. This generating function was revisited more recently by Bogna and Mason in [174] where it was substantiated further. See for instance equation (6.4) in that paper. It seems likely that this generating function should be derivable from first principles as a Bardeen-esque anomaly term in twistor space. Section 6 of [174] contains an interesting discussion of possible approaches one might take. It would also be interesting to concoct a similar generating function for gravity, although this would be much more difficult given that there is not, as of yet, a known MHV formalism for gravity to act as a guide.

### 15.2 U(1) electric-magnetic

Another anomaly interpretation for the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes is due to Doran, Monteiro, and Wikeley [175]. These authors show that the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes can be thought of as arising from a chiral anomaly of a $U(1)$ -electric-magnetic symmetry, similar to that of the 2d Schwinger model. They also argue the amplitudes are related to the trace anomaly which explains their conformal properties. In an earlier paper by Monteiro, Stark-Muchão, and Wikeley [128] the amplitudes were also related to an infinite tower of non-local classically conserved currents. These currents were used to guide the computation of the non-local “quantum corrected” action where off-shell integrated one-loop-all-plus $n$ -gons define the quantum-corrected tree-level vertices. Interestingly, in SDYM the even parity terms of the amplitude turned out to be more easily described by such vertices.

### 15.3 The Celestial Chiral Algebra program

Perhaps the work which has most directly realized Bardeen’s suggestion is due to Costello [27], who showed that the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes are anomalies which prevent the theory of pure SDYM from being being lifted from 4-dimensional spacetime to 6-dimensional twistor space at the quantum level. Let us elaborate on this. It is well known that classical SDYM can be lifted to twistor space by a Penrose-Ward transform. The original 4d theory and the lifted 6d theory are equivalent to each other, but the ability to lift to twistor space makes manifest many properties of SDYM, including its classical integrability. Now quantum SDYM, defined on spacetime $\mathbb{R}^{4}$ , is of course invariant under the usual gauge transformations in four dimensions. However, if we attempt to lift the quantum theory from $\mathbb{R}^{4}$ to twistor space $\mathbb{R}^{4}\times\mathbb{C}P^{1}$ in the same way that we did for the classical theory, the six-dimensional gauge transformations on twistor space are anomalous. The source of this anomaly turns out to be the gluon one-loop-all-plus box amplitude.

However, if special matter content is added to the theory, this anomaly can be cancelled and integrability can be restored. One possible type of matter which could be added is an axion with a fourth-order kinetic term and an explicit overall factor of $\hbar$ in the action. This cancels the one-loop gauge theory anomaly with a tree-level internal axion exchange diagram. The introduction of this axion also renders the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes zero for all $n$ , not just $n=4$ . So if one computes the internal-axion-tree contribution to the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes, and negates it, one computes the pure SDYM one-loop-all-plus amplitudes. This was done by Costello and Paquette in [28]. The way they did this was by introducing the Celestial Chiral Algebra. If one places an operator in the self-dual theory to compute a form factor, one can then integrate over the position of the form factor in $\mathbb{R}^{4}$ to compute amplitudes which can live in the non-self-dual theory. The form factors can be computed very easily, by simply “doing” the OPEs recursively in the sense of what we’ve called Ward identities, which have only holomorphic collinear singularities simply because the anomaly free theory is tautologically holomorphic. It turns out, for instance, that the correct operator to integrate over to compute the internal axion contribution to the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes is $(\Box\rho)^{2}$ , where $\rho$ is the axion field. If one wanted to compute, say, pure tree-level YM amplitudes, one would instead insert powers of $\tr(B^2)$ which deform SDYM to full YM. To compute pure YM tree-level MHV amplitudes, one inserts one instance of $\tr(B^2)$ . Every additional negative helicity gluon then requires an extra insertion of another $\tr(B^2)$ . At loop-level of course internal axion exchange will affect the amplitudes. To be completely clear, the amplitudes being computed all belong to the 4-dimensional theory, and the CCA is being used as a tool for computing 4d amplitudes. The general program of computing form-factor integrands for various theories using 2d chiral algebras has become a rich area study over the last few years. See for instance [176, 177, 178, 179, 180]. As a bit of extra background, the operator placed in the spacetime defines a $\mathbb{C}P^{1}$ defect above it in twistor space, and the particles, which are lines in twistor space, puncture this $\mathbb{C}P^{1}$ at isolated points which can also be thought of as points on the celestial sphere. The duality between the physics on the defect and the bulk physics is then said to be given by Koszul duality.

For gravity, it was shown that quantum SDG is similarly anomalous when lifted to twistor space, and that the anomaly can also be cancelled by a fourth-order axion [120, 181].

The axion with the fourth-order kinetic term is however somewhat undesirable due to its unphysical nature. One can also cancel the anomaly with more realistic fermionic matter in particular representations. For instance, if the gauge group is $SU(N_{c})$ , then the fermions can be taken to be 8 Dirac fermions transforming under the fundamental representation and one Dirac fermion transforming under the antisymmetric tensor representation of the fundamental representation. For $SU(3)$ this is equivalent to having 9 Dirac fermions in the fundamental representation. Fascinatingly, in these QCD theories one can compute all- $n$ two-loop-all-plus amplitudes using this 2d chiral algebra which are extremely difficult to compute using standard Feynman diagrammatics and loop integration [37]. Because these are specially chosen theories, these particular two-loop amplitudes turn out to be rational. This is not the case for real world two-loop-all-plus QCD amplitudes. In the work [182] by Dixon and Morales, the two-loop computation was explicitly done with Feynman diagrams for $n=4$ and shown to match the CCA result exactly in a favorable regularization scheme. We also note that in another paper [183], they showed that the CCA explains certain color identities involving gluons and photons in one-loop-all-plus/one-minus amplitudes. See also [184]. One can also cancel the anomaly by using a supersymmetric theory [185, 177].

We note here that the $\text{L}\mathfrak{s}$ algebra itself is only the leading $\mathcal{O}(\hbar^{0})$ term in the full chiral algebra. It will also recieve loop corrections, which deform the chiral algebra to a “quantum group.” There will for instance also be a double-pole which comes from the triangle diagram, as we discussed in section 9.3, and other terms as well. Nonetheless, the full OPE does remain associative on general grounds, and the associativity allows one to compute higher order terms in the OPE from the leading terms [121]. In supersymmetric gauge theory the all-orders OPE was computed in [185].

Note that the quantum-corrected double-pole, which is naturally described by the CCA, is quite difficult to deal with in BCFW loop amplitude computations. If one wants to use the BCFW method to compute loop amplitudes [114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119] one must know how to exactly account for the extra pole (and any other coincident lower-order-pole terms) using extra information in order to enact the usual contour deformation arguments. In the CCA however, they are handled quite naturally and beautifully.

## 16 More literature

Here we review a bit more literature surrounding SDYM and SDG. This is in no way exhaustive. We have in particular ignored the entire existence of twistor theory [186] twistor strings [158, 187, 101, 188, 189] ambitwistor strings [190, 191, 192, 193] nonlinear twistor sigma models [99, 194, 100] and higher spin theories [195, 196, 197].

### 16.1 Old-school MHV calculation and self-duality

In this section we discuss the original historical connection of SDYM to the Parke-Taylor formula [91] for MHV tree-level amplitudes, due to Selivanov and Rosly [198, 199, 200].

The connection uses the notion of “perturbiners.” A perturbiner is a classical solution in which one begins with a sum of free plane waves, each multiplied by its own tiny infinitesimal parameter, and then recursively solves for the rest of the solution by repeatedly plugging it back into the equations of motion and solving for higher order terms in the infinitesimal parameters.

There are two different ways that perturbiners can be used to compute amplitudes. In the first way, one realizes that classical perturbiner solutions are exactly the same as off-shell Berends-Giele currents where the momentum of the off-shell leg is swapped for a spacetime position by a Fourier transform. We review this connection in appendix H. See also the recent review [201]. In the second way, one takes the full perturbiner expansion and plugs it into the action, which calculates the amplitude at tree-level. This idea has been revisited in more modern treatments in for instance [202, 203]. A more terse review is provided in section 4 of [61].

The Selivanov and Rosly calculation uses the second scheme to compute the MHV amplitudes, where one plugs the perturbiner solution into the action and evaluates it on-shell. The amplitude is equal to the “maximum” term that contains each infinitesimal parameter, belonging to each of the original particle plane waves, exactly once. For MHV amplitudes this can be done efficiently using the following “trick”. The Yang-Mills action is essentially $\tr(F \wedge\star F)$ . One can add any multiple of a topological term $\tr(F \wedge F)$ to the action without affecting the scattering amplitudes. If one defines $F^{\pm}=F\pm i\star F$ , this means that the Yang-Mills action can be argued to be equivalent to $\tr(F^- \wedge\star F^-)$ . A self-dual solution, with only positive-helicity gluons satisfies $F^{-}=0$ .
