$$ \displaystyle(*) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\ell^{2}}\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1,n}|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle-\sum_{1\leq k<b\leq n}\frac{(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1})b|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}} \displaystyle+\sum_{1\leq k<b\leq n}\frac{((\ell+p_{1,k}+b)^{2}{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}-(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}})\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k})k|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}} \displaystyle+\sum_{1\leq k<b\leq n}\frac{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k})b|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}} \displaystyle+\sum_{k=1}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}n-1}}p_{k+1,n}^{2}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k})k|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}} $$

Next we replace in $(\ell+p_{1,k}+b)^{2}-(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}=2b\cdot(\ell+p_{1,k})$ for the third term. Then, we perform the sums over $b$ in the second, third, and fourth term. We get

$$ \displaystyle(*) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\ell^{2}}\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1,n}|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle-\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}1\leq k<n}}\frac{(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1}){\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\mathbf{p_{k+1,n}}}|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}} \displaystyle+\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}1\leq k<n}}\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}2p_{k+1,n}\cdot(\ell+p_{1,k})}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k})k|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}} \displaystyle+\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}1\leq k<n}}\frac{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k}){\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p_{k+1,n}}|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}} \displaystyle+\sum_{1\leq k<n}p_{k+1,n}^{2}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k})k|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}}. $$

$$ \displaystyle(*) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\ell^{2}}\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1,n}|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle-\sum_{1\leq k<n}\frac{(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1}){\color[rgb]{0,0,1}p_{k,n}}|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}} \displaystyle+\sum_{1\leq k<n}\frac{2p_{k+1,n}\cdot(\ell+p_{1,k})\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k})k|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}} \displaystyle+\sum_{1\leq k<n}\frac{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k})p_{k+1,n}|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}} \displaystyle+\sum_{1\leq k<n}p_{k+1,n}^{2}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k})k|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}} \displaystyle+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\sum_{1\leq k<n}\frac{(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1})k|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}}}. $$

Now it’s time for some simplifications. $$ \displaystyle(*) \displaystyle=\cancel{\frac{1}{\ell^{2}}\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1,n}|\alpha}\rangle} \displaystyle\underbrace{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}+\sum_{1\leq k<n}\left(-\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1})p_{k,n}|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}}+\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k})p_{k+1,n}|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}}\right)}}_{\cancel{-\frac{\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1,n}|\alpha}\rangle}{\ell^{2}}}+\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,n-1})n|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,n-1})^{2}}} \displaystyle+(\ell+p_{1,n})^{2}\sum_{1\leq k<n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1})k|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}} $$

$$ \displaystyle(*)=\frac{(\ell+p_{1,n})^{2}}{(\ell+p_{1,n})^{2}}\times\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,n-1})n|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,n-1})^{2}}+(\ell+p_{1,n})^{2}\sum_{1\leq k<n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1})k|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}} $$

and this completes the proof.

### F.2 $4-2\epsilon$ -dimensional current

In this section we compute the $4-2\epsilon$ dimensional SDYM double-off-shell current $J_{\rm YM}(L;N)$ (188). This current is defined in by going up “one step” in the recursion relation for the double-off-shell current and replacing all the 4-dimensional propagators with the $4-2\epsilon$ -dimensional ones. We write

$$ J_{\rm YM}(L\,;\,N)\equiv\frac{i\sqrt{2}g}{(L+p_{N})^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=0\\
A=\{1,\ldots,j\}\\
B=\{j+1,\ldots,n\}\end{subarray}}^{n-1}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{A})p_{B}|\alpha}\rangle J_{\rm YM}(\ell\,;\,A)\Big\rvert_{\ell\,\mapsto L}J_{\rm YM}(B). $$

Note that the substitution $\ell\mapsto L$ does not affect the numerators of $J_{\rm YM}(\ell;A)$ , only the propagators in the denominator via the relation $(L+p)^{2}=(\ell+p)^{2}-\mu^{2}$ . Our goal then is to separate out all the extra terms generated by the identity

$$ \frac{(\ell+p)^{2}}{(L+p)^{2}}=1+\frac{\mu^{2}}{(L+p)^{2}}. $$

Anticipating this moment, we have conveniently isolated the only steps in the previous subsection where such a division occurs. The first place occurs at equation (447). The second place occurs at the end, after our penultimate equation (449), when we are to divide by $(L+p_{N})^{2}$ which cancels out an overall factor of $(\ell+p_{N})^{2}$ . Note also that we, in the final step of our proof in the last section, also multiplied a term by a factor of $1=\frac{(\ell+p_{1,n})^{2}}{(\ell+p_{1,n})^{2}}$ , which we must now replace with $1=\frac{(L+p_{1,n})^{2}}{(L+p_{1,n})^{2}}$ .

Let us bring all these terms together. We port the terms over from (449) in blue and write the additional terms generated by the cancellations of (447) in purple. The result is

$$ \displaystyle J_{\rm YM}(L\;;N) \displaystyle=\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}(-i)}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n-1,n}\rangle\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\Bigg( \displaystyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\displaystyle\frac{1}{(L+p_{1,n})^{2}}\times\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,n-1})n|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{1,n-1})^{2}}+\frac{(\ell+p_{1,n})^{2}}{(L+p_{1,n})^{2}}\sum_{1\leq k<n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1})k|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(L+p_{1,k})^{2}}} \displaystyle\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}{\displaystyle+\frac{\mu^{2}}{(L+p_{1,n})^{2}}\sum_{1\leq k<n}\left(-\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1})p_{k,n}|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(L+p_{1,k})^{2}}+\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k})p_{k+1,n}|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(L+p_{1,k})^{2}}\right)}\Bigg). $$

Using the elementary simplification

$$ \displaystyle\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1})k|\alpha}\rangle-\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1})p_{k,n}|\alpha}\rangle+\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k})p_{k+1,n}|\alpha}\rangle=-\langle{\alpha|p_{k,n}k|\alpha}\rangle $$

the expression is equal to

$$ \displaystyle J_{\rm YM}(L\;;N) \displaystyle=\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}(-i)}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n-1,n}\rangle\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\Bigg(\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1})k|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(L+p_{1,k})^{2}} \displaystyle-\frac{\mu^{2}}{(L+p_{1,n})^{2}}\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|p_{k,n}k|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(L+p_{1,k})^{2}}\Bigg) $$

which is what we wanted to show.

### F.3 A useful Clifford algebra identity

In this appendix we are going to prove a very useful identity. First, it will be useful for us to define a certain spinor object constructed out of four momenta. The object is defined as

$$ \langle{\alpha|p_{1}p_{2}p_{3}p_{4}|\alpha}\rangle\equiv-\,\alpha_{A}\,(p_{1}^{\mu}\,\sigma_{\mu}^{A\dot{A}})(p_{2,\nu}\,\sigma^{\nu}_{B\dot{A}})(p_{3}^{\rho}\,\sigma_{\rho}^{B\dot{B}})(p_{4,\gamma}\,\sigma^{\gamma}_{C\dot{B}})\,\alpha^{C}. $$

Note the minus sign out front. Recalling that $\langle{ij}\rangle=\lambda_{i}^{A}\lambda_{jA}$ , $[ij]=\tilde{\lambda}_{i}^{\dot{A}}\tilde{\lambda}_{j,\dot{A}}$ , the minus sign is there so that, if all the momenta are on-shell, we get the natural equation

$$ \displaystyle\langle{\alpha|p_{1}p_{2}p_{3}p_{4}|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle\equiv-\alpha_{A}\,(p_{1}^{\mu}\,\sigma_{\mu}^{A\dot{A}})(p_{2,\nu}\,\sigma^{\nu}_{B\dot{A}})(p_{3}^{\rho}\,\sigma_{\rho}^{B\dot{B}})(p_{4,\gamma}\,\sigma^{\gamma}_{C\dot{B}})\,\alpha^{C} \displaystyle=-\underbrace{(\alpha_{A}\lambda_{1}^{A})}_{-1}(\tilde{\lambda}_{1}^{\dot{A}}\tilde{\lambda}_{2\dot{A}})\underbrace{(\lambda_{2B}\lambda_{3}^{B})}_{-1}(\tilde{\lambda}_{3}^{\dot{B}}\tilde{\lambda}_{4\dot{B}})\underbrace{(\lambda_{4C}\alpha^{C})}_{-1} \displaystyle=\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle[12]\langle{23}\rangle[34]\langle{4\alpha}\rangle. $$

This sign is not present in the two-momentum object because

$$ \displaystyle\langle{\alpha|p_{1}p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle=\alpha_{A}\,(p_{1}^{\mu}\,\sigma_{\mu}^{A\dot{A}})(p_{2,\nu}\,\sigma^{\nu}_{B\dot{A}})\,\alpha^{B} \displaystyle=\underbrace{(\alpha_{A}\lambda_{1}^{A})}_{-1}(\tilde{\lambda}_{1}^{\dot{A}}\tilde{\lambda}_{2\dot{A}})\underbrace{(\lambda_{2B}\alpha^{B})}_{-1} \displaystyle=\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle[12]\langle{2\alpha}\rangle. $$

Using the Clifford algebra relation $\{\sigma^{\mu},\sigma^{\nu}\}=2\eta^{\mu\nu}$ , and accounting for the relative sign in between the four-momentum and two-momentum object, for any momenta $P_{1}$ , $P_{2}$ , $P_{3}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\langle{\alpha|P_{3}P_{1}P_{2}P_{3}|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle=-P_{3}^{2}\langle{\alpha|P_{1}P_{2}|\alpha}\rangle+(2P_{3}\cdot P_{2})\langle{\alpha|P_{1}P_{3}|\alpha}\rangle-(2P_{3}\cdot P_{1})\langle{\alpha|P_{2}P_{3}|\alpha}\rangle. $$

Now say $p_{1}^{2}=p_{2}^{2}=0$ and $\ell^{2}\neq 0$ . We are interested in expanding the quantity $\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1}|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1})p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle$ , which is a product of two-momentum objects, as a sum of such objects. We first massage the expression as

$$ \displaystyle\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1}|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1})p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle=\frac{\langle{1\alpha}\rangle\langle{2\alpha}\rangle}{\langle{12}\rangle}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1})p_{1}p_{2}(\ell+p_{1})|\alpha}\rangle $$

Now we plug in to (459) to get the following equation.

$$ \displaystyle=\frac{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle}{\langle{12}\rangle}\left(-(\ell+p_{1})^{2}\langle{\alpha|p_{1}p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle-2(\ell+p_{1})\cdot p_{2}\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1}|\alpha}\rangle+2\ell\cdot p_{1}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1})p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle\right) \displaystyle=\frac{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle}{\langle{12}\rangle}\left(-(\ell\!+\!p_{1})^{2}\langle{\alpha|p_{1}p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle-((\ell\!+\!p_{1}\!+\!p_{2})^{2}-(\ell\!+\!p_{1})^{2})\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1}|\alpha}\rangle+((\ell\!+\!p_{1})^{2}-\ell^{2})\langle{\alpha|(\ell\!+\!p_{1})p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle\right) \displaystyle=\frac{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle}{\langle{12}\rangle}\big(\!\!-\!(\ell\!+\!p_{1})^{2}\big(\langle{\alpha|p_{1}p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle\!-\!\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1}|\alpha}\rangle\!-\!\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1})p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle\big)\!-\!(\ell\!+\!p_{1}\!+\!p_{2})^{2}\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1}|\alpha}\rangle\!-\!\ell^{2}\langle{\alpha|(\ell\!+\!p_{1})p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle\big) $$

After one last simplification, we have now derived the very handy identity

$$ \displaystyle\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1}|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1})p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle=\frac{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle}{\langle{12}\rangle}\Big((\ell+p_{1})^{2}\langle{\alpha|\ell(p_{1}+p_{2})|\alpha}\rangle-(\ell+p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1}|\alpha}\rangle-\ell^{2}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1})p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle\Big).\;\;\;\vphantom{\Bigg\rvert} $$

## Appendix G More properties of the SDYM one-loop-all-plus formula

In this appendix we review some basic properties of the SDYM one-loop-all-plus single-trace partial amplitude formula

$$ A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;1}=-\frac{i}{3}\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}}{(4\pi)^{2}}\frac{1}{\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n1}\rangle}\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<i_{3}<i_{4}\leq n}\langle{i_{1}i_{2}}\rangle[i_{2}i_{3}]\langle{i_{3}i_{4}}\rangle[i_{4}i_{1}]. $$

### G.1 Cyclic invariance

The numerator of (463) does not display manifest cyclic invariance amongst the particles due to the sum of the form $1\leq\ldots\leq n$ , so in this subsection we show that cyclic invariance

$$ A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;1}(1^{+},2^{+},\ldots,(n-1)^{+},n^{+})=A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;1}(n^{+},1^{+},2^{+}\ldots,(n-1)^{+}) $$

does hold on the support of momentum conservation. This elaborates on the discussion in [130].

First we decompose

$$ \sum_{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<i_{3}<i_{4}\leq n}\langle{i_{1}i_{2}}\rangle[i_{2}i_{3}]\langle{i_{3}i_{4}}\rangle[i_{4}i_{1}]=\frac{1}{2}(E_{n}+O_{n}) $$

into the parity even and odd pieces

$$ \displaystyle E_{n} \displaystyle=\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<i_{3}<i_{4}\leq n}\tr(\slashed{p_{i_1}} \slashed{p_{i_2}} \slashed{p_{i_3}} \slashed{p_{i_4}} ), \displaystyle O_{n} \displaystyle=\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<i_{3}<i_{4}\leq n}\tr(\slashed{p_{i_1}} \slashed{p_{i_2}} \slashed{p_{i_3}} \slashed{p_{i_4}} \gamma^5 ). $$

Here we use

$$ \displaystyle\tr(\slashed{p_{1}} \slashed{p_{2}} \slashed{p_{3}} \slashed{p_{4}} ) \displaystyle=\langle{12}\rangle[23]\langle{34}\rangle[41]+[12]\langle{23}\rangle[34]\langle{41}\rangle, \displaystyle\tr(\slashed{p_{1}} \slashed{p_{2}} \slashed{p_{3}} \slashed{p_{4}} \gamma^5 ) \displaystyle=\langle{12}\rangle[23]\langle{34}\rangle[41]-[12]\langle{23}\rangle[34]\langle{41}\rangle. $$

Note also the relations

$$ \displaystyle\tr(\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma) \displaystyle=4(\eta^{\mu\nu}\eta^{\rho\sigma}-\eta^{\mu\rho}\eta^{\nu\sigma}+\eta^{\mu\sigma}\eta^{\nu\rho}), \displaystyle\tr(\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma\gamma^5) \displaystyle=-4i\varepsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}, $$

which can be shown to be equivalent to the previous identities using Schouten and (312).

It is easy to see that $E_{n}$ is cyclically symmetric using the cyclicity of the trace. Therefore we only need to focus on $O_{n}$ . Only the terms where $i_{4}=n$ will not obviously be equal in (464). So we need to show

$$ \sum_{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<i_{3}\leq n-1}\tr( \slashed{p_{i_1}} \slashed{p_{i_2}} \slashed{p_{i_3}} \slashed{p_n}\gamma^5)\overset{?}{=}\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<i_{3}\leq n-1}\tr( \slashed{p_n} \slashed{p_{i_1}} \slashed{p_{i_2}} \slashed{p_{i_3}} \gamma^5) $$

which using $\not{p_{n}}\gamma^{5}=-\gamma^{5}\not{p_{n}}$ becomes

$$ \sum_{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<i_{3}\leq n-1}\tr( \slashed{p_{i_1}} \slashed{p_{i_2}} \slashed{p_{i_3}} \slashed{p_n}\gamma^5)\overset{?}{=}0. $$

Using momentum conservation, we can replace $p_{n}$ with a (negative) sum of all the other momenta. Then using the antisymmetry of the epsilon pseudotensor, we can remove all the momenta which coincide with one of $i_{1}$ , $i_{2}$ , $i_{3}$ . The result is

$$ \sum_{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<i_{3}\leq n-1}\sum_{i_{4}\neq i_{1},i_{2},i_{3},n}\varepsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}p_{i_{1}}^{\mu}p_{i_{2}}^{\nu}p_{i_{3}}^{\rho}p_{i_{4}}^{\sigma}\overset{?}{=}0. $$

However, this sum is zero as we’ll now explain. Imagine you pick some distinct $i_{1}$ , $i_{2}$ , $i_{3}$ from $1$ to $n-1$ that are in order. Then you pick a distinct $i_{4}$ from $1$ to $n-1$ . Let’s say you want to re-order the indices so that $i_{4}$ is placed in ascending order with the rest of the indices. So for instance if $i_{2}<i_{4}<i_{3}$ , you would reorder $\varepsilon(i_{1},i_{2},i_{3},i_{4})$ to $-\varepsilon(i_{1},i_{2},i_{4},i_{3})$ at the cost of a minus sign. This organizes all the terms in a unique way. After doing this, they all cancel out for the following reason. Picking $i_{1},i_{2},i_{3}$ in order and then $i_{4}$ is the same thing as just picking four distinct integers from $1$ to $n-1$ , and then singling out one of the integers to be designated as the “special” $i_{4}$ . However, the choice of $i_{4}$ will cancel out with its neighbor as shown in figure 54, which proves the whole sum is zero.

### G.2 Holomorphic collinear limit of planar partial amplitude

In this section we check that

$$ \lim_{\langle{i,i+1}\rangle\to 0}A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;1}(1,\ldots,n)=\frac{-i\sqrt{2}g}{\langle{i,i+1}\rangle}A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n-1;1}(1,\ldots,|i\rangle,|i]+|i{+}1],\ldots,n). $$

Note that analogous relation also holds for the full amplitude. In fact, the appropriate formula holds for the single-trace and double-trace parts of the amplitude independently. (Note (463) was shown to hold for the full collinear limit $\langle{i,i+1}\rangle\to 0$ , $[i,i+1]\to 0$ in [130], which is actually how it was originally conjectured.)

Because (463) is cyclically symmetric, we assume for simplicity that $i\neq n$ . In this case, it is easy to check that

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\langle{i,i+1}\rangle\to 0}A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;1}(1,\ldots,n) \displaystyle=\frac{-i\sqrt{2}g}{\langle{i,i+1}\rangle}A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n-1;1}(1,\ldots,|i\rangle,|i]+|i{+}1],\ldots,n) \displaystyle+\lim_{\langle{i,i+1}\rangle\to 0}-\frac{i}{3}\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}}{(4\pi)^{2}}\frac{1}{\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n1}\rangle}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i_{1}<i\\
i+1<i_{4}\leq n\end{subarray}}t(i_{1},i,i+1,i_{4}). $$

The first term is what we desire, and the second term is defined by

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\langle{i,i+1}\rangle\to 0}t(i_{1},i,i+1,i_{4}) \displaystyle=\lim_{\langle{i,i+1}\rangle\to 0}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i_{1}<i\\
i+1<i_{4}\leq n\end{subarray}}\langle{i_{1}i}\rangle[i,i{+}1]\langle{i{+}1,i_{4}}\rangle[i_{4}i_{1}] \displaystyle=\lim_{\langle{i,i+1}\rangle\to 0}[i,i+1]\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i_{1}<i\\
i+1<i_{4}\leq n\end{subarray}}\langle{i+1|i_{4}i_{1}|i}\rangle. $$

In the full collinear limit $[i,i+1]\to 0$ and this is trivially zero. In the holomorphic collinear limit, however, to show it is zero one must use momentum conservation

$$ \sum_{i+1<i_{4}\leq n}p_{i_{4}}=-p_{i}-p_{i+1}-\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<i}p_{i_{1}} $$

and then plug it in the previous formula. The $p_{i}+p_{i+1}$ will go away when hit by $\langle i+1|$ , so

$$ \lim_{\langle{i,i+1}\rangle\to 0}t(i_{1},i,i+1,i_{4})=-\lim_{\langle{i,i+1}\rangle\to 0}[i,i+1]\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<i}\sum_{1\leq i_{1}^{\prime}<i}\langle{i+1|i_{1}^{\prime}i_{1}|i}\rangle=0. $$

This disappears by the antisymmetric identity $\langle{\alpha|PP|\alpha}\rangle=0$ , completing the proof.

## Appendix H Relationship between classical solutions, Berends-Giele currents, and amplitudes

In this appendix we will review the connection between tree-level off-shell Berends-Giele currents and classical solutions [201]. For simplicity, consider the scalar $\varphi^{3}$ theory with action

$$ S[\varphi]=\int d^{4}x\left(\frac{1}{2}(\partial\varphi)^{2}-\frac{g}{3!}\varphi^{3}\right) $$

and classical equation of motion

$$ \Box\varphi+\frac{g}{2}\varphi^{2}=0. $$

We start by following the usual discussion, found e.g. in [204]. Denoting the sourced action as

$$ S_{J}[\varphi]=S[\varphi]+\int d^{4}xJ(x)\,\varphi(x), $$

we define the sourced path integral $Z[J]$ and its generating function $W[J]$ via

$$ Z[J]=\int\mathcal{D}\varphi\,e^{iS_{J}[\varphi]}=e^{iW[J]}. $$

Denoting correlators within the sourced path integral as

$$ \langle{\ldots}\rangle_{J}\equiv\int\mathcal{D}\varphi\,e^{iS_{J}[\varphi]}(\ldots) $$

we have the standard expression

$$ \langle{\varphi(x_{1})\ldots\varphi(x_{n})}\rangle_{0}=(-i)^{n}\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x_{1})}\ldots\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x_{n})}Z[J]\big\rvert_{J=0}. $$

The correlators can be expressed as a sum over all Feynman diagrams where the sources are external legs. If we only sum over connected Feynman diagrams instead of all diagrams, then on the RHS $Z$ is replaced with $iW$ :

$$ \langle{\varphi(x_{1})\ldots\varphi(x_{n})}\rangle_{0,\rm{connected}}=(-i)^{n}\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x_{1})}\ldots\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x_{n})}iW[J]\big\rvert_{J=0}. $$

At tree-level (i.e. $\hbar\to 0$ ) the path integral is equal to its on-shell value. If we define $\varphi_{{\rm cl},J}$ as classical solution which extremizes the sourced action given vanishing boundary conditions (due to the implicit $i\epsilon$ ) then we have

$$ W[J]=S_{J}[\varphi_{{\rm cl},J}] $$

which implies

$$ \frac{\delta}{\delta J(x)}W[J]=\varphi_{{\rm cl},J}(x)+\int d^{4}y\left(\frac{\delta S_{J}}{\delta\varphi(y)}[\varphi_{{\rm cl},J}]\right)\frac{\delta\varphi_{{\rm cl},J}(y)}{\delta J(x)}. $$

Because the action is stationary when varied around the classical solution,

$$ \frac{\delta}{\delta J(x)}W[J]=\varphi_{{\rm cl},J}(x). $$

Plugging this into (483), we have

$$ \langle{\varphi(x)\varphi(x_{1})\ldots\varphi(x_{n})}\rangle_{0,\rm{connected}}=(-i)^{n}\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x_{1})}\ldots\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x_{n})}\varphi_{{\rm cl},J}(x)\big\rvert_{J=0}. $$

Fourier transforming both $\varphi(x_{i})$ and $J(x_{i})$ via

$$ \varphi(x)=\int\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\;e^{ik\cdot x}\tilde{\varphi}(k),\hskip 28.45274ptJ(x)=\int\frac{d^{4}k}{(2\pi)^{4}}\;e^{ik\cdot x}\tilde{J}(k), $$

we have from the chain rule

$$ \int d^{4}x\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\frac{\delta}{\delta J(x)}=(2\pi)^{4}\frac{\delta}{\delta\tilde{J}(-k)}. $$

If we Fourier transform (487) and amputate the external legs,

$$ \displaystyle(-i)^{n}(k_{1}^{2}\ldots k_{n}^{2})\langle{\varphi(x)\tilde{\varphi}(k_{1})\ldots\tilde{\varphi}(k_{n})}\rangle_{0,\rm{connected}} \displaystyle=(2\pi)^{4n}\;(-k_{1}^{2})\frac{\delta}{\delta\tilde{J}(-k_{1})}\ldots(-k_{n}^{2})\frac{\delta}{\delta\tilde{J}(-k_{n})}\varphi_{{\rm cl},J}(x)\big\rvert_{\tilde{J}=0}. $$

We now wish to remove the currents from the RHS of the equation. Because we are differentiating with respect to $\tilde{J}$ and then setting them equal to zero, let us defined a current $j(x)$ to be a sum of plane waves multiplied by infinitesimal parameters $\epsilon_{i}$ along with the prefactors $(-k_{i}^{2})$ :

$$ j(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}(-k_{i}^{2})e^{-ik\cdot x},\hskip 28.45274pt\tilde{j}(k)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}(-k_{i}^{2})\,(2\pi)^{4}\delta^{(4)}(k+k_{i}). $$

With this current, (490) becomes

$$ (-i)^{n}(k_{1}^{2}\ldots k_{n}^{2})\langle{\varphi(x)\tilde{\varphi}(k_{1})\ldots\tilde{\varphi}(k_{n})}\rangle_{0,\rm{connected}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\epsilon_{1}}\ldots\frac{\partial}{\partial\epsilon_{n}}\varphi_{{\rm cl},j}(x)\Big|_{\epsilon_{i}=0\;\forall i}. $$

If we want to solve

$$ \Box\varphi_{{\rm{cl}},j}+\frac{g}{2}\varphi_{{\rm{cl}},j}^{2}=j $$

we can Taylor expand the solution in the coupling in $g$ via

$$ \varphi_{{\rm{cl}},j}=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}g^{m}\varphi_{{\rm{cl}},j}^{(m)} $$

and recursively solve for the coefficients through

$$ \varphi^{(0)}_{{\rm{cl}},j}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}e^{-ik_{i}\cdot x},\hskip 28.45274pt\Box\varphi_{{\rm{cl}},j}^{(m+1)}=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{l=0}^{m}\varphi_{{\rm{cl}},j}^{(l)}\varphi_{{\rm{cl}},j}^{(m-l)}. $$

The above equation is nothing more than the Berends-Giele recursion relation. Note that $\varphi^{(m)}_{{\rm{cl}},j}$ is of order $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{m})$ .

Let us now take the on-shell limits $k_{i}^{2}\to 0$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$ . In this limit, $\varphi_{{\rm{cl}},j}$ clearly becomes a solution to the unsourced equations of motion.

We define the “perturbiner expansion” $\varphi^{\rm(ptb)}$ to be $\varphi_{{\rm{cl}},j}$ where we take the $\epsilon_{i}$ ’s to square to zero.

$$ \varphi^{\rm(ptb)}\equiv\lim_{k_{i}^{2}\to 0}\varphi_{{\rm{cl}},j}\Big|_{\epsilon_{i}^{2}=0\;\forall i} $$

In other words, the perturbiner expansion is a solution to the equation of motion where the leading (free) term is a sum of on-shell plane waves multiplied by infinitesimal parameters

$$ \varphi^{\rm(ptb)}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}\;e^{-ik_{i}\cdot x}+\ldots $$

and the higher-order terms are found by recursively plugging the solution into the interacting equations of motion. While the infinitesimal parameters are defined such that each individual parameter squares to zero, the product of distinct parameters is not zero. (If you wish, this definition is adopted for economy because we will be setting all $\epsilon_{i}$ to zero at the end of the calculation anyway after we differentiate by each of them once.)

$$ (\epsilon_{i})^{2}=0\hskip 28.45274pt\epsilon_{i}\epsilon_{i^{\prime}}\neq 0\text{ for }i\neq i^{\prime} $$

Having defined the perturbiner classical solutions, we may now write

$$ \lim_{k_{i}^{2}\to 0}(-i)^{n}(k_{1}^{2}\ldots k_{n}^{2})\langle{\varphi(x)\tilde{\varphi}(k_{1})\ldots\tilde{\varphi}(k_{n})}\rangle_{0,\rm{connected}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\epsilon_{1}}\ldots\frac{\partial}{\partial\epsilon_{n}}\varphi^{\rm(ptb)}(x)\Big|_{\epsilon_{i}=0\;\forall i}. $$

Fourier transforming $x$ to the off-shell momentum $k$ , we get

$$ \boxed{\lim_{k_{i}^{2}\to 0}(-i)^{n}(k_{1}^{2}\ldots k_{n}^{2})\langle{\tilde{\varphi}(k)\tilde{\varphi}(k_{1})\ldots\tilde{\varphi}(k_{n})}\rangle_{0,\rm{connected}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\epsilon_{1}}\ldots\frac{\partial}{\partial\epsilon_{n}}\tilde{\varphi}^{\rm(ptb)}(k)\Big|_{\epsilon_{i}=0\;\forall i}.} $$

The LHS of the above equation is the definition of a Berends-Giele current with one off-shell leg, and the RHS is the top piece of a classical perturbiner solution. Furthermore, if we amputate the final leg and take $k^{2}\to 0$ , we get

$$ \boxed{\mathcal{A}(k,k_{1},\ldots,k_{n})=-i\lim_{k^{2}\to 0}k^{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial\epsilon_{1}}\ldots\frac{\partial}{\partial\epsilon_{n}}\tilde{\varphi}^{\rm(ptb)}(k)\Big|_{\epsilon_{i}=0\;\forall i}} $$

in the all-outgoing convention.

Let’s look at the example of the 3-pt amplitude in $\varphi^{3}$ theory. The full perturbiner expansion with two seed particles is easily solved to be

$$ \tilde{\varphi}^{\rm(ptb)}(x)=\epsilon_{1}e^{-ik_{1}\cdot x}+\epsilon_{2}e^{-ik_{2}\cdot x}+\epsilon_{1}\epsilon_{2}\frac{g}{(k_{1}+k_{2})^{2}}e^{-i(k_{1}+k_{2})\cdot x} $$

and plugging this in to (501) we get

$$ \mathcal{A}(k,k_{1},k_{2})=-ig\,(2\pi)^{4}\delta^{(4)}(k_{1}+k_{2}+k) $$

where in the above expression we’ve restored the often-suppressed delta function which is produced naturally from the formula.

This concludes our discussion of perturbiner expansions and amplitudes, with (501) being the equation which relates the two. Having said this, there is also another way that tree-level amplitudes can be calculated using perturbiners. It involves simply plugging the perturbiner expansion into the action itself. The position $x$ of the solution is integrated over spacetime, producing the delta function, so only the on-shell legs comprise the particles in the amplitude. It is interesting how there are two quite different formulae which both relate perturbiners to amplitudes.

P6116:
# Path integral games with de Sitter $\alpha$ -vacua

**Authors:** Noah Miller Affiliation: School of Natural Sciences, Institute for Advanced Study, 1 Einstein Drive, Princeton, NJ 08540 USA Affiliation: Princeton Gravity Initiative, Princeton University, Jadwin Hall, Washington Road, Princeton NJ 08544, USA Email: noahmiller@ias.edu

## Abstract

The $\alpha$ -vacua are a 1-parameter family of quantum field vacua in de Sitter space which are invariant under the isometry group $SO(1,d)$ . In this work give a path integral construction of the de Sitter $\alpha$ -vacua. We explain that these states can be prepared by acting on the Bunch-Davies vacuum with a certain non-local charge operator. While most conserved charges live on a single codimension-1 manifold, we show that this particular charge lives on a pair of two codimension-1 manifolds which are antipodal mirrors of each other. The rules for the manipulation of this charge as an insertion in the path integral are explained. We further explain how this charge can be used to solve for the wavefunctionals of the $\alpha$ -vacua at ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ (in the regime that $\alpha$ is small) by deforming the equator of de Sitter space to $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ / $\mathcal{I}^{-}$ .

We also discuss the special $\alpha$ -vacua known as the “in” and “out” vacua, for both heavy and light scalars. It is well known that the “in” and “out” vacua are equal in odd dimensions, but we also show that they are equal in even dimensions when $\sqrt{(d-1)^{2}/4-m^{2}}$ is a half-integer.

Finally, we investigate the question of whether the $\alpha$ -vacua can be constructed in interacting quantum field theories. Using the fact that the antipodal charge operator is only conserved in a free theory, we give a symmetry based argument that in general they cannot be, explaining why interactions and $SO(1,d)$ invariance of the vacua are in tension.

## 1 Introduction

A free quantum field theory of a scalar field in Minkowski space or Anti-de Sitter space has only a single vacuum state that is invariant under the full isometry group of the spacetime. The situation is different in de Sitter space, where there exists a 1-parameter family of states, called the $\alpha$ -vacua, which are invariant under the full de Sitter isometry group $SO(1,d)$ Chernikov and Tagirov (1968); Schomblond and Spindel (1976); Mottola (1985); Allen (1985); Burges (1984). The special case $\ket{\alpha= 0}$ is the Bunch-Davies vacuum Bunch and Davies (1978), also called the euclidean vacuum or the Hartle-Hawking vacuum Hartle and Hawking (1983).

These states have become a somewhat niche topic of recurring interest since their discovery in 1968 Chernikov and Tagirov (1968). Because the $\alpha$ -vacua are homogeneous and isotropic, many works have considered the possibility that the $\alpha$ -vacua (or states which look like the $\alpha$ -vacua above some short distance cut off) could have been initial conditions for the inflaton field in the early universe, and investigated what high energy physics would be imprinted in these states Kaloper et al. (2002); de Boer et al. (2005); Danielsson (2002a); Danielsson (2002b); Easther et al. (2001); Easther et al. (2003); Easther et al. (2002); Collins and Holman (2005). In quantum cosmology, Chen et al. (2024) found $\alpha$ -like states emerging in a system of two dS spacetimes connected by a euclidean wormhole. The $\alpha$ -vacua were also conjectured to be dual to marginal deformations of a dual CFT in the context of the dS/CFT correspondence Bousso et al. (2002); Ng and Strominger (2013); Spradlin and Volovich (2002). In the field of celestial holography, analog $\alpha$ -vacua have recently been defined in flat space which are not invariant under the full Poincaré group but are invariant under the Lorentz subgroup Melton et al. (2024). See Joung et al. (2006); Joung et al. (2007) for a group theory construction of the $\alpha$ -vacua. See also Kanno et al. (2014); Polyakov (2008); Nguyen (2017); Chopping et al. (2024); Ansari et al. (2024); Cotler and Strominger (2023).

The purpose of this note is, simply, to understand how the $\alpha$ -vacua are constructed using the Feynman path integral.

In 1984, it was noted by Burges11 1 who referenced an unpublished note by Gross and Witten Burges (1984) that there exists a certain non-local charge operator $\hat{Q}^{A}$ which generates the $\alpha$ -vacua from the Bunch-Davies vacuum via $\ket{\alpha}=e^{i\alpha\hat{Q}^{A}}\ket{0}$ . However, something was conspicuously missing from Burges’ paper which motivated this present investigation: it was not explained how the codimension-1 surface on which this charge was defined could be continuously deformed, in the way that surfaces can naturally be deformed when charges are conserved.

Let us be more precise. If we cover de Sitter space $dS_{d}=\mathbb{R}\times S_{d-1}$ with global coordinates $(t,\Omega)$ , with $\Omega\in S_{d-1}$ , as

$$ ds^{2}=-dt^{2}+\cosh^{2}(t)d\Omega_{d-1}^{2} $$

then Burges gave an expression for the charge that only holds on the $t=0$ slice:

$$ \hat{Q}^{A}=\int d^{d-1}\Omega\,\hat{\phi}(0,\Omega)\hat{\pi}(0,\Omega^{A}). $$

Here $\Omega^{A}$ is the point antipodal to $\Omega$ on the $S_{d-1}$ sphere. In this work we will explain how this charge can be defined beyond the $t=0$ slice. In fact, we will see that this charge actually lives on two antipodal slices in spacetime, and will study the consequences of this fact. This fact did not appear in Burges’ original analysis because the $t=0$ slice happens to be its own antipodal surface.

In section 2 we review global coordinates in de Sitter spacetime and in its euclidean analytic continuation.

In section 3 we review the path integral construction of the Bunch-Davies vacuum for a free scalar on a de Sitter background using the euclidean path integral on the half-sphere. We explain why this state is invariant under the dS isometry group.

In section 4 we discuss the well known fact that annihilation operators constructed out of “euclidean modes” (solutions to the dS Klein-Gordon equation which are non-singular when analytically continued to the lower half euclidean sphere) annihilate the Bunch-Davies state. We prove this fact with Noether’s theorem, which we are able to do because annihilation operators are the Noether charges of a linear symmetry that only exists in free theories.

In section 5 we discuss the antipodal map in de Sitter space, and use it to construct a non-local symmetry variation $\delta\phi=\epsilon\,\phi^{A}$ of the free scalar field. We calculate the associated classical conserved current using Noether’s theorem. This conserved current is unusual in that it is non-local, in the sense that the current evaluated a point in de Sitter space depends on the value of the field and its derivatives at that point and at the antipodal point. After quantization, we show that this classical conserved current is indeed promoted to a conserved insertion in the path integral à la a Ward–Takahashi identity, although the proof of this is slightly subtler than one might expect.

In section 6 we explain “why” extra dS isometry invariant states can be constructed aside from the Bunch-Davies vacuum. To briefly outline the argument, one would expect that a dS isometry invariant state could be constructed by acting on the Bunch-Davies state by some conserved charge, producing a state like $\hat{Q}\ket{0}$ for some $\hat{Q}$ which is defined as the integral over a codimension-1 surface of a locally-defined conserved current. However, the Bunch-Davies state is prepared by a path integral over the half-sphere, and the half-sphere is a simply-connected space, meaning the surface on which the conserved charge lives (the equator) is able to be contracted to zero, implying $\hat{Q}\ket{0}=0$ . However, due to the strange nature of the non-local “antipodal” charge $\hat{Q}^{A}$ , the equator together with its antipodal mirror are not able to be contracted on the lower half-sphere, so $\hat{Q}^{A}\ket{0}\neq 0$ and we can construct a family of dS-invariant states $\ket{\alpha}=e^{i\alpha\hat{Q}^{A}}\ket{0}$ .

In section 7 we explain which $\alpha\in\mathbb{C}$ result in $\ket{\alpha}$ being a normalizable state.

In section 8 we turn our attention to the so-called “in” and “out” vacuum states, which are special $\alpha$ -vacua that contain no particles in the infinite past/infinite future. Using a simple analytic argument, we are able to calculate which values of $\alpha$ produce these states. The argument uses the fact that the antipodal map in de Sitter space can be continuously connected to the identity via an analytic continuation through the euclidean section $t\mapsto t+i\pi$ . This argument works for all spacetime dimensions $d$ and mass $m$ . While it is well known that for heavy masses $m>\tfrac{d-1}{2}$ the in vacuum equals the out vacuum in odd dimensions Bousso et al. (2002); Lagogiannis et al. (2011), we show that for light masses $m<\tfrac{d-1}{2}$ the in vacuum also equals the out vacuum when $\sqrt{(d-1)^{2}/4-m^{2}}$ is a half-integer. This includes the massless and conformally coupled scalars.

In section 9 we discuss the $\alpha$ -vacua wavefunctionals at the infinite future of de Sitter space $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ . We use a path integral argument to find the operation which maps the Bunch-Davies wavefunctional at $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ to the $\alpha$ -vacuum wavefunctional at $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ when $\alpha$ is small. If $\alpha$ is finite, operator ordering problems prevent us from using our path integral argument to solve for the wavefunctional at $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ , which we explain.

In section 10 we address the question of whether or not the $\alpha$ -vacua can be defined in interacting field theories. We argue that they cannot be. This is congruous with the findings of the previous works Collins et al. (2003); Danielsson (2002c); Einhorn and Larsen (2003a); Einhorn and Larsen (2003b); Goldstein and Lowe (2003); Goldstein and Lowe (2004); Goldstein (2005); Akhmedov (2014); Kaloper et al. (2002); Banks and Mannelli (2003); Akhmedov et al. (2023).

## 2 Global coordinates in lorentzian and euclidean de Sitter

Let us define a $d+1$ dimensional Minkowski embedding space with coordinates $X^{M}$ for $M=0,\ldots,d$ and metric $ds^{2}=-(dX^{0})^{2}+(dX^{1})^{2}+\ldots+(dX^{d})^{2}=\eta_{MN}dX^{M}dX^{N}$ . $d$ -dimensional de Sitter space $dS_{d}$ can be defined as a hyperboloid cut out of the embedding space

$$ -(X^{0})^{2}+(X^{1})^{2}+\ldots+(X^{d})^{2}=1 $$

where we have set the de Sitter length scale to 1. Euclidean de Sitter space can then be defined via the analytic continuation

$$ X^{0}=-i\tilde{X}^{0} $$

where $\tilde{X}^{0}$ is taken to be real. Euclidean de Sitter space is a $d$ dimensional sphere $S_{d}$

$$ (\tilde{X}^{0})^{2}+(X^{1})^{2}+\ldots+(X^{d})^{2}=1 $$

in an embedding space with metric $ds^{2}=(d\tilde{X}^{0})^{2}+(dX^{1})^{2}+\ldots+(dX^{d})^{2}$ . Let us also define the lower half of the sphere $S_{d,-}\subset S_{d}$ to be

$$ S_{d,-}\equiv\{\tilde{X}^{0},\ldots,X^{d}\;|\;\tilde{X}^{0}\leq 0,(\tilde{X}^{0})^{2}+\ldots+(X^{d})^{2}=1\} $$

and the $X^{0}=\tilde{X}^{0}=0$ “equator” $E$ to be

$$ E\equiv\{X^{0},\ldots,X^{d}\;|\;X^{0}=0,(X^{1})^{2}+\ldots+(X^{d})^{2}=1\}. $$

The equator $E$ can be understood as a subset of either the lorentzian $dS_{d}$ or the euclidean $S_{d}$ .

*Figure 1: Lorentzian de Sitter space $dS_{d}$ and euclidean de Sitter space $S_{d}$ . The equator $E$ , defined at $X^{0}=\tilde{X}^{0}=0$ , exists on both. The halves of the euclidean sphere above and below $E$ are denoted $S_{d,+}$ and $S_{d,-}$ , respectively.*

Let $\Omega$ denote a set of sphere coordinates which cover the unit sphere $S_{d-1}$ with metric $d\Omega_{d-1}^{2}$ , and let $n^{a}(\Omega)$ with $a=1,\ldots,d$ be the unit vector on the sphere parameterized by $\Omega$ with $n(\Omega)^{2}=1$ . Then $dS_{d}$ may be parameterized with global coordinates $x^{\mu}=(t,\Omega)$ , for $\mu=0,\ldots,d-1$ , by

$$ \displaystyle X^{0}(t,\Omega) \displaystyle=\sinh(t) \displaystyle X^{a}(t,\Omega) \displaystyle=\cosh(t)n^{a}(\Omega) $$

with metric

$$ ds^{2}=-dt^{2}+\cosh^{2}(t)d\Omega^{2}_{d-1}. $$

If we analytically continue $t=-i\tilde{t}$ and take $\tilde{t}$ to be real, we make $X^{0}$ imaginary just as in (4). Euclidean de Sitter space $S_{d}$ is then parameterized as

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{X}^{0}(-i\tilde{t},\Omega) \displaystyle=\sin(\tilde{t}) \displaystyle X^{a}(-i\tilde{t},\Omega) \displaystyle=\cos(\tilde{t})n^{a}(\Omega) $$

where $\tilde{t}\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ . $\tilde{t}=-\pi/2$ is the south pole and $\tilde{t}=\pi/2$ is the north pole. The euclidean metric is

$$ ds^{2}=d\tilde{t}^{2}+\cos^{2}(\tilde{t})d\Omega^{2}_{d-1}. $$

We denote $\tilde{x}^{\mu}=(\tilde{t},\Omega)$ .

## 3 The Bunch-Davies state

In this section we review the path integral construction of the Bunch-Davies state in $dS_{d}$ . The euclidean action for a free scalar field $\phi$ of mass $m$ on a spacetime patch of the euclidean sphere $U\subset S_{d}$ is

$$ S_{U}[\phi]=\frac{1}{2}\int_{U}d^{d}\tilde{x}\sqrt{g}\left((\nabla\phi)^{2}+m^{2}\phi^{2}\right). $$

The Bunch-Davies state, denoted as $\ket{0}$ , can be defined on the $\tilde{t}=0$ time slice $E$ as the euclidean path integral over the half-sphere with open boundary conditions. If $\varphi(\Omega)$ is some function on the equatorial $d-1$ sphere, then let us define the field “position eigenvector” state $\ket{\varphi}$ to be the state that satisfies

$$ \hat{\phi}(0,\Omega)\ket{\varphi}=\varphi(\Omega)\ket{\varphi}. $$

The Bunch-Davies wavefunctional evaluated at $\varphi$ is then given by the path integral over all fields $\phi$ on the half-sphere which are equal to $\varphi$ on $E$ . See figure 2.

$$ \Psi^{E}_{0}[\varphi]=\innerproduct{\varphi}{0}=\int_{\evaluated{\phi}_{E}=\,\varphi}\mathcal{D}\phi\;e^{-S_{S_{d,-}}[\phi]}. $$

*Figure 2: Definition of the Bunch-Davies wavefunctional $\Psi^{E}_{0}[\varphi]$ as a euclidean path integral on the half-sphere with boundary conditions $\evaluated{\phi}_{E}=\varphi$ .*

The group of isometries of $dS_{d}$ is $SO(1,d)$ . Let us define the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(1,d)$ vector fields as

$$ L^{MN}\equiv\eta^{NP}X^{M}\partialderivative{X^P}-\eta^{MP}X^{N}\partialderivative{X^P} $$

and denote $\hat{L}^{MN}$ to be the corresponding quantum operators. Generators of the form $L^{0M}$ are “boost” vector fields, while generators of the form $L^{MN}$ with $M,N=1,\ldots,d$ are “spatial rotation” vector fields which generate a $SO(d)\subset SO(1,d)$ subgroup. Only the spatial rotations map $E$ into itself.

One might wonder if $\ket{0}$ is invariant under all of these symmetries. Clearly, $\ket{0}$ is invariant under the $SO(d)$ subgroup because the euclidean half-sphere itself is symmetric under these rotations. But what about the boost generators $\hat{L}^{0M}$ ? Do they annihilate $\ket{0}$ ? Without loss of generality we focus on $\hat{L}^{01}$ .

*Figure 3: The Killing vector field $L^{01}$ generates a boost in lorentzian de Sitter and a rotation in euclidean de Sitter.*

Notice that in the euclidean section, the vector field is

$$ -iL^{01}=-\tilde{X}^{0}\partialderivative{X^1}+X^{1}\partialderivative{\tilde{X}^0} $$

and generates a $U(1)$ rotation in the $\tilde{X}^{0}$ - $X^{1}$ plane. See figure 3. This means that, if $\epsilon$ is a tiny angle, then in euclidean de Sitter space the operator $1-\epsilon\,\hat{L}^{01}$ has the effect of rotating the path integral by an angle of $\epsilon$ in said plane. (For a review on how the quantum operators corresponding to spacetime vector fields shift the spacetime boundary of path integration, see appendix A.)

However, due to the $SO(d+1)$ symmetry of $S_{d}$ , we can trivially see that the rotated path integral equals the original path integral, and thus $\hat{L}^{01}\ket{0}=0$ . See figure 4. If our path integral had, say, contained insertions on the lower half-sphere, then the state would not have been annihilated by $\hat{L}^{01}$ . See figure 5.

*Figure 4: Proof of the de Sitter invariance of the Bunch-Davies state. $\epsilon\hat{L}^{01}$ rotates the euclidean half-sphere by angle $\epsilon$ , which does not actually change the path integral.*

*Figure 5: If we were to add some insertions into the half-sphere path integral, the corresponding state would not be annihilated by $\hat{L}^{01}$ because the rotation of the equator by a tiny angle $\epsilon$ would not leave the path integral invariant.*

We have now seen that the Bunch-Davies state is invariant under the full dS isometry group. This is a special property, and one may wonder if there are more states invariant under this group. As we will see, the $\alpha$ -vacua are a 1-parmeter family of states which are also dS-invariant.

## 4 Noether’s theorem and annihilation operators

In this section we review some properties of annihilation operators, euclidean modes, and their relation to the Bunch-Davies state.

Consider a function $f$ on $dS_{d}$ which satisfies the free de Sitter Klein-Gordon equation of motion

$$ (\nabla^{2}-m^{2})f=0. $$

$f$ can also be understood as a function on the sphere $S_{d}$ upon analytic continuation.

On the euclidean sphere $S_{d}$ , the eigenvalues of the Laplace operator $\nabla^{2}$ are given by $-l(l+d-1)$ for all $l=0,1,2\ldots$ . Notice, then, that $\nabla^{2}$ only has negative eigenvalues while any $f$ which solves (17) will be an eigenfunction of $\nabla^{2}$ with the positive eigenvalue $m^{2}$ . This implies that, strictly speaking, there exists no such $f$ which is defined on the whole sphere. Any $f$ that solves (17) must be ill-defined at some points on $S_{d}$ , where there will be non-analyticities such as poles or branch cuts.

If the analytic continuation of a function $f_{e}$ that solves (17) is well-defined on the whole lower half-sphere $S_{d,-}$ , we call it a “euclidean mode.” As a consequence of the previous discussion, all euclidean modes must necessarily have non-analyticities or singularities in the upper half-sphere $S_{d,+}$ .

Every solution $f$ to the Klein-Gordon equation can be used to define an associated “annihilation operator” $\hat{a}(f)$ . It turns out that any annihilation operator built out of a euclidean mode will annihilate the Bunch-Davies state, $\hat{a}(f_{e})\ket{0}=0$ . We will now present a proof of this fact using Noether’s theorem.

Classically, the free euclidean action of a scalar field $S_{U}[\phi]$ possesses a symmetry

$$ \delta\phi=\epsilon f $$

where $\epsilon$ is a tiny constant and $f$ is any function which satisfies (17). This symmetry only exists because the free equation of motion is linear, and any two solutions can be added together to produce a new solution.

We will now preform the Noether trick to find the conserved current corresponding to this symmetry. To do this, we promote $\epsilon$ to an infinitesimal function $\varepsilon(\tilde{x})$ which vanishes at the boundary of $U$ , and consider the change in the action corresponding to $\delta\phi(\tilde{x})=\varepsilon(\tilde{x})f(\tilde{x})$ . It turns out to be

$$ \delta S_{U}[\phi]=\int_{U}d^{d}\tilde{x}\sqrt{g}\left((\partial^{\mu}\varepsilon)(f\overset{\leftrightarrow}{\partial}_{\mu}\phi)-(\varepsilon\,\phi)(\nabla^{2}f-m^{2}f)\right) $$

where $f_{1}\overset{\leftrightarrow}{\partial}_{\mu}f_{2}\equiv f_{1}(\partial_{\mu}f_{2})-(\partial_{\mu}f_{1})f_{2}$ . Because $f$ satisfies (17) and $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, this implies that the Noether current

$$ J(f)_{\mu}\equiv f\overset{\leftrightarrow}{\partial}_{\mu}\phi $$

is conserved on shell, satisfying $\nabla_{\mu}J(f)^{\mu}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{g}}\partial_{\mu}(\sqrt{g}J(f)^{\mu})=0$ . Let us define the associated conserved charge

$$ a_{\Sigma}(f)\equiv i\int_{\Sigma}d\Sigma^{\mu}J(f)_{\mu}. $$

which is defined on a codimension- $1$ surface $\Sigma$ . This conserved charge is the classical version of the annihilation operator corresponding to the mode $f$ . (We note that the standard definition of the annihilation operator differs from the one above by an extra complex conjugation, replacing $f$ above with $f^{*}$ .)

We now turn to the quantum path integral on the lower half euclidean sphere. If we define $\phi^{\prime}=\phi+\varepsilon f_{e}$ , then $\mathcal{D}\phi^{\prime}=\mathcal{D}\phi$ because the addition of $\varepsilon f_{e}$ simply shifts the measure. Crucially, because $f_{e}$ is a euclidean mode, the change in measure $\phi^{\prime}=\phi+\varepsilon f_{e}$ is well defined everywhere on the lower half-sphere.

Using this symmetry variation, one can derive a corresponding quantum Ward identity in the usual way, and it will read

$$ \int_{\evaluated{\phi}_{E}=\,\varphi}\mathcal{D}\phi\;e^{-S_{S_{d,-}}[\phi]}\nabla_{\mu}J(f_{e})^{\mu}(\tilde{x})=0 $$

where $\tilde{x}$ can be any point in $S_{d,-}$ .

The above equation implies that, if one inserts the charge $a_{\Sigma}(f_{e})$ into the path integral, $\Sigma$ can be deformed without changing the path integral.

Let us now define the quantum annihilation operator22 2 In this paper we use hatted symbols to denote operators acting on states, such as $\hat{a}(f)$ , and non-hatted symbols to denote insertions in the path integral, like $a_{\Sigma}(f)$ .

$$ \hat{a}(f)\equiv i\int_{E}dE^{\mu}f\overset{\leftrightarrow}{\partial}_{\mu}\hat{\phi} $$

where we set the codimension-1 surface $\Sigma$ to be the equator $E$ .

*Figure 6: If $f_{e}$ has no singularities on $S_{d,-}$ , then $\hat{a}(f_{e})$ annihilates $\ket{0}$ because the equator is contractible.*

Because $E$ is contractable on the half-sphere, the annihilation operator $\hat{a}(f_{e})$ annihilates the Bunch-Davies state, as shown in figure 6.

$$ (\hat{a}(f_{e})\Psi_{0}^{E})[\varphi]=\int_{\evaluated{\phi}_{E}=\,\varphi}\mathcal{D}\phi\;e^{-S_{S_{d,-}}[\phi]}a_{E}(f_{e})=0. $$

This completes the proof.

## 5 The antipodal symmetry, classically and quantumly

One can define an antipodal map on de Sitter space, which takes the form $X\mapsto-X$ in the embedding space. This map commutes with the dS isometry group $SO(1,d)$ .

Interestingly, one cannot define an analogous antipodal map in Anti-de Sitter space. This is essentially because Anti-de Sitter space is defined as the universal cover of the hyperboloid $-(X^{0})^{2}-(X^{1})^{2}+(X^{2})^{2}+\ldots+(X^{d})^{2}=-1$ in flat space with signature $(2,d-1)$ , which has closed timelike curves and must be “unwrapped.” Once unwrapped, however, the point $-X$ has an infinite number of representatives in the covering space, and as a result there is no way to continuously lift the antipodal map.33 3 Furthermore, a $SO(1,d-1)$ invariant antipodal map cannot be defined in euclidean Anti-de Sitter space (EAdS) either. EAdS can be defined as the “top cap” of the hyperboloid $-(X^{0})^{2}+(\tilde{X}^{1})^{2}+\ldots+(X^{d})^{2}=-1$ . The natural embedding space antipodal map $X\mapsto-X$ maps the “top cap” with $X^{0}>0$ into the “bottom cap” with $X^{0}<0$ , and thus does not map EAdS into itself. If one tries to adopt an ad-hoc discontinuous definition of the antipodal map on the universal cover, said map will not be $SO(2,d-1)$ invariant. See figure 7.
