# Proof of the graviton MHV formula using Plebański’s second heavenly equation

**Authors:** Noah Miller Affiliation: Center for the Fundamental Laws of Nature, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA Email: noahmiller@g.harvard.edu

## Abstract

Self-dual spacetimes can be thought of as spacetimes containing only positive helicity gravitons. In this work we give a perturbiner expansion for self-dual spacetimes based on Plebański’s second heavenly equation. The expansion is naturally organized as a sum over “marked tree graphs” where each node corresponds to a positive helicity graviton and can have an arbitrary number of edges. Negative helicity gravitons must be added in by hand.

We then use this perturbiner expansion to give a first principles derivation of the NSVW tree formula for the MHV amplitude in Einstein gravity. A unique feature of this proof is that it does not use BCFW recursion or twistor theory. It works by plugging the spacetime with arbitrarily many $+$ gravitons and two $-$ gravitons into the on-shell gravitational action and evaluating it. The action we use is the self-dual Plebański action plus an additional boundary term, and the amplitude itself comes entirely from the boundary term. Along the way, we also find an interesting new generalization of the NSVW formula which has not previously appeared in the literature.

In the appendix we give another way to express the perturbiner expansion using binary tree graphs instead of marked tree graphs, and prove the equivalence of these two expansions diagrammatically. We also provide an introduction to self-dual gravity aimed at non-experts, as well as a proof of the Parke-Taylor formula in Yang Mills theory analogous to our proof of the NSVW formula in gravity.

## 1 Introduction

In pure Einstein gravity, the amplitude for an arbitrary number of positive helicity gravitons to scatter is zero at tree-level. If a single negative helicity graviton is added, the amplitude is still zero. If two negative helicity gravitons are added, however, the amplitude is non-zero. This is the so-called gravitational maximal helicity violating (MHV) amplitude, and it is the simplest non-vanishing amplitude in Einstein gravity.

While gravitational Feynman diagrammatics are notoriously complex even at tree-level, there are a number of miraculous closed form expressions for the MHV amplitude with arbitrarily many positive helicity gravitons Nguyen et al. (2010); Berends et al. (1988); Elvang and Freedman (2008); Hodges (2012).

The first was given by Berends, Giele, and Kuijf (BGK) in 1988 Berends et al. (1988), although their formula did not make manifest the permutation symmetry of the positive helicity gravitons. A nicer formula was later found by Nguyen, Spradlin, Volovich, and Wen (NSVW) Nguyen et al. (2010) in 2009. Their formula expressed the MHV amplitude as a sum over “marked tree graphs” (which are not the usual tree-level Feynman diagrams) where each node of the graph corresponds to a positive helicity graviton. In some sense, their formula was anticipated 10 years prior by Bern, Dixon, Perelstein, and Rozowsky Bern et al. (1999), who discovered a set of recursive rules to compute the MHV amplitude. While the NSVW formula does not appear explicitly in that earlier work, it can be obtained from the rules laid out in that paper Krasnov and Scarinci (2013). In 2012 Hodges (2012), Hodges provided a more compact expression for the MHV amplitude as the determinant of a certain matrix which depends on two arbitrary reference spinors. Once the reference spinors are set to the negative helicity gravitons, it can be shown that Hodges’ formula is equivalent to NSVW’s through the use of a combinatorial “matrix tree theorem,” in which Hodges’ determinant can be rewritten as a sum over NSVW’s trees Feng and He (2012). See Trnka (2021) for a review of the various formulae.

It is not understood how the NSVW formula or Hodges’ formula arise via the explicit summation of tree-level Feynman diagrams. Instead, they were both originally proven with a different method, by showing that they satisfied the BCFW recursion relation Britto et al. (2005b); Britto et al. (2005a).

However, there do exist “direct” (i.e., non BCFW) proofs of the NSVW/Hodges’ formulae. These proofs exploit the existence of an integrable subsector of Einstein gravity known as “self-dual gravity” (SDG), which is the main object of study of twistor theory Penrose (1976b); Penrose (1976a). These twistorial proofs of the MHV formulae include Mason and Skinner’s 2008 proof of the original BGK formula Mason and Skinner (2010) and Adamo, Mason, and Sharma’s separate 2021 proof of the NSVW/Hodges’ formula Adamo et al. (2021).

Roughly speaking, both of these proofs operate by computing a classical gravitational action on-shell, whose value equals the tree-level MHV scattering amplitude itself. There is no fundamental reason that this action could not have been computed without the use of twistor theory, although in those works it was an indispensable tool.

We now summarize the two main results of this present paper:

- 1. We explain how to perturbatively generate self-dual solutions to Einstein’s equation using a perturbative expansion written in terms of “marked tree graphs” instead of Feynman diagrams. These self-dual metrics correspond to spacetimes containing an arbitrary number of positive helicity gravitons.

- 2. Using the tree formula for self-dual metrics (and adding in two ASD perturbations by hand), we will provide a new first-principles proof of the NSVW formula by plugging this spacetime into the on-shell gravitational action. The only non-zero part of the action will come from a boundary term. This proof of NSVW is the first which does not make use of BCFW recursion or twistor theory.

Throughout this paper, we will use a formulation of SDG due to Jerzy Plebański Plebanski (1975), who showed that any SD metric can be written in the form

$$ ds^{2}=4\big(du\,d{\bar{u}}-dw\,d{\bar{w}}+(\partial_{w}^{2}\phi)\,d{\bar{u}}^{2}+(2\partial_{u}\partial_{w}\phi)\,d{\bar{u}}d{\bar{w}}+(\partial_{u}^{2}\phi)\,d{\bar{w}}^{2}\big) $$

where $\phi$ is a scalar field that satisfies an equation of motion known as “Plebański’s second heavenly equation”

$$ \Box\phi-\{\partial_{u}\phi,\partial_{w}\phi\}=0. $$

Here, $\Box$ is the flat space wave operator and $\{\cdot,\cdot\}$ is a spacetime Poisson bracket defined with the two coordinates $u,w$ , as

$$ \Box\equiv\partial_{u}\partial_{\bar{u}}-\partial_{w}\partial_{\bar{w}},\hskip 28.45274pt\{f,g\}\equiv\partialderivative{f}{u}\,\partialderivative{g}{w}-\partialderivative{f}{w}\,\partialderivative{g}{u}. $$

Classical solutions to (2) can be generated with Feynman diagrams using standard methods, see for instance Monteiro and O’Connell (2011), and Monteiro (2023); Armstrong-Williams et al. (2022). Having said that, we emphasize that we will not prove the validity of the marked tree expansion through the use of Feynman diagrams, even though it certainly must somehow be possible.

This paper is organized as follows.

- • In section 2, we present and prove the tree formula to perturbatively calculate self-dual metrics using marked tree diagrams.

- • In section 3, we study linear SD and ASD perturbations to self-dual metrics using our tree formula. We then show how the tree formula can be used to explicitly calculate the action of a certain “recursion operator” $\mathcal{R}$ , familiar to the study of integrability in SDG, on these linear perturbations. This will come in handy at multiple points when it comes time to prove the NSVW formula.

- • In section 4, we briefly review the relationship between tree-level scattering amplitudes and on-shell actions.

- • In section 5 we provide the proof of the NSVW formula using the marked tree formula for the Plebański scalar.

- • In section 6 we discuss our results.

- • In appendix A, we give a second way to build up self-dual metrics using binary tree graphs instead of the marked tree graphs from section 2. This binary tree expansion provides a recursive way to compute the self-dual metric containing $N+1$ positive helicity gravitons if one already has an expression for the metric containing $N$ positive helicity gravitons. We give a diagrammatic proof that this binary tree expansion is equivalent to our earlier marked tree expansion.

- • In appendix B we provide the first principles derivations of many key equations of SDG used in this paper that are spread throughout the literature. This will hopefully be useful to readers new to the subject, and will culminate in the proofs of Plebański’s first and second heavenly equations.

- • In appendix C we provide an analogous proof of the Parke-Taylor formula for the Yang Mills MHV amplitude.

In the language of Berends-Giele currents, we note that our calculation of the perturbiner expansion for Plebański’s second scalar is essentially equivalent to the computation of the tree-level all-plus graviton current with one off-shell leg Bern et al. (1999); Krasnov and Scarinci (2013); Krasnov (2017).

There are two possible advantages the proof we give here has over the BCFW proof. The first is that our perturbiner expansion can potentially be generalized to non-flat backgrounds Lipstein and Nagy (2023); Bittleston et al. (2024); Adamo et al. (2024a), although we leave this for future work. The second is that it produces an interesting new generalization of the NSVW formula, equation (127), which is distinct from Hodges formula and has not previously appeared in the literature. (It would also be interesting if some connection could be made between our perturbiner expansion and Hodges formula, although we are unsure how this could be done.)

In a partner paper Miller (2025), we also use the marked tree expansion of the Plebański scalar to write down an explicit formula for the action of the so-called $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ algebra on self-dual spacetimes.

## 2 A perturbiner expansion for Plebański’s second heavenly equation

We are interested in solutions to the equation (2). Once we have $\phi$ , we can plug it into (1) to get a self-dual metric, so knowing $\phi$ is tantamount to knowing the metric. When $\phi=0$ , the metric reduces to flat space in lightcone coordinates

$$ \displaystyle u \displaystyle=(X^{0}-X^{3})/2\,, \displaystyle{\bar{u}} \displaystyle=(X^{0}+X^{3})/2\,, \displaystyle w \displaystyle=(X^{1}+iX^{2})/2\,, \displaystyle{\bar{w}} \displaystyle=(X^{1}-iX^{2})/2\,. $$

Note that ${\bar{u}}\neq(u)^{*}$ , as both $u$ and ${\bar{u}}$ are real independent variables. We have adopted this convention in the pursuit of notational symmetry.

It is straightforward to check that $\phi=Ae^{ip\cdot X}$ solves (2) for any $A$ as long as $p^{2}$ = 0. This solution corresponds to a finite size (complex) positive helicity gravitational wave $h_{\mu\nu}=A\,\varepsilon^{+}_{\mu\nu}e^{ip\cdot X}$ where $\varepsilon^{+}_{\mu\nu}$ is given below. Because (2) is non-linear, the sum of two plane waves will in general not also satisfy (2). One could imagine, however, taking a sum of plane waves and then recursively solving for higher order terms in the coefficients “ $A$ ” in order to arrive at a full solution.

This motivates the idea of a “perturbiner expansion” Rosly and Selivanov (1997a) which we now define. First, note that the equation of motion (2) can be split up into a free part (which is just the wave equation) and a quadratic interacting part. Imagine starting with a solution to the free equation

$$ \phi=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\epsilon_{i}\,e^{ip_{i}\cdot X} $$

where $p_{i}^{2}=0$ , and the $\epsilon_{i}$ ’s are infinitesimal parameters. We will define the square of any particular infinitesimal parameter to be 0, but the product of distinct infinitesimal parameters to not be zero:

$$ (\epsilon_{i})^{2}=0,\hskip 28.45274pt\epsilon_{i}\epsilon_{j}\neq 0\hskip 5.69046pt\text{ if }i\neq j. $$

With this in mind, we define the plane wave “seed” functions to be

$$ \phi_{i}\equiv\epsilon_{i}\,e^{ip_{i}\cdot X}. $$

A perturbiner expansion is then defined as a solution to the full equation of motion which contains (5) as its linear piece. The linear piece is the boundary condition which specifies the rest of the solution. For example, when there are two seed functions, the perturbiner expansion will take the form

$$ \phi=\phi_{1}+\phi_{2}+\epsilon_{1}\epsilon_{2}(\ldots) $$

and when there are three seed functions the expansion will take the form

$$ \phi=\phi_{1}+\phi_{2}+\phi_{3}+\epsilon_{1}\epsilon_{2}(\ldots)+\epsilon_{1}\epsilon_{3}(\ldots)+\epsilon_{2}\epsilon_{3}(\ldots)+\epsilon_{1}\epsilon_{2}\epsilon_{3}(\ldots). $$

The exact expression for the $(\ldots)$ ’s will be given soon. Note however that the expansion for $N$ seed functions terminates with a highest order term containing all $N$ infinitesimal parameters $\epsilon_{1}\ldots\epsilon_{N}$ .

We now define some useful conventions. We parameterize the momenta with an energy scale $\omega$ and two stereographic coordinates ${\bar{z}},z\in\mathbb{C}$ as

$$ p_{i}^{\mu}\equiv\omega_{i}q^{\mu}({\bar{z}}_{i},z_{i})\equiv\frac{\omega_{i}}{2}(1+z_{i}{\bar{z}}_{i},z_{i}+{\bar{z}}_{i},-i(z_{i}-{\bar{z}}_{i}),1-z_{i}{\bar{z}}_{i}). $$

In lightcone coordinates,

$$ p_{i}\cdot X=\omega_{i}(u+z_{i}{\bar{z}}_{i}{\bar{u}}-{\bar{z}}_{i}w-z_{i}{\bar{w}}). $$

We also define spinor variables

$$ p^{A\dot{A}}=p^{a}\sigma_{a}^{A\dot{A}}=\begin{pmatrix}p^{0}+p^{3}&p^{1}-ip^{2}\\
p^{1}+ip^{2}&p^{0}-p^{3}\end{pmatrix} $$

where $a=0,1,2,3$ are flat space indices. We then decompose the momenta as

$$ p^{A\dot{A}}_{i}=\kappa_{i}^{A}\tilde{\kappa}_{i}^{\dot{A}} $$

with the explicit choice of spinor parameterization

$$ \kappa_{i}^{A}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\
z_{i}\end{pmatrix},\hskip 28.45274pt\tilde{\kappa}_{i}^{\dot{A}}=\omega_{i}\begin{pmatrix}1\\
{\bar{z}}_{i}\end{pmatrix},\hskip 28.45274pt\kappa^{i}_{A}=\begin{pmatrix}-z_{i}\\
1\end{pmatrix},\hskip 28.45274pt\tilde{\kappa}^{i}_{\dot{A}}=\omega_{i}\begin{pmatrix}-{\bar{z}}_{i}\\
1\end{pmatrix}. $$

We have the angle and square brackets

$$ \displaystyle\langle ij\rangle \displaystyle=\varepsilon_{AB}\kappa_{i}^{A}\kappa_{j}^{B}=z_{ij}, \displaystyle[ij] \displaystyle=\varepsilon^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\tilde{\kappa}^{i}_{\dot{A}}\tilde{\kappa}^{j}_{\dot{B}}=-\omega_{i}\omega_{j}{\bar{z}}_{ij}. $$

A full list of spinor conventions can be found in appendix B.1. We also define the spin-2 polarization tensors for the positive and negative helicity gravitons as

$$ \varepsilon^{\mu\nu}_{\pm,i}=\varepsilon^{\mu}_{\pm,i}\varepsilon^{\nu}_{\pm,i},\hskip 28.45274pt\varepsilon^{\mu}_{+,i}=-2i\,\partial_{z}p^{\mu}_{i},\hskip 28.45274pt\varepsilon^{\mu}_{-,i}=\frac{2i}{\omega^{2}}\partial_{\bar{z}}p^{\mu}_{i}, $$

which when necessary are to be raised and lowered with the flat metric. These satisfy $\varepsilon_{+,i}^{A\dot{A}}=2i\,r^{A}\tilde{\kappa}_{i}^{\dot{A}}/\langle\kappa_{i}r\rangle$ and $\varepsilon_{-,i}^{A\dot{A}}=2i\,\kappa_{i}^{A}\tilde{r}^{\dot{A}}/[\tilde{\kappa}_{i}\tilde{r}]$ for $r^{A}=(0,1)$ , $\tilde{r}^{\dot{A}}=(0,1)$ .

Let us now return to our study of the perturbiner expansion for Plebański’s second heavenly equation.

#### Definition 1.

We denote the perturbiner expansion with

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N})\equiv\;\;\begin{matrix}\text{full perturbiner expansion of Plebański}\\
\text{scalar $\phi$ with seed functions }\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N}.\end{matrix} $$

Note the use of the large font.

We will soon show how to write this perturbiner expansion as a sum over marked tree graphs. We now define these graphs.

#### Definition 2.

Let $\mathcal{T}_{N}$ denote the set of marked, connected, tree graphs with $N$ or fewer nodes where each note has a distinct label contained in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ .

#### Example.

.

*Figure 1: Examples of graphs in $\mathcal{T}_{9}$ .*

Next we define a differential operator $\partial_{\mu}^{(i)}$ which only acts on the seed $\phi_{i}$ , but not on $\phi_{j}$ for $i\neq j$ .

$$ \partial_{\mu}^{(i)}\phi_{i}\equiv\partial_{\mu}\phi_{i},\hskip 28.45274pt\partial_{\mu}^{(i)}\phi_{j}\equiv 0\hskip 14.22636pt\text{ for }i\neq j $$

For example

$$ \partial_{\mu}^{(1)}(\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\phi_{3})=(\partial_{\mu}\phi_{1})\phi_{2}\phi_{3}. $$

We then define the differential operator $D^{ij}$ as

$$ D^{ij}\equiv\partial_{u}^{(i)}\partial_{w}^{(j)}-\partial_{u}^{(j)}\partial_{w}^{(i)}. $$

Note, for instance,

$$ D^{12}(\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\phi_{3})=\{\phi_{1},\phi_{2}\}\phi_{3} $$

and

$$ D^{12}D^{12}(\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\phi_{3})=\{\partial_{u}\phi_{1},\partial_{w}\phi_{2}\}\phi_{3}-\{\partial_{w}\phi_{1},\partial_{u}\phi_{2}\}\phi_{3}. $$

Using the operator $D^{ij}$ , we will now explain what an “edge” in one of these graphs corresponds to. Two nodes, labelled $i$ and $j$ , correspond to the two seed functions $\phi_{i}$ and $\phi_{j}$ , while an edge between them corresponds to $D^{ij}/z_{ij}$ , where $z_{i}$ and $z_{j}$ are just the same $z$ ’s which parameterized the momenta in (10).

*Figure 2: A edge in a graph corresponds to $D^{ij}/z_{ij}$ .*

More generally, we can express a term corresponding to an arbitrary graph in the following way.

#### Definition 3.

For each graph $\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}_{N}$ we define the associated term $\phi_{\mathbf{t}}$ via

$$ \phi_{\mathbf{t}}\equiv\left(\prod_{e_{ij}\,\in\,\text{edges of }\mathbf{t}}\frac{D^{ij}}{z_{ij}}\right)\left(\prod_{k\,\in\,\text{nodes of }\mathbf{t}}\phi_{k}\right)\hskip 14.22636pt\text{ for }\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}_{N}. $$

#### Example.

.

*Figure 3: An example of a graph $\mathbf{t}$ and its corresponding $\phi_{\mathbf{t}}$ .*

#### Theorem 2.1.

The complete perturbiner expansion of the Plebański scalar is given by a sum over all marked tree graphs in $\mathcal{T}_{N}$ via

$$ \displaystyle\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N})=\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}}. $$

#### Proof.

To prove this statement, we will plug the above expression into Plebański’s second heavenly equation (2) and check that it is a solution. This boils down to checking

$$ \Box\left(\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}}\right)\overset{?}{=}\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}\sum_{\mathbf{t}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}\big(\left\{\partial_{u}\phi_{\mathbf{t}},\partial_{w}\phi_{\mathbf{t}^{\prime}}\right\}-\left\{\partial_{w}\phi_{\mathbf{t}},\partial_{u}\phi_{\mathbf{t}^{\prime}}\right\}\big). $$

Let us start by evaluating the LHS of (25). Recall that

$$ \Box=\partial_{u}\partial_{\bar{u}}-\partial_{w}\partial_{\bar{w}} $$

and note the relations

$$ \partial_{\bar{u}}\phi_{i}=-z_{i}\partial_{w}\phi_{i},\hskip 28.45274pt\partial_{\bar{w}}\phi_{i}=-z_{i}\partial_{u}\phi_{i}, $$

which hold for our $\phi_{i}$ defined as plane waves (see (11)).

Let us think about what happens when we act $\Box$ on a string of $\phi_{i}$ ’s. Of course, for each $\phi_{i}$ we have $\Box\,\phi_{i}=0$ . Furthermore, using (27), a single line of algebra shows that

$$ \Box(\phi_{i}\phi_{j})=z_{ij}D^{ij}(\phi_{i}\phi_{j}). $$

From the product rule of differentiation, if we act $\Box$ on a longer string of seed functions, say $\phi_{i}\phi_{j}\phi_{k}$ , we must sum over all pairs of the seed functions in the following way:

$$ \Box(\phi_{i}\phi_{j}\phi_{k})=(z_{ij}D^{ij}+z_{jk}D^{jk}+z_{ik}D^{ik})(\phi_{i}\phi_{j}\phi_{k}). $$

Therefore, in order to express the action of $\Box$ using our diagrammatic language, we shall define a new kind of edge, now denoted with a double line, that corresponds to the operator $z_{ij}D^{ij}$ instead of $D^{ij}/z_{ij}$ .

*Figure 4: A edge corresponding to $\Box(\phi_{i}\phi_{j})$ .*

If we act $\Box$ on a sum of graphs (like what we have on the LHS of (25)) we must therefore sum over a different set of marked graphs which we shall now define.

#### Definition 4.

Let $\mathcal{T}^{\Box}_{N}$ denote the set of all graphs which can be constructed by taking a marked tree graph in $\mathcal{T}_{N}$ and placing a single extra double line between two of the nodes.

That is, the “data” of a graph $\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{\Box}_{N}$ is identical to the “data” of a graph $\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}_{N}$ save for the addition of a single double-lined edge. The term $\phi_{\mathbf{t}}$ corresponding to these graphs is given by

$$ \phi_{\mathbf{t}}\equiv\left(z_{ab}D^{ab}\right)\Bigg\rvert_{\begin{subarray}{c}e_{ab}\text{ is}\\
\text{double}\\

We can now write $\Box$ acting on our sum of tree graphs as

$$ \Box\left(\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}}\right)=\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{\Box}_{N}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}}. $$

We now turn to the RHS of (25). Let us begin by exploring what happens when two graphs are placed in two different slots of the Poisson bracket. To represent two seed functions in the Poisson bracket $\{\phi_{i},\phi_{j}\}$ , we would need to create an edge corresponding to $D^{ij}(\phi_{i}\phi_{j})$ . However, due to the antisymmetry of the Poisson bracket ( $D^{ij}=-D^{ji})$ , this edge must be a bit different from the other edges because it must be given an orientation. We display this orientation with an arrow, and draw this particular edge with a wiggly line.

*Figure 5: A edge corresponding to $D^{ij}\phi_{i}\phi_{j}$ .*

Now, say we have two graphs $\mathbf{t}_{\alpha}$ and $\mathbf{t}_{\beta}$ which could look like the following.

What sum of graphs will the expression $\{\phi_{\mathbf{t}_{\alpha}},\phi_{\mathbf{t}_{\beta}}\}$ be? From the product rule of differentiation, the Poisson bracket will be equal to a sum of terms which will correspond to all possible ways a wiggly line could be drawn from a node on $\mathbf{t}_{\alpha}$ to a node on $\mathbf{t}_{\beta}$ . Let us denote such a graph with a wiggly line starting at node $i$ and ending on node $j$ as $\mathbf{t}_{\{\alpha,\beta\}_{ij}}$ .

$$ \{\phi_{\mathbf{t}_{\alpha}},\phi_{\mathbf{t}_{\beta}}\}=\sum_{i\,\in\,\text{nodes of }\mathbf{t}_{\alpha}}\sum_{j\,\in\,\text{nodes of }\mathbf{t}_{\beta}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}_{\{\alpha,\beta\}_{ij}}} $$

Of course, because $(\phi_{i})^{2}=0$ due to the infinitesimal nature of $\epsilon_{i}$ , if there are any shared nodes between the two graphs, the Poisson bracket will actually be zero.

$$ \{\phi_{\mathbf{t}_{\alpha}},\phi_{\mathbf{t}_{\beta}}\}=0\hskip 14.22636pt\text{if }\mathbf{t}_{\alpha}\text{ and }\mathbf{t}_{\beta}\text{ both have a node with the same label}. $$

Now we return to the RHS of (25) as written. We can see that this term contains not just a Poisson bracket, which would correspond to a single wiggly line being drawn between two graphs, but also contains an extra set of $\partial_{u}$ , $\partial_{w}$ derivatives which have the effect of requiring that two wiggly lines be drawn between the two graphs! (See for instance (22).) Let us now give a name to the set of all such graphs.

#### Definition 5.

Let $\mathcal{T}^{P^{2}}_{N}$ denote the set of all graphs which can be constructed by taking two graphs in $\mathcal{T}_{N}$ that share no common nodes and drawing two wiggly lines between them, with each wiggly line connecting one node in one graph to another node in the other graph. The orientation of these two wiggly lines must be arranged such that they both point in the same direction (i.e., from the same one of the original graphs to the other).

We write the term corresponding to a graph in $\mathcal{T}^{P^{2}}_{N}$ as

$$ \phi_{\mathbf{t}}\equiv\left(\prod_{\vec{e}_{ab}\,\in\,\begin{subarray}{c}\text{wiggly}\\
\text{edges of }\mathbf{t}\end{subarray}}D^{ab}\right)\left(\prod_{e_{ij}\,\in\,\begin{subarray}{c}\text{single-lined}\\
\text{edges of }\mathbf{t}\end{subarray}}\frac{D^{ij}}{z_{ij}}\right)\left(\prod_{k\,\in\,\text{nodes of }\mathbf{t}}\phi_{k}\right)\hskip 14.22636pt\text{ for }\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}_{N}^{P^{2}} $$

(where the vector notation $\vec{e}_{ab}$ is used to denote the fact that the wiggly edges have an orientation pointing from $a$ to $b$ ) such that

$$ \frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}\sum_{\mathbf{t}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}\big(\left\{\partial_{u}\phi_{\mathbf{t}},\partial_{w}\phi_{\mathbf{t}^{\prime}}\right\}-\left\{\partial_{w}\phi_{\mathbf{t}},\partial_{u}\phi_{\mathbf{t}^{\prime}}\right\}\big)=\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{P^{2}}_{N}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}}. $$

The factor of $1/2$ accounts for the symmetry factor of 2 associated with the indistinguishability of the two wiggly lines.

Therefore, in order to prove (25), using (31) and (35) we have now shown that it is equivalent to check

$$ \sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}_{N}^{\Box}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}}\overset{?}{=}\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}_{N}^{P^{2}}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}}. $$

Let’s now look at some examples of graphs in $\mathcal{T}_{N}^{\Box}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{N}^{P^{2}}$ and show how we can re-organize the above sums in a way that enables us to prove the above equality.

## 3 Linear perturbations on a SD background

### 3.1 Linear SD perturbations and the recursion operator

Here we study the set of linear perturbations to Plebański’s second scalar. A linear perturbation $\phi+\delta\phi$ satisfies the linearized e.o.m.

$$ \Box\delta\phi-\{\partial_{u}\delta\phi,\partial_{w}\phi\}-\{\partial_{u}\phi,\partial_{w}\delta\phi\}=0. $$

If $\phi$ can be expressed as a perturbiner expansion of some set of seed functions, then we can always construct a $\delta\phi$ which is created by adding in one extra seed function to the set. As a useful piece of notation, let us denote the change in the perturbiner associated to the addition of this single seed function with a vertical line by

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N}\rvert\phi_{I})\equiv\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N},\phi_{I})-\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N}) $$

where $I$ is a new index not contained in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ .

#### Definition 6.

Let $\mathcal{T}_{N|I}$ denote the set of all marked tree graphs, necessarily containing the node $I$ , with distinct node labels in the set $\{1,\ldots,N\}\cup\{I\}$ .

It is straightforward to see that

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N}\rvert\phi_{I})=\sum_{\mathbf{t}\,\in\,\mathcal{T}_{N|I}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}}. $$

Furthermore, as stated above, we know that

$$ \phi=\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N})\,,\hskip 28.45274pt\delta\phi=\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N}\rvert\phi_{I})\,, $$

satisfies (40).

#### Example.

Let us explicitly write out $\delta\phi$ above when $N=2$ , $I=3$ , and draw all the corresponding graphs in $\mathcal{T}_{2|3}$ .

$$ \displaystyle\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\phi_{2}|\phi_{3}) \displaystyle=\phi_{3}+\frac{1}{z_{13}}\{\phi_{1},\phi_{3}\}+\frac{1}{z_{23}}\{\phi_{2},\phi_{3}\} \displaystyle+\frac{D^{12}}{z_{12}}\frac{D^{23}}{z_{23}}\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}+\frac{D^{13}}{z_{13}}\frac{D^{32}}{z_{32}}\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}+\frac{D^{21}}{z_{21}}\frac{D^{13}}{z_{13}}\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\phi_{3} $$

In SDG there exists a certain “recursion operator” $\mathcal{R}$ which is related to the integrability of the theory Dunajski (2009). This operator maps the space of linear perturbations of the Plebański scalar into itself, meaning if $\delta\phi$ satisfies (40) then $\mathcal{R}\delta\phi$ will also satisfy (40).

In particular, $\mathcal{R}\delta\phi$ is defined as the solution to the pair of differential equations

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{u}(\mathcal{R}\delta\phi) \displaystyle=\partial_{\bar{w}}\delta\phi+\{\partial_{u}\phi,\delta\phi\}, \displaystyle\partial_{w}(\mathcal{R}\delta\phi) \displaystyle=\partial_{\bar{u}}\delta\phi+\{\partial_{w}\phi,\delta\phi\}. $$

The compatibility of the two equations (45) follows from the fact that $\delta\phi$ is a linear perturbation of $\phi$ :

$$ \partial_{u}(\partial_{w}(\mathcal{R}\delta\phi))-\partial_{w}(\partial_{u}(\mathcal{R}\delta\phi))=\Box\delta\phi-\{\partial_{u}\delta\phi,\partial_{w}\phi\}-\{\partial_{u}\phi,\partial_{w}\delta\phi\}=0. $$

Furthermore, $\mathcal{R}\delta\phi$ is guaranteed to solve the linearized e.o.m. by

$$ \Box\,\mathcal{R}\delta\phi-\{\partial_{u}\mathcal{R}\delta\phi,\partial_{w}\phi\}-\{\partial_{u}\phi,\partial_{w}\mathcal{R}\delta\phi\}=\{\Box\phi-\{\partial_{u}\phi,\partial_{w}\phi\},\delta\phi\}=0. $$

A explicit set of solutions $\phi$ and $\delta\phi$ was provided by our perturbiner expansion in (43). One might wonder how $\mathcal{R}$ acts on such a $\delta\phi$ . The result is given by the following theorem.

#### Theorem 3.1.

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}\,\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N}\rvert\phi_{I})=-z_{I}\times\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N}\rvert\phi_{I}) $$

#### Proof.

Proving this statement is equivalent to checking the following equality,

$$ \partial_{u}\left(-z_{I}\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}_{N|I}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}}\right)\overset{?}{=}\partial_{{\bar{w}}}\left(\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}_{N|I}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}}\right)+\Big\{\partial_{u}\left(\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}}\right),\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}_{N|I}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}}\Big\} $$

which is the first equation of (45). The second equation will follow by an analogous argument.

Let us think about which graphs appear in each of the three terms in the above equation. In the first term, by the product rule of differentiation, we simply sum over all graphs in $\mathcal{T}_{N|I}$ where $-z_{I}\partial_{u}$ is to “decorate” any of the nodes in the graph. (If $-z_{I}\partial_{u}$ decorates the node $i$ , this amounts to acting with $-z_{I}\partial_{u}^{(i)}$ on the corresponding graph in the perturbiner expansion.) In the second term, we similarly sum over all graphs in $\mathcal{T}_{N|I}$ but decorate one node with $\partial_{{\bar{w}}}$ instead of $-z_{I}\partial_{u}$ . For the third term, we sum over all graphs which consist of a wiggly line pointing from a graph in $\mathcal{T}_{N}$ with a node decorated by $\partial_{u}$ to a graph containing the node $I$ .

Notice that all of the graphs described above have one thing in common: they all contain the node $I$ , and they all contain one “decorated” node, whether that be by $-z_{I}\partial_{u}$ , $\partial_{\bar{w}}$ , or $\partial_{u}$ . Of course, some of the graphs also contain a wiggly line. Let us therefore partition the graphs in groups where all the graphs in each group would look the same if we were to convert any wiggly line into a straight line, and if we were to regard all possible “decorations” as the same. If we can check that all of the graphs contained in such a group satisfy (49), then we are done. An example for a typical set of graphs in such a group is given below in the first line.

Because all of our graphs are tree graphs, there is always exactly one path between any two nodes in the graph. Therefore, there is always one path between the node $I$ and the decorated node. When it comes to the graphs containing a wiggly line, this wiggly line will always lie somewhere on this path.

We then simplify the RHS of the above graphical equation using two facts. The first fact is that $\partial_{{\bar{w}}}\phi_{i}=-z_{i}\partial_{u}\phi_{i}$ , (27). The second fact is that a wiggly line going from $i$ to $j$ can be replaced with a straight line if we multiply by $z_{ij}$ . (See Figures 2 and 5.) The RHS then becomes a numerical factor times the very graph on the LHS. However, if we sum up the numerical factors along the chain from $i$ to $I$ , we see they equal $-z_{I}$ , matching precisely with the LHS and completing the proof. ∎

### 3.2 Linear ASD perturbations

An incredible fact is that linearized anti-self-dual perturbations on a self-dual background satisfy the exact same equation of motion as the linearized self-dual perturbations! This fact will become very important when it comes time to add two negative helicity gravitons to our spacetime and compute the MHV amplitude.

In appendix B we review many basic facts about SDG, and we refer the reader there to find the proofs of the statements below. If we define $\Psi_{ABCD}$ to be the ASD part of the Riemann curvature tensor, then this object satisfies the Bianchi identity

$$ \displaystyle 0=\nabla^{A}_{\;\;\dot{A}}\Psi_{ABCD}=(e^{A}_{\;\;\dot{A}})^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}\Psi_{ABCD} \displaystyle-(\Gamma_{A}^{\;\;\;E})^{A}_{\;\;\dot{A}}\Psi_{EBCD}-(\Gamma_{B}^{\;\;\;E})^{A}_{\;\;\dot{A}}\Psi_{AECD} \displaystyle-(\Gamma_{C}^{\;\;\;E})^{A}_{\;\;\dot{A}}\Psi_{ABED}-(\Gamma_{D}^{\;\;\;E})^{A}_{\;\;\dot{A}}\Psi_{ABCE} $$

where $\Gamma_{AB}$ is the ASD part of the spin connection 1-form and $e_{A\dot{A}}$ denotes a basis of four vierbein vector fields. If $\theta^{A\dot{A}}=\theta^{A\dot{A}}_{\mu}dx^{\mu}$ are a basis of tetrad 1-forms satisfying $ds^{2}=\tfrac{1}{2}\varepsilon_{AB}\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\theta^{A\dot{A}}\theta^{B\dot{B}}$ , then the vierbein is given by $e_{A\dot{A}}^{\mu}=g^{\mu\nu}\varepsilon_{AB}\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\theta^{B\dot{B}}_{\nu}$ . For a SD metric of the form (1), a convenient choice of tetrads is given by

$$ \displaystyle\theta^{1\dot{1}}=2d{\bar{u}}\,, \displaystyle\theta^{2\dot{1}}=2(dw-(\partial_{u}\partial_{w}\phi)d{\bar{u}}-(\partial_{u}^{2}\phi)d{\bar{w}})\,, \displaystyle\theta^{1\dot{2}}=2d{\bar{w}}\,, \displaystyle\theta^{2\dot{2}}=2(du+(\partial_{w}^{2}\phi)d{\bar{u}}+(\partial_{u}\partial_{w}\phi)d{\bar{w}})\,, $$

with the associated vierbein being

$$ \displaystyle e^{\mu}_{1\dot{1}}\partial_{\mu} \displaystyle=\partial_{{\bar{u}}}+(\partial_{u}\partial_{w}\phi)\partial_{w}-(\partial_{w}^{2}\phi)\partial_{u}\,, \displaystyle e^{\mu}_{2\dot{1}}\partial_{\mu} \displaystyle=\partial_{w}\,, \displaystyle e^{\mu}_{1\dot{2}}\partial_{\mu} \displaystyle=\partial_{{\bar{w}}}+(\partial_{u}^{2}\phi)\partial_{w}-(\partial_{u}\partial_{w}\phi)\partial_{u}\,, \displaystyle e^{\mu}_{2\dot{2}}\partial_{\mu} \displaystyle=\partial_{u}\,. $$

In a SD background, $(\Psi_{0})_{ABCD}=0$ and $(\Gamma_{0})_{AB}=0$ for our above choice of vierbein. If we then denote $\psi_{ABCD}$ to be a linearized perturbation around $(\Psi_{0})_{ABCD}$ , it therefore satisfies

$$ 0=(e^{A}_{\;\;\dot{A}})^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}\psi_{ABCD} $$

where $e_{A\dot{A}}$ above is the vierbein of the SD background.

Plugging in the formula for $e_{A\dot{A}}$ , this reduces to the two equations, for $\dot{A}=\dot{1},\dot{2}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\dot{A}=\dot{1}: \displaystyle 0=-\partial_{w}\psi_{1BCD}+\partial_{\bar{u}}\psi_{2BCD}+\{\partial_{w}\phi,\psi_{2BCD}\}\,, \displaystyle\dot{A}=\dot{2}: \displaystyle 0=-\partial_{u}\psi_{1BCD}+\partial_{\bar{w}}\psi_{2BCD}+\{\partial_{u}\phi,\psi_{2BCD}\}\,. $$

After a comparison with (45), we identify that (54) is simply the equation

$$ \psi_{1BCD}=\mathcal{R}\,\psi_{2BCD}. $$

The two equations (54) can be rearranged to show that both $\psi_{1BCD}$ and $\psi_{2BCD}$ satisfy (40) (see (46) and (47)):

$$ \Box\psi_{ABCD}-\{\partial_{u}\psi_{ABCD},\partial_{w}\phi\}-\{\partial_{u}\phi,\partial_{w}\psi_{ABCD}\}=0. $$

Furthermore, Theorem 3.1 tells us that (55) implies $\psi_{1BCD}=-z_{I}\psi_{2BCD}$ , and the index symmetry $\psi_{ABCD}=\psi_{(ABCD)}$ implies

$$ \psi^{I}_{ABCD}=-\frac{1}{8}\,\kappa^{I}_{A}\kappa^{I}_{B}\kappa^{I}_{C}\kappa^{I}_{D}\,\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N}\rvert\phi_{I}) $$

will always be a solution to (54), where $\kappa^{I}_{A}=(-z_{I},1)$ . In fact, this is the solution that corresponds to adding one ASD graviton $h_{\mu\nu}=\epsilon_{I}\varepsilon_{\mu\nu}^{-,I}e^{ip_{I}\cdot X}$ to our SD background! The prefactor of $-1/8$ can be fixed by matching with the trivial $N=0$ case where one ASD graviton is added to flat space.

## 4 Scattering amplitudes and on-shell actions

In this section we briefly review the connection between tree-level scattering amplitudes and on-shell actions. The general idea is that “in” and “out” states can be thought of as boundary conditions for the path integral, and by the stationary phase approximation, if we plug the classical solution with said boundary conditions into the action we compute the transition amplitude to the leading order in $\hbar$ .11 1 There is another way that classical solutions can be used to compute scattering amplitudes in which one leg of a Feynman diagram is taken to be off shell Boulware and Brown (1968); Monteiro and O’Connell (2011). A formalism for computing amplitudes in this way was developed by Arefeva, Faddeev, and Slavnov Arefeva et al. (1974) and was revisited recently in Kim et al. (2023); Kraus and Myers (2024). Further pedagogical treatments can be found in Shrauner et al. (1978); Balian and Zinn-Justin (1976). This formalism is often used to calculate amplitudes in non-trivial backgrounds Adamo et al. (2018); Adamo et al. (2022); Gonzo et al. (2022); Adamo et al. (2023a); Adamo et al. (2024b); Adamo et al. (2024a). See also Fabbrichesi et al. (1994).

For simplicity, say we have a scalar field $\varphi$ which has some self-interaction. A scattering amplitude is defined as

$$ \mathcal{A}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{N})=\bra{0}\hat{a}_{p_{1}}\ldots\hat{a}_{p_{M}}\,\mathcal{S}\,\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{p_{M+1}}\ldots\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{p_{N}}\ket{0}. $$

One can also define finite-amplitude “coherent states”

$$ \displaystyle\bra{A_1, \ldots, A_M} \displaystyle=\bra{0}e^{A_{1}\hat{a}_{p_{1}}}\ldots e^{A_{M}\hat{a}_{p_{M}}}\,, \displaystyle\ket{A_{M+1}, \ldots, A_N} \displaystyle=e^{A_{M+1}\hat{a}_{p_{M+1}}^{\dagger}}\ldots e^{A_{N}\hat{a}_{p_{N}}^{\dagger}}\ket{0}\,, $$

which correspond, classically, to fields that are sums of plane waves with finite amplitudes $A_{i}$ . In a free theory, these are the solutions

$$ \varphi(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}A_{i}e^{ip_{i}\cdot X}. $$

Here we are using a convention in which the energy of $p_{i}^{\mu}$ is positive (negative) for ingoing (outgoing) particles. Therefore, in the above field, the positive frequency part of $\varphi$ which we label $\varphi^{+}$ is determined by the ingoing momenta while the negative frequency part $\varphi^{-}$ is determined by the outgoing momenta.

Using the coherent state path integral, one can in principle compute transition amplitudes between such states in the interacting theory. In the coherent state path integral, the field “paths” one is integrating over are naturally complexified, and it turns out that the initial state is given by specifying the positive-frequency part of the field at $t=-T/2$ and the final state is given by specifying the negative-frequency part of the field at $t=T/2$ :

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{T\to\infty}\varphi^{-}(+T/2) \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{M}A_{i}e^{ip_{i}X},\hskip 14.22636pt\lim_{T\to\infty}\varphi^{+}(-T/2) \displaystyle=\sum_{i=M+1}^{N}A_{i}e^{ip_{i}X}. $$

One must be conscientious about what boundary terms are included in the action $S$ because the fields in the path integral have non-trivial boundary conditions. In principle the boundary terms should be fixed by demanding that the solutions to the e.o.m. render the action stationary given these boundary conditions, but they can also be determined by other means, like by using time-slicing regularization.

$$ \displaystyle\bra{A_1, \ldots, A_M}\mathcal{S}\ket{A_{M+1}, \ldots, A_N}=\lim_{T\to\infty}\int_{\varphi^{+}(-T/2)=\sum_{i=M+1}^{N}A_{i}e^{ip_{i}X}}^{\varphi^{-}(T/2)=\sum_{i=1}^{M}A_{i}e^{ip_{i}X}}\mathcal{D}\varphi\;e^{iS[\varphi]} $$

In the stationary phase approximation, one is instructed to find the $\varphi$ that solves the equation of motion with boundary conditions (69) and plug it into the action. Then, to compute a standard scattering amplitude of elementary quanta at tree-level, one can simply differentiate the on-shell integrand by all of the $A_{i}$ ’s as

$$ \mathcal{A}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{N})=\frac{\partial^{N}}{\partial A_{1}\ldots\partial A_{N}}e^{iS[\varphi]}\Big\rvert_{A_{i}=0\;\forall A_{i}}. $$

Note that because we differentiate by $A_{i}$ and then evaluate $A_{i}=0$ , for all intents and purposes we can replace $A_{i}\mapsto\epsilon_{i}$ such that $(\epsilon_{i})^{2}=0$ when we solve the classical e.o.m.. This justifies our prescription (6).

Furthermore, as $A_{i}\to 0$ , the boundary conditions are dominated by the leading “free” solution (68), as higher order terms in the solution necessary to solve the interacting e.o.m. will be higher order in the $\epsilon_{i}$ ’s. Therefore we are just instructed to find a perturbative solution of the form

$$ \varphi=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\epsilon_{i}e^{ip_{i}X}+\sum_{i<j}\epsilon_{i}\epsilon_{j}(\ldots)e^{i(p_{i}+p_{j})\cdot X}+\ldots $$

which is nothing but a perturbiner expansion, and plug it into the action.

Upon Taylor expanding the exponential in (71), there will be a zeroth order term 1 which will not contribute to the amplitude, a first order term $iS$ , and higher order terms $(iS)^{n}$ . The higher order terms are clearly products of lower-point amplitudes, so if we’re only interested in the connected part of the amplitude we only need to evaluate the action itself:

$$ \mathcal{A}_{\rm connected}(p_{1},\ldots,p_{N})=\frac{\partial^{N}}{\partial\epsilon_{1}\ldots\partial\epsilon_{N}}iS[\varphi]\Big\rvert_{\epsilon_{i}=0\;\forall\epsilon_{i}}. $$

Henceforth, it will be implicitly understood we’re only interested in connected amplitudes and will drop the explicit subscript.

## 5 The Gravitational MHV Amplitude

### 5.1 MHV scattering and the Plebański Action

From the last section, we know that we can compute the graviton MHV amplitude in two steps. First, we must solve for the classical spacetime containing $N$ positive helicity gravitons and 2 negative helicity gravitons. Second, we must plug this spacetime into the action. Actually, using a standard trick we can circumvent having to do some of step 1, which we’ll explain shortly.

The commonly used Einstein-Hilbert (EH) action (with possible boundary terms included) is ill suited for our task because its dependence on the metric is very complicated. A better action for us is the so-called chiral Plebański action, which we’ll now review.

If $\theta^{A\dot{A}}=\theta^{A\dot{A}}_{\mu}dx^{\mu}$ is a basis of tetrad 1-forms, we can define a basis of three ASD 2-forms $\Sigma^{AB}=\Sigma^{(AB)}$ and three SD 2-forms $\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=\widetilde{\Sigma}^{(\dot{A}\dot{B})}$

$$ \Sigma^{AB}\equiv\theta^{A\dot{A}}\wedge\theta^{B}_{\;\;\dot{A}}\,,\hskip 28.45274pt\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\equiv\theta^{A\dot{A}}\wedge\theta_{A}^{\;\;\dot{B}}\,. $$

We’ll also take the spin-connection 1-form $\Gamma_{ab}=\Gamma_{ab\mu}dx^{\mu}$ , satisfying $\Gamma_{ab}=\Gamma_{[ab]}$ , and break it up into ASD and SD parts as

$$ \Gamma_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}}=2\,\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\Gamma_{AB}+2\,\varepsilon_{AB}\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}} $$

with $\Gamma_{AB}=\Gamma_{(AB)}$ and $\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=\widetilde{\Gamma}_{(\dot{A}\dot{B})}$ . From the spin connection one can define the Riemann curvature 2-form $R_{ab}=\differential\Gamma_{ab}+\Gamma_{ac}\wedge\Gamma^{c}_{\;\;b}$ and similarly break it into ASD and SD parts $R_{AB}=R_{(AB)}$ and $\widetilde{R}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=\widetilde{R}_{(\dot{A}\dot{B})}$ . These objects are related to the spin connection by

$$ \displaystyle R_{AB} \displaystyle=\differential\Gamma_{AB}+\Gamma_{AC}\wedge\Gamma^{C}_{\;\;\;B}\,, \displaystyle\widetilde{R}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}} \displaystyle=\differential\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}+\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{C}}\wedge\widetilde{\Gamma}^{\dot{C}}_{\;\;\;\dot{B}}\,. $$

If one uses the vacuum Einstein equation, $R_{AB}$ and $\widetilde{R}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}$ can also be expressed as

$$ \displaystyle R_{AB} \displaystyle=\Psi_{ABCD}\Sigma^{AB}\,, \displaystyle\widetilde{R}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}} \displaystyle=\widetilde{\Psi}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}\dot{C}\dot{D}}\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{C}\dot{D}}\,, $$

using the scalars $\Psi_{ABCD}=\Psi_{(ABCD)}$ and $\widetilde{\Psi}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}\dot{C}\dot{D}}=\widetilde{\Psi}_{(\dot{A}\dot{B}\dot{C}\dot{D})}$ . See appendix B for a more thorough review of these objects.

The EH Lagrangian can be expressed with

$$ \displaystyle 2\,R\,\mathrm{dvol} \displaystyle=\varepsilon_{abcd}R^{ab}\wedge\theta^{c}\wedge\theta^{d} \displaystyle=i\;R_{AB}\wedge\Sigma^{AB}-i\;\widetilde{R}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\wedge\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}} $$

where we have used the identity for the Levi-Civita pseudotensor

$$ \varepsilon_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}C\dot{C}D\dot{D}}=4i\,\varepsilon_{AC}\varepsilon_{BD}\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\varepsilon_{\dot{C}\dot{D}}-4i\,\varepsilon_{AB}\varepsilon_{CD}\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{C}}\varepsilon_{\dot{B}\dot{D}}. $$

The other linear combination of the SD and ASD parts of the curvature 2-form comes from the so-called Holst term,

$$ R_{ab}\wedge\theta^{a}\wedge\theta^{b}=\frac{1}{2}R_{AB}\wedge\Sigma^{AB}+\frac{1}{2}\widetilde{R}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\wedge\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}. $$

In fact, the Holst term is identically zero due to the Bianchi identity $R_{ab}\wedge\theta^{a}=0$ . This implies we can express the EH action as

$$ \frac{1}{2}\int R\,\mathrm{dvol}=\frac{i}{2}\int R_{AB}\wedge\Sigma^{AB}=\frac{i}{2}\int\big(\differential\Gamma_{AB}+\Gamma_{AC}\wedge\Gamma^{C}_{\;\;B}\big)\wedge\Sigma^{AB} $$

where we set $\kappa_{G}^{2}=8\pi G=1$ .

If we want to use the above action on-shell to compute scattering amplitudes, we run into the issue that $R=0$ when $R_{\mu\nu}=0$ . A boundary term must be appended to this action to make it non-zero.

While we would like to provide the reader with a principled derivation of the appropriate boundary term, it is not yet known how to extend the AFS formalism to Einstein gravity using tetrad variables and we will unfortunately not be solving that problem here. However, an eminently natural choice of boundary term is the one which arises by an “integration by parts” in the action,

$$ \displaystyle S[\theta^{A\dot{A}},\Gamma_{AB}] \displaystyle=\frac{i}{2}\int\big(R_{AB}\wedge\Sigma^{AB}-\differential(\Gamma_{AB} \wedge\Sigma^{AB} )\big) \displaystyle=\frac{i}{2}\int\big(\Gamma_{AB}\wedge\differential\Sigma^{AB}+\Gamma_{AC}\wedge\Gamma^{C}_{\;\;B}\wedge\Sigma^{AB}\big)\,. $$

This boundary term has appeared previously in different contexts Corichi and Wilson-Ewing (2010); Corichi and Reyes (2015); Ashtekar et al. (2008); Corichi et al. (2014), see also De Paoli and Speziale (2018).

The action (82) (without boundary term) is known as the Plebański action, and though it only depends on the ASD 2-forms and ASD spin connection it remarkably is still an action for full Einstein gravity Capovilla et al. (1991a); Plebański (1977); Capovilla (1993). It is in fact the Lagrangian counterpart to Ashtekar’s SD Hamiltonian formulation for GR Ashtekar (1987). The equations of motion arising from the variations $\delta\theta^{A\dot{A}}$ and $\delta\Gamma_{AB}$ are

$$ R_{AB}\wedge\theta^{A\dot{A}}=0,\hskip 28.45274pt\differential\Sigma^{AB}=-2\Gamma^{(A}_{\;\;\;\;C}\wedge\Sigma^{B)C}. $$

The first equation is equivalent to the vacuum Einstein equation and the second equation is the first Cartan structure equation. Plugging the second equation of motion (83) into the action, we get the further on-shell expression

$$ S=-\frac{i}{2}\int\big(\Sigma^{AB}\wedge\Gamma_{AC}\wedge\Gamma^{C}_{\;\;B}\big). $$

On a self-dual background, which we’ll denote with the subscript 0, we have the equations

$$ (R_{0})_{AB}=0,\hskip 28.45274pt(\Gamma_{0})_{AB}=0,\hskip 28.45274pt\differential(\Sigma_0)^{AB}=0,\hskip 28.45274pt(\Psi_{0})_{ABCD}=0. $$

Consider a SD background made out of $N$ positive helicity gravitons, and let us define the integers

$$ \displaystyle I \displaystyle\equiv N+1 \displaystyle J \displaystyle\equiv N+2 $$

to be the labels corresponding to the two negative helicity gravitons. A linear perturbation to a SD background $(\gamma_{AB},\psi_{ABCD})\equiv(\delta\Gamma_{AB},\delta\Psi_{ABCD})$ satisfies

$$ \differential\gamma_{AB}=\psi_{ABCD}\Sigma_{0}^{CD},\hskip 42.67912pt\differential\Sigma^{AB}=-2\gamma^{(A}_{\;\;\;\;C}\wedge\Sigma_{0}^{B)C}. $$

Something nice happens if we have two ASD perturbations and wish to evaluate the action. In general, we would expect that we would have to solve for second order, non-linear corrections in $\gamma$ proportional to $\epsilon_{I}\epsilon_{J}$ coming from the two ASD perturbations interacting with each other. However, because $S$ from (84) is quadratic in $\Gamma_{AB}$ , and $(\Gamma_{0})_{AB}=0$ , these second order corrections will not affect the scattering amplitude.

If we define $\gamma^{I}$ and $\gamma^{J}$ to be the linearized ASD perturbations corresponding to the negative helicity gravitons labelled $I$ and $J$ , then by (73) we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{\rm MHV}(1^{+},\ldots,N^{+},I^{-},J^{-}) \displaystyle=\evaluated{ \frac{\partial^{N+2}}{\partial\epsilon_1 \ldots\partial\epsilon_{N+2}} \int(\Sigma_0)^{AB} \wedge(\gamma^{I})_{AC} \wedge(\gamma^{J})^C_{\;\;B} }_{\epsilon_i = 0 \, \forall\epsilon_i}. $$

This is the well-known MHV generating function Mason and Skinner (2010); Adamo et al. (2021). We shall now evaluate it using the marked-tree perturbiner expansion for the Plebański scalar we developed in section 2.

### 5.2 Massaging the MHV generating function

If we wish to evalaute (88), the first task is to compute $\gamma^{I}$ corresponding to the ASD graviton labelled $I$ . From (87), we can do this if we know what $\psi^{I}_{ABCD}$ is.

Fortunately, we have already found the expression for $\psi^{I}_{ABCD}$ in (57) when we noted that $\psi$ solved the same equation of motion as a SD perturbation to $\phi$ in a SD background. We showed that such perturbations can be written as the exponential of a function $F_{I}$ (60), where $F_{I}$ is a sum over a certain special set of graphs (61) which were given in definition 7.

$$ \psi_{ABCD}^{I}=-\frac{1}{8}\,\epsilon_{I}\,\kappa^{I}_{A}\kappa^{I}_{B}\kappa^{I}_{C}\kappa^{I}_{D}\exp(i F_I). $$

With $\psi^{I}_{ABCD}$ in hand, we now just need to find a $\gamma^{I}$ that solves (87). There is a known formula for this Adamo et al. (2023b), which review here in the following claim.

#### Claim 5.1.

$$ (\gamma^{I})_{AB}=-i\epsilon_{I}\kappa^{I}_{A}\kappa^{I}_{B}\frac{\kappa^{I}_{C}\xi_{\dot{C}}(H_{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\;\dot{C}}\theta^{C\dot{A}}}{2[\xi I]}\exp(i F_I) $$

where the tensor $(H^{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\dot{B}}$ is defined by

$$ e_{A\dot{A}}^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}F_{I}^{\dot{B}}=\kappa_{A}^{I}(H^{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\dot{B}}\,, $$

$\xi_{\dot{A}}$ is an arbitrary spinor,22 2 The choice of $\xi$ corresonds to the choice of Lorentz frame for the tetrad. A change in frame sends $\gamma^{I}_{AB}\mapsto\gamma^{I}_{AB}+\differential f_{AB}$ for some zero-form $f_{AB}$ , just as the change $\xi\mapsto a\xi+b\tilde{\kappa}^{I}$ does. and $\theta^{A\dot{A}}$ / $e_{A\dot{A}}$ is the tetrad/vierbein of the SD background.

#### Proof.

To prove this claim, we must show that (90) and (89) solve (87).

We begin by expressing the exterior derivative $\differential$ as

$$ \differential=dx^{\mu}\wedge\partial_{\mu}=\theta^{a}\wedge e_{a}^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}=\frac{1}{2}\theta^{A\dot{A}}\wedge e_{A\dot{A}}^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}. $$

The above expression can be used to rewrite (91) as

$$ 2\;\differential F_{I}^{\dot{B}}=\kappa^{I}_{A}(H^{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\dot{B}}\theta^{A\dot{A}} $$

which implies

$$ \differential\left(\kappa^{I}_{A}(H^{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\dot{B}}\theta^{A\dot{A}}\right)=0. $$

We now act with the expression for $\gamma^{I}$ in (90) by $\differential$ :

$$ \displaystyle\differential(\gamma^I)_{AB} \displaystyle=-i\epsilon_{I}\kappa^{I}_{A}\kappa^{I}_{B}\frac{\kappa^{I}_{C}\xi_{\dot{C}}(H_{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\;\dot{C}}\theta^{C\dot{A}}}{2[\xi I]}\wedge\differential\exp(i F_I) \displaystyle=-i\epsilon_{I}\kappa^{I}_{A}\kappa^{I}_{B}\frac{\kappa^{I}_{C}\xi_{\dot{C}}(H_{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\;\dot{C}}\theta^{C\dot{A}}}{2[\xi I]}\wedge\left(\frac{i}{2}\tilde{\kappa}^{I}_{\dot{B}}\kappa^{I}_{D}(H_{I})_{\dot{D}}^{\;\;\dot{B}}\theta^{D\dot{D}}\right)\exp(i F_I) \displaystyle=\epsilon_{I}\kappa^{I}_{A}\kappa^{I}_{B}\kappa^{I}_{C}\kappa^{I}_{D}\frac{\tilde{\kappa}^{I}_{\dot{B}}\xi_{\dot{C}}}{{4[\xi I]}}\left((H_{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\;\dot{C}}(H_{I})_{\dot{D}}^{\;\;\dot{B}}\theta^{C\dot{A}}\wedge\theta^{D\dot{D}}\right)\exp(i F_I)\,. $$

It turns out that the tensor $(H_{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\dot{B}}$ satisfies the property

$$ (H_{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\dot{C}}(H_{I})_{\dot{D}}^{\;\;\dot{B}}\varepsilon^{\dot{A}\dot{D}}=-\varepsilon^{\dot{B}\dot{C}}. $$

We will show the above equation is true later (see Claim 5.3) but for now use it as a given. (96) implies

$$ \displaystyle(H_{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\;\dot{C}}(H^{I})_{\dot{D}}^{\;\;\dot{B}}\theta^{C\dot{A}}\wedge\theta^{D\dot{D}} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}(H_{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\;\dot{C}}(H^{I})_{\dot{D}}^{\;\;\dot{B}}(\varepsilon^{\dot{A}\dot{D}}\Sigma_{0}^{CD}+\varepsilon^{CD}\widetilde{\Sigma}_{0}^{\dot{A}\dot{D}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon^{\dot{B}\dot{C}}\Sigma_{0}^{CD}-\frac{1}{2}(H_{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\;\dot{C}}(H^{I})_{\dot{D}}^{\;\;\dot{B}}\varepsilon^{CD}\widetilde{\Sigma}_{0}^{\dot{A}\dot{D}} $$

which we can plug into (95) to get

$$ \displaystyle\differential(\gamma^I)_{AB} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{8}\epsilon_{I}\kappa^{I}_{A}\kappa^{I}_{B}\kappa^{I}_{C}\kappa^{I}_{D}\exp(i F_I)\Sigma_{0}^{CD} \displaystyle=\psi^{I}_{ABCD}\Sigma_{0}^{CD} $$

as desired.

∎

The careful reader may have noticed that $(H_{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\dot{B}}$ , defined in (91), was not yet proven to be well-defined. We rectify the situation below.

#### Claim 5.2.

There exists some matrix $(H_{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\dot{B}}$ such that (91) is satisfied.

#### Proof.

We begin with (62), reproduced below

$$ F_{I}=\tilde{\kappa}^{I}_{\dot{A}}F_{I}^{\dot{A}} $$

where $\tilde{\kappa}^{I}_{\dot{A}}=\omega_{I}(-{\bar{z}}_{I},1)$ . Because $F_{I}$ can be written as a sum of graphs where the (diamond) $I$ node only has one edge (see (61)), we know that $F_{I}$ is linear in $\tilde{\kappa}^{I}$ and $F_{I}^{\dot{A}}$ is therefore independent of $\omega_{I}$ and ${\bar{z}}_{I}$ . which we can write as

We now use the explicit formula for the vierbein of the SD background (52),

$$ \displaystyle e^{\mu}_{1\dot{1}}\partial_{\mu} \displaystyle=\partial_{{\bar{u}}}+\{\partial_{w}\phi,\cdot\}=\partial_{w}\mathcal{R}\,, \displaystyle e^{\mu}_{1\dot{2}}\partial_{\mu} \displaystyle=\partial_{{\bar{w}}}+\{\partial_{u}\phi,\cdot\}=\partial_{u}\mathcal{R}\,, \displaystyle e^{\mu}_{2\dot{1}}\partial_{\mu} \displaystyle=\partial_{w}\,, \displaystyle e^{\mu}_{2\dot{2}}\partial_{\mu} \displaystyle=\partial_{u}\,. $$

With the vierbein (102), we may write

$$ \displaystyle e_{A\dot{A}}^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}F_{I}^{\dot{B}}=\frac{1}{\omega_{I}}\evaluated{ \begin{pmatrix} - \partial_{\bz_I} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}^{\dot B} \left( \frac{-i}{e^{i F_I}} ( e_{A \dot A}^\mu\partial_\mu) e^{i F_I} \right) }_{\bz_I = 0}. $$

The key feature of this equation is that, for the $e_{1\dot{A}}$ ’s, we are acting with a recursion operator on the linear perturbation $e^{iF_{I}}$ on the RHS, which we know differs from $e_{2\dot{A}}$ by a relative factor of $-z_{I}$ via claim 3.1.

for some proportionality matrix $(H^{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\dot{B}}$ . This completes the proof. ∎

Note that from $e_{2\dot{1}}=\partial_{w}$ , $e_{2\dot{2}}=\partial_{u}$ , the equation (107) reduces to the simple expression for $(H_{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\dot{B}}$

$$ (H_{I})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\;\dot{B}}=\begin{pmatrix}\partial_{w}\\
\partial_{u}\end{pmatrix}_{\dot{A}}F_{I}^{\dot{B}}. $$

### 5.3 Proof of the NSVW formula

Now that we have an expression for the MHV generating function (112), we can use it to calculate the MHV amplitude (88). In the end, the dependence on the arbitrary reference spinors $\xi_{\dot{A}}$ and $\chi_{\dot{B}}$ will drop out.

We begin by finding a visual representation of the term $\{\xi_{\dot{A}}F_{I}^{\dot{A}},\chi_{\dot{B}}F_{J}^{\dot{B}}\}$ . It will end up being expressed in terms of the following graphs.

#### Definition 9.

Let $\mathcal{T}^{\meddiamond,\xi,\chi}_{N|I,J}$ be the set of graphs which can be formed by taking a graph in $\mathcal{T}_{N}$ and appending to it two diamond nodes with labels $I$ and $J$ , which are connected by a $\xi$ -edge and a $\chi$ -edge, respectively. We also include in $\mathcal{T}^{\meddiamond,\xi,\chi}_{N|I,J}$ the exceptional graph which is just the two diamond nodes $I$ and $J$ connected by a paired $\xi\chi$ -edge.

#### Examples.

Here are some examples of graphs in $\mathcal{T}^{\meddiamond,\xi,\chi}_{N|I,J}$ for $N=7$ .

#### Claim 5.4.

$$ -\{\xi_{\dot{A}}F_{I}^{\dot{A}},\chi_{\dot{B}}F_{J}^{\dot{B}}\}=\langle IJ\rangle\sum_{\mathbf{t}\,\in\,\mathcal{T}^{\meddiamond,\xi,\chi}_{N|I,J}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}} $$

#### Proof.

From the graphical equation for $\xi_{\dot{A}}F_{I}^{\dot{A}}$ (63), we may write the LHS of the above expression as

$$ \displaystyle-\{\xi_{\dot{A}}F_{I}^{\dot{A}},\chi_{\dot{B}}F_{J}^{\dot{B}}\}= \displaystyle\,\{\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{\meddiamond,\xi}_{N|I}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}},\sum_{\mathbf{t}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}^{\meddiamond,\chi}_{N|J}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}^{\prime}}\} \displaystyle-i(\xi_{\dot{1}}\partial_{u}-\xi_{\dot{2}}\partial_{w})\sum_{\mathbf{t}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}^{\meddiamond,\chi}_{N|J}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}^{\prime}}+i(\chi_{\dot{1}}\partial_{u}-\chi_{\dot{2}}\partial_{w})\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{\meddiamond,\xi}_{N|I}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}} \displaystyle+[\xi\chi] $$

where we used the fact that

$$ -\{\xi_{\dot{1}}(w-z_{I}{\bar{u}})+\xi_{\dot{2}}(u-z_{I}{\bar{w}}),\chi_{\dot{1}}(w-z_{I}{\bar{u}})+\chi_{\dot{2}}(u-z_{I}{\bar{w}})\}=[\xi\chi]. $$

There are now four types of graphs to be summed, arising from the four terms in the RHS of (115).

The first type of graph, corresponding to the first term, is constructed by taking two graphs in $\mathcal{T}^{\meddiamond,\xi}_{N|I}$ and $\mathcal{T}^{\meddiamond,\chi}_{N|J}$ and drawing one wiggly line from a circle node in the first graph to a circle node in the second graph. A typical example of such a graph we should sum over is shown below.

#### Definition 13.

However, this expression has an issue: it is not invariant under rescalings of the spinor variables $|i\rangle\mapsto t|i\rangle$ , $|i]\mapsto t^{-1}|i]$ because the graphs we are summing over have different little group weights for the various spinor variables. The above equation only holds for our particular spinor parameterization (14), and would fail if we were to rescale the spinors.

To remedy this, we shall now add two auxiliary spinors $|\iota\rangle$ and $|o\rangle$ to this expression to make it reparameterization invariant. We start by setting

$$ \iota^{A}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\
1\end{pmatrix},\hskip 28.45274pto^{A}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\
1\end{pmatrix}, $$

such that in our parameterization (14)

$$ \langle\iota i\rangle=\langle oi\rangle=1. $$

We now multiply our amplitude by $1$ in such a way that the final expression has the correct little group weights. The resulting amplitude (with $\mathcal{A}=i(2\pi)^{4}\delta^{(4)}(\ldots)\mathcal{M}$ ) is

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{\rm MHV}= \displaystyle-\frac{\langle IJ\rangle^{4}\langle I\iota\rangle\langle Io\rangle\langle J\iota\rangle\langle Jo\rangle}{[\xi I][\chi J]}\left(\sum_{\mathbf{t}\in\mathcal{T}^{\xi,\chi,\mathrm{max}}_{N|I,J}}K(\mathbf{t})\prod_{e_{ij}\,\in\,\text{edges of }\mathbf{t}}\frac{[ij]}{\langle ij\rangle}\prod_{a=1}^{N+2}\Big(\langle a\iota\rangle\langle ao\rangle\Big)^{\mathrm{deg}(a)-2}\right) $$

where $\mathrm{deg}(a)$ is defined as the number of edges connected to node $a$ . The above expression now has the correct little group weights of $+4$ for $I$ and $J$ , and $-4$ for all $i\neq I,J$ , and 0 for $\iota$ , $o$ , $\xi$ , and $\chi$ . To check the value of all the weights, one must use

$$ \sum_{a\,\in\,\text{nodes of }\mathbf{t}}(\mathrm{deg}(a)-2)=-2 $$

which holds for any connected tree diagram $\mathbf{t}$ .

(127) is in fact a new generalization of the NSVW formula. It is expressed as a sum over trees where all $N+2$ gravitons have a corresponding node, instead of just the $N$ positive helicity gravitons as in the NSVW formula. It should be emphasized, however, that the two negative helicity graviton nodes $I$ and $J$ obey different rules from the other nodes, as one of each of their edges depends on a reference spinor $\xi$ and $\chi$ respectively. We now show how it can be reduced to the NSVW formula.

#### Claim 5.6.

Equation (127) does not depend on the reference spinors $|\iota\rangle$ and $|o\rangle$ .

#### Proof.

Without loss of generality we focus on $|\iota\rangle$ . Because the expression is invariant under the rescaling of $|\iota\rangle$ , we can think of the two components $(\iota_{1},\iota_{2})$ as homogenous coordinates and the expression (127) as a function on $\mathbb{C}P^{1}$ . We can therefore prove that (127) is constant as a function of $|\iota\rangle$ if we show that the expression has no poles in $|\iota\rangle$ .

The only potential poles occur for $\langle i\iota\rangle\to 0$ when $i\neq I,J$ and $i$ is a node with $\mathrm{deg}(i)=1$ . Clearly, all graphs where $\mathrm{deg}(i)=1$ can be formed by taking a graph without $i$ and appending $i$ to any of the pre-existing $N+1$ nodes the graph. Summing over the $N+1$ possible nodes we could append $i$ to introduces a multiplicative factor of

$$ \frac{1}{\langle i\iota\rangle\langle io\rangle}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=1\\
j\neq i\end{subarray}}^{N+2}\frac{[ij]}{\langle ij\rangle}\langle j\iota\rangle\langle jo\rangle $$

to an otherwise nonsingular term. But then notice that the residue of the amplitude is

$$ \displaystyle\underset{\langle i\iota\rangle\to 0}{\Res}\mathcal{M}_{\rm MHV} \displaystyle=\underset{\langle i\iota\rangle\to 0}{\Res}\left(\frac{1}{\langle i\iota\rangle\langle io\rangle}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=1\\
j\neq i\end{subarray}}^{N+2}\frac{[ij]}{\langle ij\rangle}\langle j\iota\rangle\langle jo\rangle\right)(\text{non sing.}) \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{\langle io\rangle}[i|\left(\sum_{j=1}^{N+2}|j]\langle j|\right)|o\rangle(\text{non sing.})=0 $$

and vanishes due to momentum conservation. The overall function therefore has no poles in $|\iota\rangle$ , completing the proof. ∎

Using Claim 5.6, we can now redefine the auxiliary spinors to be

$$ |\iota\rangle\to|I\rangle,\hskip 28.45274pt|o\rangle\to|J\rangle, $$

without changing the amplitude.

## 6 Discussion

In this work, we developed a perturbiner expansion for Plebański’s second heavenly equation which was written as a sum over marked tree graphs, given in Theorem 2.1. This allowed us to explicitly write down expressions for spacetime metrics containing arbitrary numbers of positive helicity gravitons in the Plebański gauge (1). This gauge is particularly natural because it can be thought of as an exact, non-linear version of transverse traceless gauge, satisfying

$$ \eta^{\mu\nu}h_{\mu\nu}=g^{\mu\nu}h_{\mu\nu}=0,\hskip 28.45274pt\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\mu}h_{\nu\rho}=g^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\mu}h_{\nu\rho}=0. $$

Using this perturbiner expansion we were able to write down visual formulae for a variety of mathematical objects familiar to the study of self-dual gravity, and we were able to manipulate and combine these formulae in useful ways using a relatively small number of graphical tricks. Ultimately, this allowed us to give a self contained proof of the NSVW formula for graviton MHV scattering.

While we have not computed any amplitudes aside from MHV, it seems likely that our marked tree expansion could be a useful tool in the computation of other amplitudes. We leave this for future work.

Our tree diagrams strongly resonate with other tree diagrams that have appeared previously Adamo et al. (2021); Adamo and Mason (2013); Adamo and Mason (2014); Adamo (2013); Cao and Zhang (2023); Adamo and Klisch (2024). Notably, Adamo et al. (2021) proved the NSVW/Hodges’ formula utilizing a similar looking set of diagrams which have an unclear relationship to our diagrams. The main difference between their proof of NSVW and our proof is that their proof was based upon the use of the first Plebański scalar (also known as the Kähler scalar), whereas our work is based upon the use of the second Plebański scalar. Due to their use of the first scalar, they were able to choose a gauge in which the expressions for the ASD spin connections $\gamma^{I}$ and $\gamma^{J}$ became trivial, whereas in this work a good deal of effort was expended accounting for the spin connections.

The unique offering of this paper is a new theory of the second scalar. What interpretation our formulae have in twistor-theoretic terms will be left for future work. Perhaps the use of the second scalar may be advantageous in certain situations.

## Appendix A A binary tree expansion for Plebański’s second heavenly equation

In section 2, we saw the perturbiner expansion for $\phi$ given $N$ seed functions could be written as a sum over trees in $\mathcal{T}_{N}$ . We will now turn our attention to a different (but related) method of expressing the perturbiner expansion based a recursion relation. Essentially, if one knows what the perturbiner expansion is for $N-1$ gravitons, there is a formula which allows one to find the expansion for $N$ gravitons.

In order to write down this recursive formula, we must first break up our perturbiner expansion into a sum of sub-terms labelled by the seed functions present in that term. We will denote these sub-terms as $\phi^{(k)}$ , with $1\leq k\leq N$ , where $\phi^{(k)}$ depends linearly on $k$ seed functions appearing in its arguments.

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}\,(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N})=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\}\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}\end{subarray}}\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(k)}(\phi_{i_{1}},\ldots,\phi_{i_{k}}) $$

#### Example.

For $N=1$ ,

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1})=\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(1)}(\phi_{1}) $$

where

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(1)}(\phi_{i})=\phi_{i}. $$

For $N=2$ ,

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})=\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(1)}(\phi_{1})+\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(1)}(\phi_{2})+\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(2)}(\phi_{1},\phi_{2}) $$

where

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(2)}(\phi_{i},\phi_{j})=\frac{D^{ij}}{z_{ij}}\phi_{i}\phi_{j}. $$

For $N=3$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}(\phi_{1},\phi_{2},\phi_{3}) \displaystyle=\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(1)}(\phi_{1})+\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(1)}(\phi_{2})+\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(3)}(\phi_{3}) \displaystyle+\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(2)}(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})+\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(2)}(\phi_{2},\phi_{3})+\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(2)}(\phi_{1},\phi_{3}) \displaystyle+\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(3)}(\phi_{1},\phi_{2},\phi_{3}) $$

where

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(3)}(\phi_{i},\phi_{j},\phi_{k})=\left(\frac{D^{ij}}{z_{ij}}\frac{D^{jk}}{z_{jk}}+\frac{D^{ik}}{z_{ik}}\frac{D^{kj}}{z_{kj}}+\frac{D^{ji}}{z_{ji}}\frac{D^{ik}}{z_{ik}}\right)\phi_{i}\phi_{j}\phi_{k}. $$

Notice that the $\phi^{(N)}$ expansion of $N$ seed functions is a sum of all marked tree graphs in $\mathcal{T}^{\rm max}_{N}$ , which are graphs that contain all $N$ labeled nodes.

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(N)}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N})=\sum_{\mathbf{t}\,\in\,\mathcal{T}^{\rm max}_{N}}\phi_{\mathbf{t}}. $$

We are now ready to give the recursive formula which allows one to solve for the perturbiner expansion of $N$ particles in terms of the perturbiner expansion of $N-1$ particles. We note that it is closely related to the “inverse soft” construction Krasnov and Scarinci (2013).

#### Theorem A.1.

$$ \displaystyle\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(N)}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N})=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(N-1)}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N-1})\bigg\rvert_{\displaystyle{\phi_{i}\mapsto\frac{1}{z_{iN}}\{\phi_{i},\phi_{N}\}}} $$

#### Proof.

Let us first explain the notation used in the above formula. On the right we have a sum over all $N-1$ original seed functions $\phi_{i}$ where we replace them with $\tfrac{1}{z_{iN}}\{\phi_{i},\phi_{N}\}$ . This means that if a term in the original expression includes a certain set of seed functions with a certain set of derivatives acting on $\phi_{i}$ , then we must replace $\phi_{i}$ with $\tfrac{1}{z_{iN}}\{\phi_{i},\phi_{N}\}$ in the term such that those same derivatives are now to act on $\tfrac{1}{z_{iN}}\{\phi_{i},\phi_{N}\}$ instead. However, all of the pre-existing factors of $1/{z_{ij}}$ , corresponding to nodes $j$ which previously attached to $i$ , will remain the same.

In order to understand this recursive operation diagrammatically, so that we may prove it, we will need to introduce two new objects to our graphical dictionary.

The first new object we define is a straight lined edge with an arrow on it. This edge works quite differently than all previous edges.

In the edge above, if another node $k$ connects to the node $j$ , then one should not multiply the graph by $1/z_{jk}$ as per usual, but one should rather multiply it by $1/z_{ik}$ . The numerator, $D^{jk}$ , should stay the same.
