*Figure 13: An example of how a binary tree graph can be converted into an object built from gray dotted circles, which should be thought of as a sum over a certain type of graph.*

To explain how the gray dotted circle notation works in this context, if an edge is shared between two gray dotted circles, then one is instructed to sum over all possible connections of that edge to all pairs of nodes, where one node is contained in one circle and the other node is contained in the other circle. One example of a graph to we should include in the sum is given below:

We reiterate that the kinds of marked graphs which arise from this procedure are not the graphs of $\mathcal{T}_{N}^{\rm max}$ , due to the special $ab$ -labelled edges.

In any case, the full term which Figure 13 corresponds to is

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{z_{14}}\frac{1}{z_{45}}\frac{1}{z_{12}}\frac{1}{z_{32}}\{\{\phi_{1},\{\phi_{4},\phi_{5}\}\},\{\phi_{3},\phi_{2}\}\}= \displaystyle\frac{1}{z_{14}}\frac{1}{z_{45}}\frac{1}{z_{12}}\frac{1}{z_{32}}D^{45}D^{32}(D^{15}+D^{14})(D^{12}+D^{13}+D^{42}+D^{43}+D^{52}+D^{53})\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\phi_{3}\phi_{4}\phi_{5}. $$

It is interesting to note that this recursive formula has a similar flavor to a Ward identity in a conformal field theory.

One might wonder if this binary tree expansion of $\phi^{(N)}$ can be used to prove any facts which are difficult to see using the marked tree graphs of $\mathcal{T}_{N}^{\rm max}$ . Indeed it can, and here is one such fact we’ll give as an application.

#### Claim A.1.

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(N)}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N})=0\hskip 14.22636pt\text{if}\hskip 14.22636pt\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}^{\mu}=0 $$

#### Proof.

Before beginning the proof, it is worth noting that the equation $\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}^{\mu}=0$ , which colloquially one might say corresponds to “momentum conservation,” is not a requirement for a perturbiner expansion to solve the classical equations of motion. One is always allowed to perturbatively solve the classical equations of motion using any collection of seed functions as long as $p_{i}^{2}=0$ for all $i$ .

In any case, the condition that the momenta sum to zero is equivalent to the four equations

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{N}\omega_{i}=0,\hskip 21.33955pt\sum_{i=1}^{N}\omega_{i}{\bar{z}}_{i}=0,\hskip 21.33955pt\sum_{i=1}^{N}\omega_{i}z_{i}=0,\hskip 21.33955pt\sum_{i=1}^{N}\omega_{i}z_{i}{\bar{z}}_{i}=0. $$

Using the first two of the above equations, one can show that, for any $j\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ , we have

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{N}\omega_{i}{\bar{z}}_{ij}=0. $$

Now, let us think about the final step in evaluating any particular binary tree in the diagrammatic expansion. At the highest level, every graph will always look like two large gray dotted circles with a “12” labelled edge connecting them. Let us call the collection of nodes in the two circles $A$ and $B$ , such that $1\in A$ , $2\in B$ , and

$$ A\cup B=\{1,\ldots,N\}. $$

A schematic representation of the graph, (where the exact sub-structure contained within each of the two largest dotted circles is supressed) is drawn below.

Noting that

$$ D^{ij}\phi_{1}\ldots\phi_{N}=-(\omega_{i}\omega_{j}{\bar{z}}_{ij})\phi_{1}\ldots\phi_{N} $$

we can see that, by implementing the final sum over these pairs of nodes, we have

$$ \raisebox{0.0pt}{\Large$\phi$}^{(N)}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N})\propto\frac{1}{z_{12}}\left(-\sum_{i\in A}\sum_{j\in B}\omega_{i}\omega_{j}{\bar{z}}_{ij}\right)\phi_{1}\ldots\phi_{N} $$

where the sub-structure of the graphs contained within each of the two largest gray dotted circles only affects $\phi^{(N)}$ by a multiplicative factor.

Let us now rewrite (156) as

$$ \sum_{i\in A}\omega_{i}\omega_{j}{\bar{z}}_{ij}+\sum_{i\in B}\omega_{i}\omega_{j}{\bar{z}}_{ij}=0. $$

Summing $j$ in the above equation over all values in $B$ , we get

$$ 0=\sum_{j\in B}\left(\sum_{i\in A}\omega_{i}\omega_{j}{\bar{z}}_{ij}+\sum_{i\in B}\omega_{i}\omega_{j}{\bar{z}}_{ij}\right)=\sum_{j\in B}\sum_{i\in A}\omega_{i}\omega_{j}{\bar{z}}_{ij} $$

where the second term vanished due to antisymmetry. We finish the proof by plugging the above expression into (159). ∎

## Appendix B A crash course in self-dual gravity

The purpose of this section is to provide the background necessary to understand and prove all of the key equations of self-dual gravity used in this paper. We begin with a collection of spinor conventions in section B.1, review the tetrad formalism for Einstein gravity in section B.2, and conclude with the proof of Plebański’s first and second heavenly equations in section B.3.

We use Greek letters for curved space indices, $\mu,\nu=0,1,2,3$ , Latin letters $a,b=0,1,2,3$ for vierbein indices, and upper case letters for spin indices, $A,B=1,2$ , $\dot{A},\dot{B}=\dot{1},\dot{2}$ .

### B.1 Spinor conventions

We use the $\eta_{ab}=\text{diag}(+$ $-$ $-$ $-)$ convention. We define the 2d antisymmetric tensors $\varepsilon_{AB}$ , $\varepsilon^{AB}$ , $\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}$ , $\varepsilon^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}$ by

$$ \varepsilon^{12}=-\varepsilon_{12}=\varepsilon^{\dot{1}\dot{2}}=-\varepsilon_{\dot{1}\dot{2}}=1 $$

such that

$$ \varepsilon_{AB}\varepsilon^{BC}=\delta_{A}^{C},\hskip 28.45274pt\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\varepsilon^{\dot{B}\dot{C}}=\delta_{\dot{A}}^{\dot{C}}. $$

We raise and lower spinors from the left as

$$ \lambda_{A}=\varepsilon_{AB}\lambda^{B}=\varepsilon_{AB}(\varepsilon^{BC}\lambda_{C}). $$

We define the four-vector of Pauli matrices as

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{a}^{A\dot{A}} \displaystyle\equiv(1,\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y},\sigma_{z})\,, \displaystyle\sigma^{a}_{A\dot{A}} \displaystyle=(1,\sigma_{x},-\sigma_{y},\sigma_{z})\,, $$

where $\sigma^{a}_{A\dot{A}}=\varepsilon_{AB}\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\eta^{ab}\sigma_{b}^{B\dot{B}}$ . Note the identities

$$ \displaystyle\sigma^{a}_{A\dot{A}}\sigma_{a}^{B\dot{B}}=2\delta_{A}^{B}\delta_{\dot{A}}^{\dot{B}}\,,\hskip 28.45274pt\sigma^{a}_{A\dot{A}}\sigma^{A\dot{A}}_{b}=2\delta^{a}_{b}\,, $$

which allow us to go back and forth between objects with flat space indices $V^{a}$ and their corresponding objects with spinor indices $V^{A\dot{A}}$ via

$$ V^{A\dot{A}}=\sigma_{a}^{A\dot{A}}V^{a},\hskip 28.45274ptV^{a}=\frac{1}{2}\sigma^{a}_{A\dot{A}}V^{A\dot{A}},\hskip 28.45274ptV_{A\dot{A}}=\sigma^{a}_{A\dot{A}}V_{a},\hskip 28.45274ptV_{a}=\frac{1}{2}\sigma_{a}^{A\dot{A}}V_{A\dot{A}}. $$

Note the relation $V^{a}V_{a}=\frac{1}{2}V^{A\dot{A}}V_{A\dot{A}}$ . We further define the matrices

$$ \displaystyle(\sigma_{ab})^{A}_{\;\;B} \displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{4}\left(\sigma_{a}^{A\dot{C}}\sigma_{bB\dot{C}}-\sigma_{b}^{A\dot{C}}\sigma_{aB\dot{C}}\right)\,, \displaystyle(\widetilde{\sigma}_{ab})_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\dot{B}} \displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{4}\left({\sigma}_{aC\dot{A}}\sigma_{b}^{C\dot{B}}-{\sigma}_{bC\dot{A}}\sigma_{a}^{C\dot{B}}\right)\,, $$

which satisfy the respective anti-self-duality and self-duality equations

$$ \displaystyle(\sigma_{ab})_{A}^{\;\;B} \displaystyle=-\frac{i}{2}\varepsilon_{abcd}(\sigma^{cd})_{A}^{\;\;B}\,, \displaystyle(\widetilde{\sigma}_{ab})^{\dot{A}}_{\;\;\dot{B}} \displaystyle=\frac{i}{2}\varepsilon_{abcd}(\widetilde{\sigma}^{cd})^{\dot{A}}_{\;\;\dot{B}}\,. $$

The above identities can be used to decompose any antisymmetric rank-2 tensor $F_{ab}=F_{[ab]}$ into its ASD and SD parts using the following observation. Note that $F_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}}$ can always be written as

$$ \displaystyle F_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}}=M_{(AB)(\dot{A}\dot{B})}+N_{[AB][\dot{A}\dot{B}]}+P_{(AB)[\dot{A}\dot{B}]}+Q_{[AB](\dot{A}\dot{B})}. $$

The antisymmetry condition $F_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}}=-F_{B\dot{B}A\dot{A}}$ requires that the first two terms must be zero. Furthermore, because $\varepsilon$ is the unique 2d antisymmetric tensor up to scaling, we know that the above equation may be written as

$$ F_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}}=2\,F_{AB}\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}+2\,\widetilde{F}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\varepsilon_{AB} $$

where $F_{AB}=F_{(AB)}$ and $\widetilde{F}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=\widetilde{F}_{(\dot{A}\dot{B})}$ are some symmetric tensors. In fact, these objects can be computed from $F_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}}$ via

$$ F_{AB}=-\frac{1}{4}\varepsilon^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}F_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}},\hskip 28.45274pt\widetilde{F}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=-\frac{1}{4}\varepsilon^{AB}F_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}}. $$

Writing

$$ \displaystyle F_{ab} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sigma_{a}^{\dot{A}A}\sigma_{b}^{\dot{B}B}(F_{AB}\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}+\widetilde{F}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\varepsilon_{AB}) \displaystyle=(\sigma_{ab})^{AB}F_{AB}-(\widetilde{\sigma}_{ab})^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\widetilde{F}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}} $$

we identify $F_{AB}$ as the ASD part of $F_{ab}$ and $\widetilde{F}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}$ as the SD part of $F_{ab}$ .

### B.2 The tetrad formalism with spinor indicies

Here we review the vierbein/tetrad formulation of general relativity.

We take the vierbeins $e_{a}=e_{a}^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}$ to be a set of four vector fields satisfying

$$ g_{\mu\nu}e_{a}^{\mu}e_{b}^{\nu}=\eta_{ab}. $$

If we also define the tetrad 1-forms $\theta^{a}=\theta^{a}_{\mu}\,dx^{\mu}$ via

$$ \theta^{a}_{\mu}\equiv g_{\mu\nu}\eta^{ab}e_{b}^{\nu} $$

then we can write the metric components as

$$ g_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{ab}\theta^{a}_{\mu}\theta^{b}_{\nu}. $$

Note the identities $\delta^{a}_{b}=\theta_{\mu}^{a}e_{b}^{\mu}$ and $\delta^{\mu}_{\nu}=e_{a}^{\mu}\theta^{a}_{\nu}$ .

One can define the object $\Gamma^{a}_{cb}$ via the parallel transport of the vierbeins along each other as

$$ \nabla_{e_{c}}e_{b}=\Gamma^{a}_{cb}e_{a} $$

where the explicit formula for $\Gamma^{a}_{cb}$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma^{a}_{cb}=e^{a}_{\;\mu}e_{c}^{\;\nu}(\partial_{\nu}e_{b}^{\;\mu}+\Gamma^{\mu}_{\nu\rho}e_{b}^{\;\rho}). $$

Using $\Gamma^{a}_{cb}$ , we can define the spin-connection 1-form $\Gamma^{a}_{\;\;b}$ by

$$ \Gamma^{a}_{\;b}\equiv\Gamma^{a}_{cb}\theta^{c}. $$

One can show (see for instance Tong (2019)) that

$$ \Gamma_{ab}=-\Gamma_{ba} $$

meaning that the components of $\Gamma_{ab}$ represent infinitesimal Lorentz generators which lie in $\mathfrak{so}(1,3)$ .

We now define the curvature 2-form

$$ R_{ab}\equiv\frac{1}{2}e_{a}^{\mu}e_{b}^{\nu}R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}dx^{\rho}\wedge dx^{\sigma}. $$

Cartan’s structure equations relate $\theta^{a}$ and $R_{ab}$ to the spin connection via

$$ \displaystyle\differential\theta^{a} \displaystyle=-\Gamma^{a}_{\;\;b}\wedge\theta^{b}\,, \displaystyle R_{ab} \displaystyle=\differential\Gamma_{ab}+\Gamma_{ac}\wedge\Gamma^{c}_{\;\;b}\,. $$

In the tetrad formalism, we can write the first Bianchi identity, the vacuum Einstein equation, and the second Bianchi identity, as

$$ \displaystyle R_{ab}\wedge\theta^{a}=0\hskip 28.45274pt \displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\hskip 28.45274ptR_{\mu[\nu\rho\sigma]}=0 \displaystyle\varepsilon_{abcd}R^{ab}\wedge\theta^{c}=0\hskip 28.45274pt \displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\hskip 28.45274ptR_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}R=0 \displaystyle\differential R_{ab}+2\,\Gamma^{c}_{\;\;(a}\wedge R_{b)c}=0\hskip 28.45274pt \displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\hskip 28.45274pt\nabla_{[\mu}R_{\nu\rho]\sigma\lambda}=0 $$

where the above conversions require the identity

$$ \varepsilon^{\mu\nu\alpha\beta}\varepsilon_{\gamma\delta\rho\sigma}=-4!\,\delta^{[\mu}_{\gamma}\delta^{\nu}_{\delta}\delta^{\alpha}_{\rho}\delta^{\beta]}_{\sigma}. $$

as well as

$$ \varepsilon_{abcd}=e_{a}^{\mu}e_{b}^{\nu}e_{c}^{\rho}e_{d}^{\sigma}\varepsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma},\hskip 28.45274ptdx^{\mu}\wedge dx^{\nu}\wedge dx^{\rho}\wedge dx^{\sigma}=-\varepsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\mathrm{dvol}. $$

Because $R_{ab}=R_{[ab]}$ , we can decompose the ASD and SD parts of the $a$ , $b$ indices

$$ R_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}}=2\,R_{AB}\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}+2\,\widetilde{R}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\varepsilon_{AB} $$

with $R_{AB}=R_{(AB)}$ and $\widetilde{R}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=\widetilde{R}_{(\dot{A}\dot{B})}$ . We do the same thing with the spin connection

$$ \Gamma_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}}=2\,\Gamma_{AB}\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}+2\,\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\varepsilon_{AB} $$

where $\Gamma_{AB}=\Gamma_{(AB)}$ and $\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=\widetilde{\Gamma}_{(\dot{A}\dot{B})}$ .

It is worth reviewing what this split of Lorentz generators into ASD and SD parts means explicitly. Recall that $\mathfrak{so}(1,3)=\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})\times\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})$ , which can be seen by redefining the generators in the following way. If $j_{i},k_{i}\in\mathfrak{so}(1,3)$ , for $i=1,2,3$ , are the usual $4\times 4$ rotation and boost matrices satisfying

$$ [j_{i},j_{j}]=\varepsilon_{ijk}j_{k},\hskip 28.45274pt[j_{i},k_{j}]=\varepsilon_{ijk}k_{k},\hskip 28.45274pt[k_{i},k_{j}]=-\varepsilon_{ijk}j_{k} $$

then

$$ \begin{split}\ell_{0}&=\frac{1}{2}(-k_{3}-ij_{3})\,,\\
\ell_{1}&=\frac{1}{2}(-k_{1}+j_{2}-i(k_{2}+j_{1}))\,,\\
\ell_{-1}&=\frac{1}{2}(k_{1}+j_{2}-i(k_{2}-j_{1}))\,,\end{split}\quad\quad\quad\begin{split}\bar{\ell}_{0}&=\frac{1}{2}(-k_{3}+ij_{3})\,,\\
\bar{\ell}_{1}&=\frac{1}{2}(-k_{1}+j_{2}+i(k_{2}+j_{1}))\,,\\
\bar{\ell}_{-1}&=\frac{1}{2}(k_{1}+j_{2}+i(k_{2}-j_{1}))\,,\end{split} $$

satisfy

$$ [\ell_{m},\ell_{n}]=(m-n)\ell_{m+n}\,,\hskip 28.45274pt[\bar{\ell}_{m},\bar{\ell}_{n}]=(m-n)\bar{\ell}_{m+n}\,,\hskip 28.45274pt[\ell_{m},\bar{\ell}_{n}]=0\,, $$

and of course $(\ell_{n})_{ab}=-(\ell_{n})_{ba}$ , $(\bar{\ell}_{n})_{ab}=-(\bar{\ell}_{n})_{ba}$ . The entries of these matrices are

$$ \displaystyle(\ell_{0})^{a}_{\;\;b}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&-1\\
\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}i&\phantom{-}0\\
\phantom{-}0&-i&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0\\
-1&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0\end{pmatrix},\hskip 7.11317pt(\ell_{1})^{a}_{\;\;b}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\phantom{-}0&-1&-i&\phantom{-}0\\
-1&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}1\\
-i&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}i\\
\phantom{-}0&-1&-i&\phantom{-}0\end{pmatrix},\hskip 7.11317pt(\ell_{-1})^{a}_{\;\;b}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\phantom{-}0&1&-i&\phantom{-}0\\
\phantom{-}1&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}1\\
-i&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&-i\\
\phantom{-}0&-1&\phantom{-}i&\phantom{-}0\end{pmatrix}, \displaystyle(\overline{\ell}_{0})^{a}_{\;\;b}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&-1\\
\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&-i&\phantom{-}0\\
\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}i&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0\\
-1&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0\end{pmatrix},\hskip 7.11317pt(\overline{\ell}_{1})^{a}_{\;\;b}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\phantom{-}0&-1&\phantom{-}i&\phantom{-}0\\
-1&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}1\\
\phantom{-}i&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&-i\\
\phantom{-}0&-1&\phantom{-}i&\phantom{-}0\end{pmatrix},\hskip 7.11317pt(\overline{\ell}_{-1})^{a}_{\;\;b}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}1&\phantom{-}i&\phantom{-}0\\
\phantom{-}1&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}1\\
\phantom{-}i&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}0&\phantom{-}i\\
\phantom{-}0&-1&-i&\phantom{-}0\end{pmatrix}. $$

The independent $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})$ algebras generated by $\ell_{n}$ and $\bar{\ell}_{n}$ correspond to the “ASD” and “SD” halves of the Lorentz algebra because

$$ \displaystyle(\ell_{n})_{ab} \displaystyle=-\frac{i}{2}\varepsilon_{abcd}(\ell_{n})^{cd}, \displaystyle(\bar{\ell}_{n})_{ab} \displaystyle=\frac{i}{2}\varepsilon_{abcd}(\bar{\ell}_{n})^{cd}. $$

A straightforward exercise in spinor variables shows that the Cartan structure equations can be decomposed as

$$ \displaystyle\differential\theta^{A\dot{A}}=-\Gamma^{A}_{\;\;B}\wedge\theta^{B\dot{A}}-\widetilde{\Gamma}^{\dot{A}}_{\;\;\dot{B}}\wedge\theta^{A\dot{B}} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle R_{AB} \displaystyle=\differential\Gamma_{AB}+\Gamma_{AC}\wedge\Gamma^{C}_{\;\;\;B}\,, \displaystyle\widetilde{R}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}} \displaystyle=\differential\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}+\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{C}}\wedge\widetilde{\Gamma}^{\dot{C}}_{\;\;\;\dot{B}}\,. $$

We now note an identity satisfied by the tetrads Capovilla et al. (1991a)

$$ \theta^{(A}_{\;\;\;\dot{A}}\wedge\theta^{B}_{\;\;\dot{B}}\wedge\theta^{C)}_{\;\;\;\dot{C}}=0 $$

which holds because the above expression is totally antisymmetric in $[\dot{A}\dot{B}\dot{C}]$ and therefore must vanish because spin indices are 2 dimensional. The above expression further implies the if-and-only-if statement44 4 It is if-and-only-if because the $\theta^{A\dot{A}}$ comprise a basis of four 1-forms, and only wedge products of three distinct basis 1-forms are non-vanishing. One can check that the object $\theta^{A}_{\;\;\dot{A}}\wedge\theta^{B}_{\;\;\dot{B}}\wedge\theta^{C}_{\;\;\dot{C}}$ is non-zero only for four options of $(A,B,C,\dot{A},\dot{B},\dot{C})$ , with, say, $(1,1,2,\dot{1},\dot{2},\dot{2})$ being one such option. Expanding out (198) for any of these options shows that it simply reduces to the sum of two non-zero 3-forms cancelling out, and therefore corresponds to the unique expression characterizing the cancellation of such 3-forms up to scaling.

$$ M_{ABC}\,\theta^{A}_{\;\;\dot{A}}\wedge\theta^{B}_{\;\;\dot{B}}\wedge\theta^{C}_{\;\;\dot{C}}=0\hskip 21.33955pt\Longleftrightarrow\hskip 21.33955ptM_{ABC}=M_{(ABC)}. $$

We now define the ASD 2-forms $\Sigma^{AB}=\Sigma^{(AB)}$ and the SD 2-forms $\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=\widetilde{\Sigma}^{(\dot{A}\dot{B})}$

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma^{AB} \displaystyle\equiv\theta^{A\dot{A}}\wedge\theta^{B}_{\;\;\dot{A}} \displaystyle\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}} \displaystyle\equiv\theta^{A\dot{A}}\wedge\theta_{A}^{\;\;\;\dot{B}} $$

which can be written in component form as

$$ \Sigma^{AB}=\frac{1}{2}\Sigma^{AB}_{\mu\nu}dx^{\mu}\wedge dx^{\nu},\hskip 28.45274pt\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=\frac{1}{2}\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}_{\mu\nu}dx^{\mu}\wedge dx^{\nu}, $$

and can straightforwardly be shown to satisfy

$$ \Sigma^{AB}_{\mu\nu}=-\frac{i}{2}\varepsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}(\Sigma^{AB})^{\rho\sigma},\hskip 28.45274pt\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}_{\mu\nu}=\frac{i}{2}\varepsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}(\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}})^{\rho\sigma}. $$

Equation (196) also gives

$$ \displaystyle\differential\Sigma^{AB} \displaystyle=-2\Gamma^{(A}_{\;\;\;\;C}\wedge\Sigma^{B)C}, \displaystyle\differential\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}} \displaystyle=-2\widetilde{\Gamma}^{(\dot{A}}_{\;\;\;\;\dot{C}}\wedge\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{B})\dot{C}}. $$

Combining the vacuum Einstein equation (186) and the first Bianchi identity (185), we find that the Einstein equation can be written as

$$ \displaystyle R_{AB}\wedge\theta^{A\dot{A}} \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\widetilde{R}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\wedge\theta^{A\dot{A}} \displaystyle=0. $$

We are always free to decompose $R_{AB}$ , as a general spacetime 2-form, into its spacetime ASD and SD parts

$$ R_{AB}=\Psi_{ABCD}\Sigma^{CD}+\Phi_{AB\dot{A}\dot{B}}\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}. $$

Combining (205) with the statement (199), we see that the Einstein equation is only satisfied if $\Psi_{ABCD}=\Psi_{(ABCD)}$ and $\Phi_{AB\dot{A}\dot{B}}$ = 0. We therefore have

$$ R_{AB}=\Psi_{ABCD}\Sigma^{CD},\hskip 28.45274pt\widetilde{R}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=\widetilde{\Psi}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}\dot{C}\dot{D}}\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{C}\dot{D}}, $$

where $\widetilde{\Psi}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}\dot{C}\dot{D}}=\widetilde{\Psi}_{(\dot{A}\dot{B}\dot{C}\dot{D})}$ as well.

The scalars $\Psi_{ABCD}$ and $\widetilde{\Psi}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}\dot{C}\dot{D}}$ are called the Weyl scalars, which in our conventions give the coefficients in the decomposition of the Riemann tensor $R_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}C\dot{C}D\dot{D}}=e_{A\dot{A}}^{\mu}e_{B\dot{B}}^{\nu}e_{C\dot{C}}^{\rho}e_{D\dot{D}}^{\sigma}R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$ as

$$ \nabla_{a}V_{b}=e_{a}^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}V_{b}-\Gamma^{c}_{\;\;ab}V_{c}. $$

The above equation also generalizes to tensors with a larger number of indices.

We can then take the differential Bianchi identity

$$ \nabla_{[a}R_{bc]de}=0, $$

plug in (209) (and contract the appropriate indices) to find

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\nabla^{A}_{\;\;\dot{A}}\Psi_{ABCD} $$

where, using the notation $\Gamma_{BC}=\frac{1}{2}(\Gamma_{BC})_{A\dot{A}}\theta^{A\dot{A}}$ , we explicitly have

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{A\dot{A}}\Psi_{BCDE}=(e_{A\dot{A}})^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}\Psi_{BCDE} \displaystyle-(\Gamma_{B}^{\;\;\;F})_{A\dot{A}}\Psi_{FCDE}-(\Gamma_{C}^{\;\;\;F})_{A\dot{A}}\Psi_{BFDE} \displaystyle-(\Gamma_{D}^{\;\;\;F})_{A\dot{A}}\Psi_{BCFE}-(\Gamma_{C}^{\;\;\;E})_{A\dot{A}}\Psi_{BCDF}\,. $$

### B.3 Proof of Plebański’s heavenly equations

The equation for SDG is

$$ R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}=\frac{i}{2}\varepsilon_{\mu\nu\alpha\beta}R^{\alpha\beta}_{\;\;\;\;\rho\sigma}. $$

The symmetry of the Riemann tensor then implies

$$ \displaystyle R^{\mu\nu}_{\;\;\;\;\rho\sigma} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{4}\varepsilon^{\mu\nu\alpha\beta}\varepsilon_{\rho\sigma\gamma\delta}R_{\alpha\beta}^{\;\;\;\;\;\gamma\delta} $$

and by identity (188) and the Bianchi identity, we see that (214) automatically implies the vacuum Einstein equation $R_{\nu\sigma}=0$ :

$$ \displaystyle R^{\mu}_{\;\;\nu\mu\sigma} \displaystyle=-\frac{3}{2}\delta^{[\gamma}_{\sigma}\delta^{\alpha}_{\nu}\delta^{\beta]}_{\delta}R_{\alpha\beta\gamma}^{\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\delta} \displaystyle=0. $$

Using the decomposition of $R_{AB}$ (208), as well as (202), the self-duality equation (214) then implies that the ASD part of the curvature 2-form vanishes:

$$ R_{AB}=0. $$

We will now argue that the above condition implies that it is always possible to choose a vierbein frame on the spacetime such that $\Gamma_{AB}=0$ .

We can always decompose $\Gamma_{a}^{\;\;b}$ into SD and ASD parts as

$$ \Gamma_{a}^{\;\;b}=(\Gamma_{\rm sd})_{a}^{\;\;b}+(\Gamma_{\rm asd})_{a}^{\;\;b}. $$

We have previously shown (see (195)) that one can decompose the Lorentz algebra $\mathfrak{so}(1,3)$ into two $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})$ halves, one SD and one ASD. Crucially, these subalgebras commute with each other, as $[\ell_{n},\bar{\ell}_{m}]=0$ . Therefore, any path ordered exponential of the spin connection will factor into two commuting matrices which are path ordered exponentials of $\Gamma_{\rm sd}$ and $\Gamma_{\rm asd}$ respectively.

$$ \mathcal{P}\exp(\int_{x_i}^{x_f} \Gamma)_{\!\!a}^{\;\,b}=\mathcal{P}\exp(\int_{x_i}^{x_f} \Gamma_{\rm sd} )_{\!\!a}^{\;\,c}\,\mathcal{P}\exp(\int_{x_i}^{x_f} \Gamma_{\rm asd} )_{\!\!c}^{\;\,b} $$

We can then redefine our vierbein frames at each point $x$ with the ASD path ordered integral

$$ e_{A\dot{A}}(x)\mapsto e^{\prime}_{A\dot{A}}(x)=\mathcal{P}\exp( \int_{x_0}^x \Gamma)_{\!\!A}^{\;\,B}e_{B\dot{A}}(x_{0}) $$

where here we path-integrate from a chosen basepoint $x_{0}$ to $x$ . The overall integral does not depend on the particular path chosen because $R_{AB}=0$ , and $R_{AB}$ necessarily quantifies the ASD $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{R})$ holonomy around a tiny loop.

This vierbein redefinition sends

$$ \Gamma_{A}^{\;\;B}\mapsto(\Gamma_{A}^{\;\;B})^{\prime}=0. $$

as desired. This also shows that the holonomy group of a SD metric is always the restricted holonomy group $SL_{\rm sd}(2,\mathbb{R})\subset SO(1,3)$ , in a complexified sense.

If we set $\Gamma_{AB}=0$ , equation (203) implies that all three ASD 2-forms are closed when the metric is SD:

$$ \differential\Sigma^{AB}=0. $$

The SD 2-forms also satisfy

$$ \Sigma^{(AB}\wedge\Sigma^{CD)}=0 $$

which is just a consequence of their tetrad definition (200) and identity (198).

A surprising fact is that knowing of the triplet of ASD 2-forms alone is completely sufficient to reconstruct $g_{\mu\nu}$ ! This is true for all metrics, not just self-dual ones. This fact follows from Urbantke’s remarkable identity Urbantke (1984); Capovilla et al. (1991b), which using our conventions reads

$$ \sqrt{-g}g_{\mu\nu}=-\frac{i}{3\times 2^{6}}\sqrt{-g}\varepsilon^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\Sigma^{AB}_{\mu\alpha}\Sigma_{\beta\gamma\;B}^{\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;C}\Sigma_{\delta\nu CA}. $$

Note that the RHS is determined entirely by the $\Sigma^{AB}$ ’s (as $\sqrt{-g}\varepsilon^{0123}=-1$ in our definition). The Urbantke formula can be proven by raising the indices of the middle 2-form using (202).

Let us now regard (222) and (223) as our new starting points of SDG and show how the metric is determined from these equations.

Using the explicit formula

$$ \Sigma^{AB}_{\mu\nu}=2\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\theta^{A\dot{A}}_{[\mu}\theta^{B\dot{B}}_{\nu]} $$

we can define the “almost complex structure” matrix

$$ J^{\mu}_{\;\;\nu}\equiv\frac{i}{2}\,g^{\mu\rho}(\Sigma^{12})_{\rho\nu} $$

which can readily be shown to satisfy the properties

$$ J^{\mu}_{\;\;\rho}J^{\rho}_{\;\;\nu}=-\delta^{\mu}_{\nu} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle(\Sigma^{11})_{\rho\sigma}J^{\rho}_{\;\;\mu}J^{\sigma}_{\;\;\nu} \displaystyle=-(\Sigma^{11})_{\mu\nu}, \displaystyle(\Sigma^{22})_{\rho\sigma}J^{\rho}_{\;\;\mu}J^{\sigma}_{\;\;\nu} \displaystyle=-(\Sigma^{22})_{\mu\nu}. $$

We also note that the 2-forms $\Sigma^{AB}_{\mu\nu}$ satisfy an important property. Adopting the notation $\Gamma_{AB\rho}dx^{\rho}=\Gamma_{AB}$ , $\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}\rho}dx^{\rho}=\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}$ , equation (178) becomes $\nabla_{\rho}\theta^{A\dot{A}}_{\mu}=-\Gamma^{\;\;\;A}_{C\;\;\;\rho}\theta^{C\dot{A}}_{\mu}-\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{C}\;\;\;\rho}^{\;\;\;\dot{A}}\theta^{A\dot{C}}_{\mu}$ , and from this and (225) one can calculate

$$ \nabla_{\rho}\Sigma^{AB}_{\mu\nu}=-\Gamma^{\;\;\;A}_{C\;\;\;\rho}\Sigma^{CB}_{\mu\nu}-\Gamma^{\;\;\;B}_{C\;\;\;\rho}\Sigma^{AC}_{\mu\nu}=0 $$

using $\Gamma_{AB}=0$ . We note the above equation is stronger than $\differential\Sigma^{AB}=0$ which only gives $\partial_{[\rho}\Sigma^{AB}_{\mu\nu]}=\nabla_{[\rho}\Sigma^{AB}_{\mu\nu]}=0$ . Importantly for us, it implies $\nabla_{\rho}J^{\mu}_{\;\;\nu}=0$ .

The Newlander–Nirenberg theorem states that if the Nijenhuis tensor of $J$ , defined as

$$ N^{\alpha}_{\;\;\mu\nu}\equiv J^{\rho}_{\;\;\mu}\partial_{[\rho}J^{\alpha}_{\;\;\nu]}-J^{\rho}_{\;\;\nu}\partial_{[\rho}J^{\alpha}_{\;\;\mu]}=J^{\rho}_{\;\;\mu}\nabla_{[\rho}J^{\alpha}_{\;\;\nu]}-J^{\rho}_{\;\;\nu}\nabla_{[\rho}J^{\alpha}_{\;\;\mu]} $$

is equal to 0, then $J$ is an actual complex structure. From $\nabla_{\rho}J^{\mu}_{\;\;\nu}=0$ we can see that $N^{\alpha}_{\;\;\mu\nu}=0$ for any self-dual spacetime.

Now that we know $J$ gives a complex structure, we can choose a coordinate basis $(y^{1},y^{2},\bar{y}^{1},\bar{y}^{2})$ that diagonalizes $J$ with eigenvalues $\pm i$ via

$$ J\partialderivative{y^j}=i\partialderivative{y^j}\,,\hskip 28.45274ptJ\partialderivative{\by^\bj}=-i\partialderivative{\by^\bj}\,, $$

for $j=1,2$ and ${\bar{\jmath}}=1,2$ . (228) can then be understood as the equation

$$ \Sigma^{11}(Jv_{1},Jv_{2})=-\Sigma^{11}(v_{1},v_{2}),\hskip 28.45274pt\Sigma^{22}(Jv_{1},Jv_{2})=-\Sigma^{22}(v_{1},v_{2}) $$

where $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$ are arbitrary vectors, which from (231) implies that the “mixed” holomorphic-antiholomorphic components of $(\Sigma^{11})_{\mu\nu}$ and $(\Sigma^{22})_{\mu\nu}$ are 0, with

$$ (\Sigma^{11})_{j{\bar{\jmath}}}=0,\hskip 28.45274pt(\Sigma^{22})_{j{\bar{\jmath}}}=0. $$

If we then use $\Sigma^{11}\wedge\Sigma^{11}=0$ , $\Sigma^{22}\wedge\Sigma^{22}=0$ , as well as $\differential\Sigma^{11}=0$ , $\differential\Sigma^{22}=0$ , we know that $\Sigma^{11}$ and $\Sigma^{22}$ must be able to be written in the form

$$ \Sigma^{11}=f(y^{1},y^{2})dy^{1}\wedge dy^{2},\hskip 28.45274pt\Sigma^{22}=g(\bar{y}^{1},\bar{y}^{2})d\bar{y}^{1}\wedge d\bar{y}^{2}, $$

for some arbitrary functions $f(y^{j})$ and $g(\bar{y}^{{\bar{\jmath}}})$ . However, once again using $\differential\Sigma^{11}=0$ and $\differential\Sigma^{22}=0$ , Darboux’s theorem tells us there exist coordinate redefinitions $y^{j}\mapsto\tilde{y}^{j}(y^{1},y^{2})$ and $\bar{y}^{{\bar{\jmath}}}\mapsto\tilde{\bar{y}}^{{\bar{\jmath}}}(\bar{y}^{1},\bar{y}^{2})$ such that, in these new coordinates,

$$ \Sigma^{11}=8\,dy^{1}\wedge dy^{2},\hskip 28.45274pt\Sigma^{22}=8\,d\bar{y}^{1}\wedge d\bar{y}^{2}. $$

If we now use $\Sigma^{11}\wedge\Sigma^{12}=\Sigma^{22}\wedge\Sigma^{12}=0$ , we know that $\Sigma^{12}$ must be of the form

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma^{12}=4\sum_{j=1,2}\sum_{{\bar{\jmath}}=1,2}\Omega_{j{\bar{\jmath}}}dy^{j}\wedge d\bar{y}^{{\bar{\jmath}}} $$

for some set of functions $\Omega_{j{\bar{\jmath}}}$ . $\differential\Sigma^{12}=0$ then implies that these functions must be the derivatives of a single scalar $\Omega$ called the Kähler potential,

$$ \Omega_{j{\bar{\jmath}}}=\partialderivative{y^j}\partialderivative{\bar{y}^\bj}\Omega\,. $$

The equation $2\,\Sigma^{12}\wedge\Sigma^{12}+\Sigma^{11}\wedge\Sigma^{22}=0$ imposes the following constraint on the Kähler potential:

$$ \det( \Omega_{j \bj} )=1. $$

This is known as Plebański’s first heavenly equation, and $\Omega$ is known as Plebański’s first heavenly scalar.

Now that we have all of the $\Sigma^{AB}$ ’s, we could in principle use Urbantke’s formula (224) to find the metric. We can also directly write a corresponding tetrad

$$ \displaystyle\theta^{1\dot{1}}=2d\bar{y}^{1}\,, \displaystyle\theta^{2\dot{1}}=2\Omega_{1\bar{2}}dy^{1}+2\Omega_{2\bar{2}}dy^{2}\,, \displaystyle\theta^{1\dot{2}}=2d\bar{y}^{2}\,, \displaystyle\theta^{2\dot{2}}=-2\Omega_{1\bar{1}}dy^{1}-2\Omega_{2\bar{1}}dy^{2}\,, $$

which yields the metric

$$ \displaystyle ds^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_{AB}\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\theta^{A\dot{A}}\theta^{B\dot{B}}=-4\,\Omega_{j{\bar{\jmath}}}\,dy^{j}d\bar{y}^{{\bar{\jmath}}}. $$

One can show that $\det(g_{\mu\nu})=16$ , and that our 2-forms $\Sigma^{AB}$ really are ASD with respect to this metric, after an appropriate choice of orientation. We conclude that (222) and (223) alone suffice as defining equations for SDG.

From (240), we can clearly see that all 4d SD metrics are Kähler manifolds. What’s more, they are Hyper-Kähler. In addition to $J$ , one can also define two other complex structures $I$ and $K$ , via

$$ I^{\mu}_{\;\;\nu}=\frac{1}{4}g^{\mu\rho}(\Sigma^{11}+\Sigma^{22})_{\rho\nu}\,,\hskip 28.45274ptK^{\mu}_{\;\;\nu}=\frac{i}{4}g^{\mu\rho}(\Sigma^{11}-\Sigma^{22})_{\rho\nu}\,, $$

which satisfy $I^{2}=J^{2}=K^{2}=IJK=-1$ .

Let us now give the proof of Plebański’s second heavenly equation, repeating Plebański’s original derivation Plebanski (1975). We use new coordinates $(u,{\bar{u}},w,{\bar{w}})$ satisfying

$$ u=\partialderivative{\Omega}{\by^1},\hskip 28.45274ptw=\partialderivative{\Omega}{\by^2},\hskip 28.45274pt{\bar{u}}=\bar{y}^{1},\hskip 28.45274pt{\bar{w}}=\bar{y}^{2}\,, $$

which can always be found because we have the Jacobian $|\partial(u,w)/\partial(y^{1},y^{2})|=1$ from (238). The tetrad now becomes

$$ \displaystyle\theta^{1\dot{1}}=2d{\bar{u}}\,, \displaystyle\theta^{2\dot{1}}=2(dw-Bd{\bar{u}}-Ad{\bar{w}})\,, \displaystyle\theta^{1\dot{2}}=2d{\bar{w}}\,, \displaystyle\theta^{2\dot{2}}=2(du+Cd{\bar{u}}+Bd{\bar{w}})\,, $$

with $A=\partial_{\bar{y}^{2}}^{2}\Omega$ , $B=\partial_{\bar{y}^{1}}\partial_{\bar{y}^{2}}\Omega$ , $C=\partial_{\bar{y}^{1}}^{2}\Omega$ . With this tetrad,

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma^{22}=2\theta^{2\dot{2}}\wedge\theta^{2\dot{1}}= \displaystyle 8(du\wedge dw-Adu\wedge d{\bar{w}}-Cd{\bar{u}}\wedge dw \displaystyle-B(du\wedge d{\bar{u}}+dw\wedge d{\bar{w}})-(AC-B^{2})d{\bar{u}}\wedge d{\bar{w}}) $$

and $\differential\Sigma^{22}=0$ implies

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{w}A=\partial_{u}B\,, \displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt\partial_{u}C=\partial_{w}B\,, \displaystyle\partial_{u}(AC-B^{2})-\partial_{\bar{u}}A+\partial_{\bar{w}}B=0\,, \displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt\partial_{w}(AC-B^{2})-\partial_{{\bar{u}}}B+\partial_{{\bar{w}}}C=0\,. $$

(245) implies that there exists a function $\tilde{\phi}$ such that

$$ A=\partial_{u}^{2}\tilde{\phi},\hskip 28.45274ptB=\partial_{u}\partial_{w}\tilde{\phi},\hskip 28.45274ptC=\partial_{w}^{2}\tilde{\phi}. $$

Plugging the above equations into (246) gives

$$ \partial_{u}(\Box\tilde{\phi}-\{\partial_{u}\tilde{\phi},\partial_{w}\tilde{\phi}\})=\partial_{w}(\Box\tilde{\phi}-\{\partial_{u}\tilde{\phi},\partial_{w}\tilde{\phi}\})=0. $$

This implies $\Box\tilde{\phi}-\{\partial_{u}\tilde{\phi},\partial_{w}\tilde{\phi}\}=\partial_{\bar{u}}F({\bar{u}},{\bar{w}})$ for some function $F({\bar{u}},{\bar{w}})$ . If we then define $\phi=\tilde{\phi}-uF$ , we have

$$ \Box\phi-\{\partial_{u}\phi,\partial_{w}\phi\}=0 $$

which is Plebański’s second heavenly equation and $\phi$ is Plebański’s second heavenly scalar. The tetrad is now

$$ \displaystyle\theta^{1\dot{1}} \displaystyle=2d{\bar{u}} \displaystyle\theta^{1\dot{2}} \displaystyle=2d{\bar{w}} \displaystyle\theta^{2\dot{1}} \displaystyle=2(dw-(\partial_{u}\partial_{w}\phi)d{\bar{u}}-(\partial_{u}^{2}\phi)d{\bar{w}}) \displaystyle\theta^{2\dot{2}} \displaystyle=2(du+(\partial_{w}^{2}\phi)d{\bar{u}}+(\partial_{u}\partial_{w}\phi)d{\bar{w}}) $$

and the metric is

$$ \displaystyle ds^{2} \displaystyle=\theta^{1\dot{1}}\theta^{2\dot{2}}-\theta^{1\dot{2}}\theta^{2\dot{1}} \displaystyle=4(du\,d{\bar{u}}-dw\,d{\bar{w}}+(\partial_{w}^{2}\phi)d{\bar{u}}^{2}+(\partial_{u}^{2}\phi)d{\bar{w}}^{2}+2(\partial_{u}\partial_{w}\phi)d{\bar{u}}\,d{\bar{w}}). $$

This completes the proof that all SD metrics can always locally be written in the above form for some $\phi$ satisfying the second heavenly equation.

## Appendix C SDYM and the Parke-Taylor formula

In this appendix we’ll develop the theory of perturbiner expansions in SDYM in a way that mirrors our work in SDG. We’ll show how it can be used to prove the Parke-Taylor formula for the Yang-Mills tree-level MHV amplitude Parke and Taylor (1986).

Perturbiners in SDYM were previously used to prove the Parke-Taylor formula by Selivanov and Rosly Rosly and Selivanov (1997b); Selivanov (1997); Selivanov (1996). See also Berends and Giele (1988); Bardeen (1996); Cangemi (1997); Korepin and Oota (1996). The only difference between our work below and that of Selivanov and Rosly is our use of the Chalmers-Siegel scalar, which we’ll introduce below. In this appendix alone we redefine the polarization vectors to be

$$ \varepsilon^{\mu}_{+,i}=-i\,\partial_{z}p^{\mu}_{i},\hskip 28.45274pt\varepsilon^{\mu}_{-,i}=\frac{i}{\omega^{2}}\partial_{\bar{z}}p^{\mu}_{i}. $$

### C.1 Perturbiners in SDYM

Say we have a gauge field $A_{\mu}=A_{\mu}^{a}\mathbf{T}^{a}$ , where $\mathbf{T}^{a}\in\mathfrak{g}$ . The field strength is defined to be

$$ F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_{\mu}A_{\nu}-\partial_{\nu}A_{\mu}+[A_{\mu},A_{\nu}]. $$

The equation for SDYM is

$$ F_{\mu\nu}=\frac{i}{2}\varepsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}F^{\rho\sigma}. $$

In lightcone coordinates (4), $\varepsilon_{u{\bar{u}}w{\bar{w}}}=4i$ and the above equation reduces to

$$ F_{uw}=0,\hskip 14.22636ptF_{u{\bar{u}}}=F_{w{\bar{w}}},\hskip 14.22636ptF_{{\bar{u}}{\bar{w}}}=0. $$

If we set $A_{u}=0$ , then $F_{uw}=0$ implies $A_{w}=0$ . $F_{u{\bar{u}}}=F_{w{\bar{w}}}$ then implies $\partial_{u}A_{\bar{u}}=\partial_{w}A_{\bar{w}}$ which can be solved by

$$ A_{\bar{u}}=\partial_{w}\Phi,\hskip 28.45274ptA_{{\bar{w}}}=\partial_{u}\Phi, $$

where $\Phi$ is a $\mathfrak{g}$ -valued scalar we shall call the Chalmers-Siegel scalar Parkes (1992); Bardeen (1996); Chalmers and Siegel (1996). We have therefore shown that the connection can be written as

$$ A_{\mu}=\begin{pmatrix}A_{u}\\
A_{\bar{u}}\\
A_{w}\\
A_{\bar{w}}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\
\partial_{w}\Phi\\
0\\
\partial_{u}\Phi\end{pmatrix}. $$

Note this manifestly satisfies Lorenz gauge $\partial_{\mu}A^{\mu}=0$ .

The only remaining equation to use from (255) is

$$ \displaystyle F_{{\bar{u}}{\bar{w}}}=\Box\,\Phi-[\partial_{u}\Phi,\partial_{w}\Phi]=0 $$

which is the equation of motion. Finding solutions perturbatively to the above equation is the goal of this section. We define the seed functions

$$ \Phi_{i}\equiv\epsilon_{i}\,\mathbf{T}^{a_{i}}e^{ip_{i}\cdot X} $$

which are positive helicity gluons with wavefunction $A_{\mu}=\epsilon_{i}(\varepsilon_{+,i})_{\mu}\mathbf{T}^{a_{i}}e^{ip_{i}\cdot X}$ .

#### Definition 16.

We denote

$$ \raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{N})\equiv\;\;\begin{matrix}\text{full perturbiner expansion of Chalmers-Siegel}\\
\text{scalar $\Phi$ with seed functions }\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{N}.\end{matrix} $$

#### Definition 17.

For some subset of indices $\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\}\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}$ for $1\leq k\leq N$ , we define

$$ \raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(k)}(\Phi_{i_{1}},\ldots,\Phi_{i_{k}}) $$

to be the sum of terms in

$$ \raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{N}) $$

which contain the seed functions $\Phi_{i_{1}},\ldots,\Phi_{i_{k}}$ . This implies

$$ \raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}\,(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{N})=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\}\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}\end{subarray}}\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(k)}(\Phi_{i_{1}},\ldots,\Phi_{i_{k}}). $$

#### Theorem C.1.

The perturbiner expansion is given by

$$ \displaystyle\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(N)}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{N})=\sum_{\sigma\,\in\,\mathrm{Sym}(N)}\frac{\Phi_{\sigma(1)}\Phi_{\sigma(2)}\ldots\Phi_{\sigma(N)}}{z_{\sigma(1)\sigma(2)}z_{\sigma(2)\sigma(3)}\ldots z_{\sigma(N-1)\sigma(N)}}. $$

#### Proof.

This proof will work by plugging the proposed perturbiner expansion into the equation of motion (258) and showing that it is satisfied.

Let us begin by creating a visual representation of the terms in the perturbiner expansion. For a string of indices $s_{1},\ldots,s_{k}$ , we represent a single term in the expansion with a chain of nodes as follows.

Let us now consider what happens when we act with the wave operator $\Box$ on the above term. Note that $\Box\Phi_{i}=0$ and $\Box(\Phi_{i}\Phi_{j})=z_{ij}D^{ij}\Phi_{i}\Phi_{j}$ , see (28). From the product rule of differentiation, we have for instance

$$ \Box(\Phi_{1}\Phi_{2}\Phi_{3})=(z_{12}D^{12}+z_{23}D^{23}+z_{13}D^{13})(\Phi_{1}\Phi_{2}\Phi_{3}). $$

We can therefore think of the action of $\Box$ on a string of seed functions as a sum over all pairs of seed functions $\Phi_{i}$ and $\Phi_{j}$ in the string where we act by $z_{ij}D^{ij}$ . We can represent this pairing with a double-line as follows.

Let us now define a new graphical element which is just a line (or ‘cut’) drawn in between two seed functions in a chain. This line indicates that the chain of nodes before and after the cut should be evaluated independently and then multiplied together at the end (preserving order).

As we can see above, a cut drawn in between nodes $s_{i}$ and $s_{i+1}$ simply corresponds to multiplying the entire chain of nodes by $z_{s_{i}s_{i+1}}$ .

We will define one further graphical element, which is a wiggly line. A wiggly line extending from node $s_{i}$ to node $s_{j}$ corresponds to the action of $D^{s_{i}s_{j}}$ on the string of seed functions. An arrow is drawn to denote orientation because $D^{s_{i}s_{j}}=-D^{s_{j}s_{i}}$ .

Now that we have defined all of these graphical elements, we will begin checking that

$$ \Box\Phi\overset{?}{=}[\partial_{u}\Phi,\partial_{w}\Phi] $$

for our proposed $\Phi$ . To evaluate the commutator on the RHS, via the product rule of differentiation we are to sum over the action of $\partial_{u}$ and $\partial_{w}$ on all possible nodes on either side of a “cut” as follows.

In other words, $[\partial_{u}\Phi,\partial_{w}\Phi]$ corresponds to a sum over all strings of nodes where a cut can be placed anywhere within the string and a wiggly line can be placed anywhere that starts on the left of the cut and ends on the right of the cut. Note that this diagram corresponds to the term

To evaluate $\Box\Phi$ on the LHS, we simply sum over all placements of the double-lined edge that starts and ends on two distinct nodes.

The equality $\Box\Phi=[\partial_{u}\Phi,\partial_{w}\Phi]$ is then confirmed by the computation in the figure below, done with an example where the double-line/wiggly-lines start and end on $s_{i}$ and $s_{i+4}$ , respectively. We sum over all placements of the cut on the RHS in between the two end-points of the wiggly line. Because the cut between nodes $s_{i+\ell}$ and $s_{i+\ell+1}$ multiplies the whole expression by $z_{s_{i+\ell}s_{i+\ell+1}}$ , when we sum over the chain of cut placements in the example below we end up with the overall factor $z_{s_{i}s_{i+4}}$ , matching the LHS. This computation completes the proof that the perturbiner expansion satisfies the equation of motion.

#### Examples.

For $N=1$ :

$$ \raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1})=\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(1)}(\Phi_{1})=\Phi_{1}. $$

For $N=2$ :

$$ \displaystyle\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2}) \displaystyle=\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(1)}(\Phi_{1})+\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(1)}(\Phi_{2})+\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(2)}(\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2}) $$

with

$$ \raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(2)}(\Phi_{i},\Phi_{j})=\frac{1}{z_{ij}}\Phi_{i}\Phi_{j}+\frac{1}{z_{ji}}\Phi_{j}\Phi_{i}. $$

For $N=3$ :

$$ \displaystyle\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2},\Phi_{3})= \displaystyle\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(1)}(\Phi_{1})+\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(1)}(\Phi_{2})+\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(1)}(\Phi_{3}) \displaystyle+\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(2)}(\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2})+\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(2)}(\Phi_{2},\Phi_{3})+\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(2)}(\Phi_{1},\Phi_{3}) \displaystyle+\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(3)}(\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2},\Phi_{3}) $$

with

$$ \displaystyle\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(3)}(\Phi_{i},\Phi_{j},\Phi_{k})= \displaystyle\frac{1}{z_{ij}}\frac{1}{z_{jk}}\Phi_{i}\Phi_{j}\Phi_{k}+\frac{1}{z_{jk}}\frac{1}{z_{ki}}\Phi_{j}\Phi_{k}\Phi_{i}+\frac{1}{z_{ki}}\frac{1}{z_{ij}}\Phi_{k}\Phi_{i}\Phi_{j} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{z_{ji}}\frac{1}{z_{ik}}\Phi_{j}\Phi_{i}\Phi_{k}+\frac{1}{z_{kj}}\frac{1}{z_{ji}}\Phi_{k}\Phi_{j}\Phi_{i}+\frac{1}{z_{ik}}\frac{1}{z_{kj}}\Phi_{i}\Phi_{k}\Phi_{j}. $$

Now that we have a formula for the perturbiner expansion in SDYM for any $N$ , we will now present a recursive formula which allows for the perturbiner expansion of $N$ seed functions to be computed if one already knows the expansion for $N-1$ . This formula is given below.

#### Theorem C.2.

$$ \displaystyle\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(N)}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{N})=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\evaluated{\bigPhi^{(N-1)}(\Phi_1, \ldots, \Phi_{N-1} )}_{\displaystyle\Phi_i \mapsto\frac{1}{z_{iN}} [\Phi_i, \Phi_N]} $$

#### Examples.

For $N=2$ we have

$$ \raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(2)}(\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2})=\frac{1}{z_{12}}[\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2}]. $$

For $N=3$

$$ \raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}^{(3)}(\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2},\Phi_{3})=\frac{1}{z_{12}}[\frac{1}{z_{13}}[\Phi_{1},\Phi_{3}],\Phi_{2}]+\frac{1}{z_{12}}[\Phi_{1},\frac{1}{z_{23}}[\Phi_{2},\Phi_{3}]]. $$

If one expands out the above term, one finds agreement with (268).

#### Proof.

In order to prove this recursive formula, let us use theorem C.1 to write the $N-1$ case and show that the recursive formula correctly reproduces the $N$ case.

Let us consider how a certain string of seed functions in the $N$ case can be reached by a previous string in the $N-1$ case via the recursive formula. Without loss of generality, let us consider how we can achieve the mutation of the string

$$ 1,\ldots,i,j,\ldots,N-1\;\;\;\to\;\;\;1,\ldots,i,N,j,\ldots,N-1 $$

where $N$ is inserted in between some adjacent nodes $i$ and $j$ .

If we start with the $1,\ldots,i,j,\ldots,N-1$ string

$$ \frac{1}{z_{12}}\ldots\frac{1}{z_{ij}}\ldots\frac{1}{z_{N-2,N-1}}\Phi_{1}\ldots\Phi_{i}\Phi_{j}\ldots\Phi_{N-1} $$

then only way to reach the desired string from the recursive rule is to add the two terms from the substitutions

$$ \Phi_{i}\mapsto\frac{1}{z_{iN}}(\underbrace{\Phi_{i}\Phi_{N}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{only include}\\
\text{this term}\end{subarray}}\!\!\!\!-\;\Phi_{N}\Phi_{i}\;\;),\hskip 21.33955pt+\hskip 21.33955pt\Phi_{j}\mapsto\frac{1}{z_{jN}}(\;\;\Phi_{j}\Phi_{N}-\!\!\!\underbrace{\Phi_{N}\Phi_{j}}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{only include}\\
\text{this term}\end{subarray}}) $$

under which the string transforms as

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{z_{12}} \displaystyle\ldots\frac{1}{z_{ij}}\ldots\frac{1}{z_{N-2,N-1}}\Phi_{1}\ldots\Phi_{i}\Phi_{j}\ldots\Phi_{N-1} \displaystyle\mapsto \displaystyle\frac{1}{z_{12}}\ldots\frac{1}{z_{ij}}\ldots\frac{1}{z_{N-2,N-1}}\Phi_{1}\ldots\Phi_{i}\left(\frac{1}{z_{iN}}\Phi_{N}-\frac{1}{z_{jN}}\Phi_{N}\right)\Phi_{j}\ldots\Phi_{N-1} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{z_{12}}\ldots\frac{1}{z_{iN}}\frac{1}{z_{Nj}}\ldots\frac{1}{z_{N-2,N-1}}\Phi_{1}\ldots\Phi_{i}\Phi_{N}\Phi_{j}\ldots\Phi_{N-1} $$

giving the desired result. Here we have used the elementary identity

$$ \frac{1}{z_{ij}}\left(\frac{1}{z_{iN}}-\frac{1}{z_{jN}}\right)=\frac{1}{z_{iN}}\frac{1}{z_{Nj}}. $$

### C.2 Recursion operator in SDYM

Linearized perturbations $\Phi+\delta\Phi$ to the Chalmers-Siegel scalar satisfy

$$ \Box\delta\Phi-[\partial_{u}\delta\Phi,\partial_{w}\Phi]-[\partial_{u}\Phi,\partial_{w}\delta\Phi]=0. $$

There exists a recursion operator $\mathcal{R}$ which acts on the space of linear perturbations $\delta\Phi$ and is defined as the solution to the pair of differential equations

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{u}(\mathcal{R}\delta\Phi) \displaystyle=\partial_{\bar{w}}\delta\Phi+[\partial_{u}\Phi,\delta\Phi], \displaystyle\partial_{w}(\mathcal{R}\delta\Phi) \displaystyle=\partial_{\bar{u}}\delta\Phi+[\partial_{w}\Phi,\delta\Phi]. $$

The compatibility of the two equations follows from the fact that $\delta\Phi$ is a linear perturbation of $\Phi$ :

$$ \partial_{u}(\partial_{w}(\mathcal{R}\delta\Phi))-\partial_{w}(\partial_{u}(\mathcal{R}\delta\Phi))=\Box\delta\Phi-[\partial_{u}\delta\Phi,\partial_{w}\Phi]-[\partial_{u}\Phi,\partial_{w}\delta\Phi]=0. $$

Furthermore, $\mathcal{R}\delta\Phi$ is guaranteed to solve the linearized e.o.m. by

$$ \Box\,\mathcal{R}\delta\Phi-[\partial_{u}\mathcal{R}\delta\Phi,\partial_{w}\Phi]-[\partial_{u}\Phi,\partial_{w}\mathcal{R}\delta\Phi]=[\Box\Phi-[\partial_{u}\Phi,\partial_{w}\Phi],\delta\Phi]=0. $$

A natural example of a linear perturbation $\delta\Phi$ is the change incurred by adding one extra seed function into the perturbiner expansion. To that end, we define

#### Definition 18.

$$ \raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{N}|\Phi_{I})\equiv\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{N},\Phi_{I})-\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{N}) $$

which just is the change in the perturbiner expansion coming from adding in the seed function $\Phi_{I}$ , for some index $I\notin\{1,\ldots,N\}$ .

In particular,

$$ \Phi=\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{N}),\hskip 14.22636pt\delta\Phi=\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{N}|\Phi_{I}) $$

will solve the linearized e.o.m. (274).

It turns out that there is a nice formula for the action of $\mathcal{R}$ on the linear perturbation above, which we give below.

#### Theorem C.3.

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}\,\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{N}|\Phi_{I})=-z_{I}\times\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{N}|\Phi_{I}). $$

#### Proof.

First, we know what $\delta\Phi$ is because it is just a sum over all color-ordered strings which necessarily contain the node $I$ . Therefore, we can prove the above formula by checking that (275) is satisfied if we assume $\mathcal{R}\delta\Phi=-z_{I}\delta\Phi$ . We will check the first equation of (275) and the second will follow by similar logic.

The term $\partial_{u}(-z_{I}\delta\Phi)$ will be a sum of terms which each have $\partial_{u}$ acting on a seed function (which we’ll denote $i$ ) and also contain the seed function $I$ .

First, assume $i$ is to the left of $I$ in the color ordering.

On the RHS of (275) we have $\partial_{\bar{w}}\delta\Phi+[\partial_{u}\Phi,\delta\Phi]$ . For the $\partial_{\bar{w}}\delta\Phi$ piece, note that

$$ \partial_{{\bar{w}}}\Phi_{i}=-z_{i}\partial_{u}\Phi_{i}\,,\hskip 28.45274pt\partial_{\bar{u}}\Phi_{i}=-z_{i}\partial_{w}\Phi_{i}\,, $$

(see (27)). In the commutator $[\partial_{u}\Phi,\delta\Phi]$ , the term $\partial_{u}\Phi\delta\Phi$ will have $\partial_{u}$ acting on a node (let’s say $i$ ) to the left of $I$ . Furthermore, diagrammatically there will be a ‘cut’ or ‘line’ in between the $i$ and $I$ nodes.

Below we show of a group terms in a particular example where all nodes are presented in the same order and all the derivatives are acting on $i$ . Note that we have to sum over all of the positions of the ‘cut’ in between $i$ and $I$ .

It turns out that, using (281) and summing over the chain of cuts, the diagram on the left does indeed equal the sum of diagrams on the right.

Next, assume that $i$ is to the right of $I$ . We now look at the other term $-\delta\Phi\partial_{u}\Phi$ in the commutator $[\partial_{u}\Phi,\delta\Phi]$ . An analogous computation is shown below.

Finally, if $i=I$ , then the equality of diagrams follows in a straightforward manner. Therefore, the LHS of (275) does equal the RHS if $\mathcal{R}\delta\Phi=-z_{I}\delta\Phi$ .

∎

### C.3 Proof of the Parke Taylor formula

We now present a proof of the Parke Taylor formula for gluon MHV scattering which is analogous to our proof of the graviton MHV formula. We start with the Yang Mills action with an added topological term. The topological term does not affect scattering amplitudes.

$$ S=-\frac{1}{2}\int d^{4}X\Tr( F^{\mu\nu} F_{\mu\nu} - \frac{i}{2} \vep_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} F^{\mu\nu} F^{\rho\sigma} ) $$

We now write the basis of flat-space vierbeins $e_{A\dot{A}}$

$$ e_{1\dot{1}}=\partial_{\bar{u}},\hskip 14.22636pte_{1\dot{2}}=\partial_{\bar{w}},\hskip 14.22636pte_{2\dot{1}}=\partial_{w},\hskip 14.22636pte_{2\dot{2}}=\partial_{u}. $$

Changing to spinor indices by $A_{A\dot{A}}=e^{\mu}_{A\dot{A}}A_{\mu}$ and $F_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}}=e_{A\dot{A}}^{\mu}e_{B\dot{B}}^{\nu}F_{\mu\nu}$ , and decomposing the field strength into ASD and SD parts $F_{AB}$ and $\widetilde{F}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}$ by (172), the usual kinetic term and topological term then read

$$ \displaystyle F^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu} \displaystyle=2F^{AB}F_{AB}+2\widetilde{F}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\widetilde{F}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}} \displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}F^{\mu\nu}F^{\rho\sigma} \displaystyle=4i\,(F^{AB}F_{AB}-\widetilde{F}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\widetilde{F}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}) $$

implying our action can be written purely in terms of the ASD part $F_{AB}$ as

$$ S=-2\int d^{4}X\Tr( F^{AB} F_{AB} ). $$

In a SD background, $F_{AB}=0$ . The above action therefore provides a convenient way to compute the MHV amplitude. Imagine a solution which contains $N$ positive helicity gluons and $2$ negative helicity gluons. The “linear” part of the solution should be

$$ A_{\mu}=\sum_{i=1}^{N+2}\epsilon_{i}(\varepsilon_{i})_{\mu}\mathbf{T}^{a_{i}}e^{ip_{i}\cdot X}+\ldots $$

and the higher order terms in the infinitesimal parameters $\epsilon_{i}$ (the $\ldots$ above) are determined by requiring that $A_{\mu}$ solves the e.o.m.. From

$$ \mathcal{A}_{\rm MHV}=\frac{\partial^{N+2}}{\partial\epsilon_{1}\ldots\partial\epsilon_{N+2}}\evaluated{i S}_{\epsilon_i = 0 \; \forall\epsilon_i} $$

we can see that to find $\mathcal{A}_{\rm MHV}$ all we must do is compute $f^{I}_{AB}$ and $f^{J}_{AB}$ , where $I=N+1$ and $J=N+2$ are the labels corresponding to the two negative helicity gluons and $f_{AB}=\delta F_{AB}$ denote linear ASD perturbations to the SD background of the $N$ positive helicity gluons. We then have

$$ \mathcal{A}_{\rm MHV}=-4i\frac{\partial^{N+2}}{\partial\epsilon_{1}\ldots\partial\epsilon_{N+2}}\evaluated{ \int d^4 X (f^I)^{AB} (f^J)_{AB} }_{\epsilon_i = 0 \; \forall\epsilon_i}. $$

We now solve for the ASD perturbation $f^{I}_{AB}$ . This can be done as follows. Defining the covariant derivative

$$ \mathcal{D}_{\mu}=\partial_{\mu}+[A_{\mu},\cdot\,] $$

the Yang Mills e.o.m. and Bianchi identity read

$$ \mathcal{D}_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}=0\,,\hskip 28.45274pt\mathcal{D}_{\mu}(\star F)^{\mu\nu}=0. $$

These can be added and subtracted to give

$$ \mathcal{D}^{A}_{\;\;\dot{A}}F_{AB}=0\,,\hskip 28.45274pt\mathcal{D}_{A}^{\;\;\dot{A}}\widetilde{F}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=0. $$

The first of the above equations gives us an equation of motion for $f_{AB}$ , which we write explicitly as

$$ \mathcal{D}^{A}_{\;\;\dot{A}}f_{AB}=(e^{A}_{\;\;\dot{B}})^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}f_{AB}+[A^{A}_{\;\;\dot{A}},f_{AB}]=0. $$

Note that here the connection $A_{A\dot{A}}$ denotes the connection of the SD background, given by (257). The above equation can be thought of as two equations, one for $\dot{A}=1$ and $\dot{A}=2$ , which we expand out below as

$$ \displaystyle\dot{A}=\dot{1}: \displaystyle 0=-\partial_{w}f_{1B}+\partial_{\bar{u}}f_{2B}+[\partial_{w}\Phi,f_{2B}]\,, \displaystyle\dot{A}=\dot{2}: \displaystyle 0=-\partial_{u}f_{1B}+\partial_{\bar{w}}f_{2B}+[\partial_{u}\Phi,f_{2B}]\,. $$

Comparing the above with (275), we note that this implies that $f_{1B}$ is given by the recursion operator $\mathcal{R}$ acting on $f_{2B}$ :

$$ f_{1B}=\mathcal{R}\,f_{2B}. $$

In fact, the two equations of (293) can be combined to show that

$$ \Box f_{AB}-[\partial_{u}f_{AB},\partial_{w}\Phi]-[\partial_{u}\Phi,\partial_{w}f_{AB}]=0. $$

Therefore, an ASD perturbation to a SD background solves the same e.o.m. as a SD perturbation! Thankfully we have already discussed how to solve for such perturbations using (279).

Using theorem C.3 we know we can take $f_{1B}^{I}=-z_{I}f_{2B}^{I}$ and from the symmetry $f_{AB}=f_{(AB)}$ we know we can solve for $f^{I}_{AB}$ with the formula

$$ f^{I}_{AB}=\frac{1}{2}\kappa^{I}_{A}\kappa^{I}_{B}\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{N}|\Phi_{I}) $$

where $\kappa^{I}_{A}=(-z_{I},1)$ . The proportionality factor of $1/2$ was chosen so that the negative helicity gluon has wavefunction $A_{\mu}=\epsilon_{I}(\varepsilon^{-})_{\mu}\mathbf{T}^{a_{I}}e^{ip_{I}\cdot X}$ , as can be checked straightforwardly in the trivial $N=0$ case where the SD background is 0.

Plugging the above expression for $f_{I}$ and $f_{J}$ into the action, we have

$$ \displaystyle S=-\langle IJ\rangle^{2}\int d^{4}X\;\Tr\left(\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{N}|\Phi_{I})\raisebox{-1.20007pt}{\Large$\Phi$}(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{N}|\Phi_{J})\right). $$

We can draw the terms arising from this trace in the following way.

Here, the ‘cut’ on the LHS is drawn between the two terms in (297) which correspond to $f^{I}$ and $f^{J}$ . On the RHS, a second cut is drawn to where the beginning and end of the chain are linked together by the trace.

We must sum over the positions of the two cuts, which are each placed between the $I$ and $J$ nodes on opposite sides. If we, say, hold one cut fixed and sum over the position of the other cut, the result is that we can just multiply the whole diagram without said cut by $z_{IJ}$ , using the graphical computation shown below.

There are, however, two cuts whose positions must be summed over. Summing over the position of the first cut, as we’ve shown above, gets us a factor of $z_{IJ}$ , and summing over the second cut would similarly get us a factor of $-z_{IJ}$ . Therefore, summing over the positions of both cuts gets us a factor of $-(z_{IJ})^{2}$ . Plugging this back into (297), this will reproduce the overall power of $\langle IJ\rangle^{4}$ out front. The integration over $\int d^{4}X\,e^{i(p_{1}+\ldots+p_{N+2})\cdot X}$ then becomes the energy momentum conserving delta function.

In total, the final amplitude is

$$ \mathcal{A}_{\rm MHV}=i\,(2\pi)^{4}\delta^{(4)}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N+2}p_{i}\right)\langle IJ\rangle^{4}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Sym}(N+2)/\mathbb{Z}_{N+2}}\frac{\Tr(\bT^{a_{\sigma(1)}} \ldots\bT^{a_{\sigma(N+2)}})}{\langle\sigma(1)\sigma(2)\rangle\ldots\langle\sigma(N+2)\sigma(1)\rangle} $$

which is the Parke Taylor formula.

# Generating Hodges’ Graviton MHV Formula with an $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ Ward Identity

**Authors:** Alfredo Guevara Affiliation: School of Natural Sciences, Institute for Advanced Study Email: aguevara@ias.edu Elizabeth Himwich Affiliation: Princeton Center for Theoretical Science, Princeton University Affiliation: Princeton Gravity Initiative, Princeton University Email: ehimwich@princeton.edu and Noah Miller Affiliation: School of Natural Sciences, Institute for Advanced Study Affiliation: Princeton Gravity Initiative, Princeton University Email: noahmiller@ias.edu

## Abstract

Hodges’ formula expresses the tree-level all-multiplicity Einstein gravity MHV amplitude as a matrix determinant. In this work, we prove that Hodges’ determinant is generated by an $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ Ward identity on the celestial sphere. The Ward identity takes the form of a recursion relation that has not previously appeared in the literature and is unrelated to BCFW. The proof makes use of the matrix-tree theorem.

## 1 Introduction

Is there a holographic dual to the gravitational $S$ -matrix in asymptotically flat spacetime? Success in reformulating perturbative gauge theory (with and without supersymmetry) using methods agnostic to Feynman diagrams have provided strong encouragement that similar constructions may exist in gravity. The dual descriptions of gauge theory not only streamline cumbersome calculations, but also pave the way to taming divergences of the theory [1, 2, 3].

A great deal of this progress has been based on the use of extended symmetries, such as those arising from integrability [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9], which for instance played a pivotal role in the reformulation of super-Yang-Mills scattering amplitudes with twistor variables. This reformulation put forth a new paradigm by suggesting that perhaps the actual scattering fundamentally occurs not in spacetime, but in a dual space [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]. In the dual description, locality and unitarity emerge in a completely novel way and the existence of spacetime Feynman diagrams appears fortuitous.

In pursuit of an analogous construction for gravity, Hodges introduced new dual representations of gravitational amplitudes in a series of breakthrough papers culminating in the celebrated formula for tree-level MHV scattering [16, 17, 12, 18, 19]. The construction was guided by the appearance of momentum twistors and a specific theory of gravity with $\mathcal{N}=7$ supersymmetry, as well as by the NSVW tree graph formula [20, 21]. It has generated important progress in many directions [22, 23, 24, 25] but remains mysterious despite much effort to be generalized.

Jumping forward to today, new tools from the celestial holography program are providing deep hints about the structure of gravitational scattering. In particular, a new extended $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ symmetry has been identified in the tree-level amplitudes of minimally-coupled Einstein gravity [26, 27]. In analogy with gauge theory, this suggests that a dual description for gravitational scattering could exist in a space that makes the extended $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ symmetry manifest, rather than spacetime. Coincidentally, in analogy with the integrable symmetries of gauge theory, the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ symmetry is again realized in twistor space, though it can also be pulled down to a holographic description on the two-dimensional (2D) celestial sphere [28, 29, 30, 31, 32].

The discovery of $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ symmetry within gravitational scattering immediately raises the question of how it can be used concretely to constrain and construct amplitudes, particularly from the celestial dual perspective [33, 34, 35, 36]. From the spacetime perspective, $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ symmetry organizes a universal part of the soft expansion of any tree-level minimally-coupled gravitational scattering amplitude [37, 38, 31, 39], which raises another question of whether the universal part corresponds exactly to a class of known amplitudes. These questions both touch on whether a particular known set of gravitational amplitudes is specified fully by (dual) $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ symmetry. This was asked specifically about Hodges’ formula in [31, 40] where a positive partial answer was provided.11 1 See [41, 42, 43, 44] for related work on celestial OPEs in gravity MHV amplitudes and [45] for an alterative dual construction of the graviton MHV leaf correlator.

Taking a step in this direction, we demonstrate that Hodges’ formula for tree-level MHV gravitational scattering amplitudes is exactly generated by a novel recursion relation that corresponds to the 2D Ward identity of $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ symmetry in the dual celestial description.22 2 From the realization of $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ in twistor space, one might naturally expect that the amplitudes generated by $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ would be those of the self-dual sector, although self-dual amplitudes vanish at tree level. There may however be an analogous formula for the one-loop amplitude, where it is known that the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ symmetry is perturbatively exact [46, 47]. We hope to explore this in future work. We believe it provides strong evidence that a dual of the gravitational $S$ -matrix exists on the 2D celestial sphere. Related work on the gauge theory MHV amplitude has appeared in [48, 49, 29, 50, 51, 30, 52, 53, 54, 55].

### 1.1 Main Result

Consider a tree-level maximally-helicity-violating (MHV) scattering amplitude $\mathcal{M}_{n}$ in pure Einstein gravity, with external gravitons $1^{--},2^{--},3^{++},\ldots,n^{++}$ ,

$$ \mathcal{M}_{n}=i(2\pi)^{4}\delta^{4}(p_{1}+\ldots+p_{n})M_{n} $$

where $M_{n}$ is the stripped amplitude. Crucially, $M_{n}$ is regarded as a function of all the momenta $\{p_{i}\}$ without the constraint of momentum conservation. Thus it is only defined up to a function that vanishes on this constraint. However, Hodges [19] provided a simple formula for a particular choice of $M_{n}$ , and we will use Hodges’ formula as the definition of $M_{n}$ in this paper.33 3 More accurately, we use a special case of Hodges’ formula where we fix certain arbitrary choices, which we write explicitly in (13). We also set $\kappa=\sqrt{32\pi G}=2$ . See Appendix B for conventions.

Our main result is that, for $n>3$ , Hodges’ MHV formula for the stripped amplitude $M_{n}$ satisfies a simple recursion relation that allows it to be computed from $M_{n-1}$ :

$$ M_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{[ni]}{\langle ni\rangle}\frac{\langle\alpha i\rangle^{2}}{\langle\alpha n\rangle^{2}}M_{n-1}(\,\ket{1},|1],\,\cdots,|i\rangle,|i]{+}\frac{\langle\alpha n\rangle}{\langle\alpha i\rangle}|n],\,\cdots,\ket{n{-}1},|n{-}1]\,). $$

Here $\ket{\alpha}$ is an arbitrary reference spinor that appears in Hodges’ formula. We use the usual representative $M_{3}=\left(\frac{\langle 12\rangle^{4}}{\langle 12\rangle\langle 23\rangle\langle 31\rangle}\right)^{2}$ as the base of the recursion, and this generates all $M_{n>3}$ using (2).

Interestingly, the above equation has not appeared before in the literature. Its most notable feature is that it sums over all $n-1$ particles in $M_{n-1}$ . The existing well-known recursion relations for the full MHV amplitude $\mathcal{M}_{n}$ , such as (9) in [19], or (2) in [56], are based on BCFW recursion [57] and explicitly conserve momentum at each recursive step. See also [58, 59, 60, 61, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 67]. As a result, these formulas shift more than one particle at a time and always involve a sum over $n-2$ (or fewer) particles. However, any recursion relation that shifts more than one particle at a time does not act locally on the celestial sphere, so our formula is more natural from a celestial perspective.

### 1.2 Main Result Interpreted as an $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ Ward Identity

Our ansatz for the form of (2) was motivated by considerations from the celestial holography program. In order to explain these considerations, it is convenient (although strictly speaking not necessary) to parameterize null momenta as

$$ p^{\mu}_{i}=\frac{\omega_{i}}{2}(1+z_{i}{\bar{z}}_{i},\,z_{i}+{\bar{z}}_{i},\,-i(z_{i}-{\bar{z}}_{i}),\,1-z_{i}{\bar{z}}_{i}), $$

their spinor decompositions as

$$ \hskip 14.22636ptp_{i}^{A\dot{A}}=\begin{pmatrix}p^{0}_{i}+p^{3}_{i}&p^{1}_{i}-ip^{2}_{i}\\
p^{1}_{i}+ip^{2}_{i}&p^{0}_{i}-p^{3}_{i}\end{pmatrix}=\lambda_{i}^{A}\tilde{\lambda}_{i}^{\dot{A}}, $$

and the spinors as

$$ \lambda_{i}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\
z_{i}\end{pmatrix},\hskip 28.45274pt\tilde{\lambda}_{i}=\begin{pmatrix}\omega_{i}\\
\omega_{i}{\bar{z}}_{i}\end{pmatrix},\hskip 28.45274pt\alpha=\begin{pmatrix}0\\
1\end{pmatrix}. $$

With these choices, we have

$$ \langle ij\rangle=z_{ij},\hskip 28.45274pt[ij]=\omega_{i}\omega_{j}{\bar{z}}_{ij},\hskip 28.45274pt\langle\alpha i\rangle=1, $$

where $z_{ij}=z_{i}-z_{j}$ .

Within a postulated 2D celestial CFT, we define the operators $G^{\pm}(z_{i},\tilde{\lambda}_{i})$ to correspond to insertions in the bulk four-dimensional (4D) $S$ -matrix of $\pm$ helicity gravitons with momentum $p_{i}$ . If $\omega_{i}$ is negative (positive) the graviton is incoming (outgoing).

For tree-level minimally-coupled gravity amplitudes, there is a simple formula for the holomorphic collinear splitting function of two gravitons $G^{+}(z_{i},\tilde{\lambda}_{i})G^{\pm}(z_{j},\tilde{\lambda}_{j})$ , where $z_{ij}\to 0$ as $\tilde{\lambda}_{i}$ , $\tilde{\lambda}_{j}$ are held fixed. In the language of celestial CFT, this splitting function reads [31, 44]

$$ \lim_{z_{ij}\to 0}G^{+}(z_{i},\tilde{\lambda}_{i})\,G^{\pm}(z_{j},\tilde{\lambda}_{j})=\frac{[ij]}{z_{ij}}G^{\pm}(z_{j},\tilde{\lambda}_{j}+\tilde{\lambda}_{i}), $$

which in the 2D boundary theory should be interpreted as an operator product expansion (OPE) of a level-zero $\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ current algebra, also known as the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ algebra. Note that here the $\tilde{\lambda}_{i}$ are interpreted as color indices for the $\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ symmetry. (The other common celestial CFT presentation of the splitting functions in the Mellin basis [68, 26] is simply related to (7) by a change of basis for the generators of the $\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ algebra.) We have provided a review of the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ algebra, its connection to the splitting function, and its presentation in different bases in Appendix B.

We now explain how the $\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ OPE is related to our main result (2). Using the spinor choices (5), equation (2) says that Hodges’ formula for the stripped amplitude $M_{n}$ can be generated from a 2D celestial correlator that obeys the following two rules. The first rule is that the $n=3$ base case must satisfy

$$ \big\langle G^{-}(z_{1},\tilde{\lambda}_{1})\,G^{-}(z_{2},\tilde{\lambda}_{2})\,G^{+}(z_{3},\tilde{\lambda}_{3})\big\rangle=\frac{z_{12}^{8}}{z_{12}^{2}z_{23}^{2}z_{31}^{2}}, $$

which is the usual expression for $M_{3}$ . The second rule is that the $n$ -particle correlator must be determined by the $(n-1)$ -particle correlator using the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ Ward identity

$$ \begin{split}\begin{aligned} &\big\langle G^{-}(z_{1},\tilde{\lambda}_{1})\,G^{-}(z_{2},\tilde{\lambda}_{2})\ldots G^{+}(z_{n},\tilde{\lambda}_{n})\big\rangle\\
&\hskip 18.49411pt=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{[ni]}{z_{ni}}\big\langle G^{-}(z_{1},\tilde{\lambda}_{1})\,G^{-}(z_{2},\tilde{\lambda}_{2})\ldots G^{+}(z_{i},\tilde{\lambda}_{i}+\tilde{\lambda}_{n})\ldots G^{+}(z_{n-1},\tilde{\lambda}_{n-1})\big\rangle.\end{aligned}\end{split} $$

From (2), we see that these two rules automatically imply that

$$ \big\langle G^{-}(z_{1},\tilde{\lambda}_{1})\,G^{-}(z_{2},\tilde{\lambda}_{2})\ldots G^{+}(z_{n},\tilde{\lambda}_{n})\big\rangle=M_{n}, $$

and therefore the $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ Ward identity generates Hodges’ formula.

The rest of this paper is dedicated to the proof that (2) holds for any choice of the spinors $\lambda_{i}$ , $\tilde{\lambda}_{i}$ , $\alpha$ , not just the convenient ones in (5). The proof will employ the matrix-tree theorem [69],44 4 The matrix-tree theorem was also recently used to understand the MHV double copy in [70]. and is most directly inspired by recent results on perturbiner expansions in self-dual gravity and the relation of $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ symmetry to marked tree expansions [71, 72] (see in particular the proof of Theorem A.1 in [71]).

## 2 Hodges’ Formula, Forests, and Recursion

In this section, we prove (2) using Hodges’ formula [19] and the matrix-tree theorem [69]. The relevance of trees to the MHV amplitude was noted by NSVW in [20] and anticipated in [21]. We review the necessary ingredients in Subsection 2.1 and then provide the proof in Subsection 2.2.

### 2.1 Hodges’ Formula Expressed Using Forests

Consider the $n\times n$ matrix $\Psi$ with entries given by

$$ \Psi_{ij}=\begin{cases}-\frac{[ij]}{\langle ij\rangle}a_{i}a_{j}&i\neq j\\
\sum^{k=n}_{k=1,k\neq i}\frac{[ik]}{\langle ik\rangle}a_{i}a_{k}&i=j\end{cases}, $$

where

$$ a_{i}=\langle\alpha i\rangle^{2} $$

for an arbitrary reference spinor $\ket{\alpha}$ .

Hodges [19] showed that the tree-level graviton MHV amplitude can be written using the determinant of an $(n-3)\times(n-3)$ minor of $\Psi$ . In particular,55 5 In fact, Hodges [19] proved a more general form in which any three rows and any three columns can be removed and are not necessarily equal, and $a_{i}=\langle\alpha i\rangle\langle\beta i\rangle$ with $\ket{\alpha}$ and $\ket{\beta}$ separate arbitrary reference spinors. $\mathcal{M}_{n}$ is independent of $\ket{\alpha}$ , $\ket{\beta}$ and $S_{n}$ -permutation symmetric after momentum conservation is imposed [19]. We specialize to removing rows and columns 1,2,3 because our recursion will be applied to the base case $n=3$ , and we also set $\alpha=\beta$ . We further note that the NSVW tree formula [20] corresponds to the choice $\ket{\alpha}=\ket{1}$ , $\ket{\beta}=\ket{2}$ [69].

$$ M_{n}=\langle 12\rangle^{8}\,c_{123}^{2}\frac{(a_{1}a_{2}a_{3})^{2}}{(\prod_{\ell=1}^{n}a_{\ell})^{2}}|\Psi|^{123}_{123}, $$

where $|\Psi|^{123}_{123}$ denotes the determinant of the $(n-3)\times(n-3)$ minor of $\Psi$ with rows and columns $1,2,3$ removed, and

$$ c_{123}=\frac{1}{\langle 12\rangle\langle 23\rangle\langle 31\rangle}. $$

To prove (2), we use the matrix-tree theorem to rewrite $M_{n}$ , following Feng and He [69]. This theorem implies that for the matrix $\Psi$ defined in (11),

$$ |\Psi|^{123}_{123}=\sum_{F\in\mathcal{F}_{123}^{n}}\left(\prod_{e_{ij}\,\in\,\text{edges}(F)}-\Psi_{ij}\right), $$

where $\mathcal{F}_{123}^{n}$ is the set of rooted forests consisting of three rooted trees with roots $1,2,3$ and nodes taking values in $1,\ldots,n$ . A rooted tree with root $k$ is a tree containing the node $k$ , so the rooted forests have three disconnected trees with the roots $1,2,3$ each in a different tree (i.e. the nodes $1,2,3$ always appear in disconnected trees).

Using (13) and (15) we arrive at the forest formula

$$ \displaystyle M_{n} \displaystyle=\langle 12\rangle^{8}\left(c_{123}\frac{a_{1}a_{2}a_{3}}{\prod_{\ell=1}^{n}a_{\ell}}\right)^{2}\sum_{F\in\mathcal{F}_{123}^{n}}\left(\prod_{e_{ij}\,\in\,\text{edges}(F)}\frac{[ij]}{\langle ij\rangle}a_{i}a_{j}\right). $$

For concreteness, we now exhibit low-point examples at $n=3$ and $n=4$ . With $n=3$ , corresponding to

$$ M_{3}=\left(\frac{\langle 12\rangle^{4}}{\langle 12\rangle\langle 23\rangle\langle 31\rangle}\right)^{2}, $$

the only possible rooted forest of three trees is simply the three roots themselves, as illustrated in Figure 1. This will be the base of our recursion. When $n=4$ , we have

$$ M_{4}=\left(\frac{\langle 12\rangle^{4}}{\langle 12\rangle\langle 23\rangle\langle 31\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle\alpha 4\rangle^{2}}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{[14]}{\langle 14\rangle}\langle\alpha 1\rangle^{2}\langle\alpha 4\rangle^{2}+\frac{[24]}{\langle 24\rangle}\langle\alpha 2\rangle^{2}\langle\alpha 4\rangle^{2}+\frac{[34]}{\langle 34\rangle}\langle\alpha 3\rangle^{2}\langle\alpha 4\rangle^{2}\right), $$

which is represented by the sum over forests in Figure 2. In each forest, the edges carry the weights shown in Figure 3.
