## Appendix A Descendants as representations of Lorentz and Poincaré groups

### A.1 Descendants at fixed $\Delta$ as a finite dimensional irrep of the Lorentz group

At fixed conformal dimensional $\Delta=-\ell$ for $\ell\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ , there are $(\ell+1)^{2}$ descendants of the form $\mathsf{L}^{n}_{-1}\bar{\mathsf{L}}^{\bar{n}}_{-1}\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N}$ with $n$ and $\bar{n}$ ranging from $0$ to $\ell$ . (If $n>\ell$ of $\bar{n}>\ell$ , the descendant is 0.) In fact, these descendants can be understood as being built from two spin- $\ell/2$ representations of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ , which is also known as the finite dimensional $(\tfrac{\ell}{2},\tfrac{\ell}{2})$ representation of the Lorentz group. The purpose of this Appendix is to explicitly give the correspondence and illustrate how the $\mathsf{RSW}$ inner product relates to the standard inner product on $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ representations.

The $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ generators $\mathfrak{j}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,3$ have the commutation relations $[\mathfrak{j}_{i},\mathfrak{j}_{j}]=i\,\epsilon_{ijk}\mathfrak{j}_{k}.$ Defining the raising and lowering operators $\mathfrak{j}_{\pm}=\mathfrak{j}_{1}\pm i\,\mathfrak{j}_{2}$ , we have

$$ [\mathfrak{j}_{3},\mathfrak{j}_{\pm}]=\pm\mathfrak{j}_{\pm},\hskip 21.33955pt[\mathfrak{j}_{+},\mathfrak{j}_{-}]=2\mathfrak{j}_{3}. $$

In the spin $j$ representation of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ , the generators act on the state vectors $\ket{m,j}$ via

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{j}_{3}\ket{m, j} \displaystyle=m\ket{m, j} \displaystyle\mathfrak{j}_{\pm}\ket{m, j} \displaystyle=\sqrt{(j\mp m)(j\pm m+1)}\ket{m\pm 1, j} $$

where $m=j,\ldots,-j$ . Here we use the standard inner product $\innerproduct{m_1,j_1}{m_2,j_2}=\delta_{m_{1},m_{2}}\delta_{j_{1},j_{2}}$ . From (A.3), the norm of the states $\mathfrak{j}_{-}^{n}\ket{j, j}$ and $\mathfrak{j}_{+}^{n}\ket{-j, j}$ can be computed to be

$$ \bra{j,j}\mathfrak{j}_{+}^{n}\mathfrak{j}_{-}^{n}\ket{j,j}=\frac{n!(2j)!}{(2j-n)!},\hskip 28.45274pt\bra{-j,j}\mathfrak{j}_{-}^{n}\mathfrak{j}_{+}^{n}\ket{-j,j}=\frac{n!(2j)!}{(2j-n)!}. $$

If we define a second, independent set of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ generators denoted $\widetilde{\mathfrak{j}}_{\pm}$ and $\widetilde{\mathfrak{j}}_{3}$ , we can reproduce the $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C})$ commutation relations (2.4) via the identifications

$$ \begin{split}\mathfrak{j}_{+}&\leftrightarrow-\mathsf{L}_{1}\,,\\
\widetilde{\mathfrak{j}}_{+}&\leftrightarrow\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}\,,\end{split}\quad\quad\begin{split}\mathfrak{j}_{-}&\leftrightarrow\mathsf{L}_{-1}\,,\\
\widetilde{\mathfrak{j}}_{-}&\leftrightarrow-\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{+1}\,,\\
\end{split}\quad\quad\begin{split}\mathfrak{j}_{3}&\leftrightarrow-\mathsf{L}_{0}\,,\\
\widetilde{\mathfrak{j}}_{3}&\leftrightarrow\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{0}\,.\end{split} $$

In fact, using (2.3), the above identifications (A.5) are are equivalent to

$$ \begin{split}\mathfrak{j}_{i}&\;\leftrightarrow\;\frac{1}{2}(\mathsf{K}_{i}+i\mathsf{J}_{i})\,,\\
\widetilde{\mathfrak{j}}_{i}&\;\leftrightarrow\;\frac{1}{2}(-\mathsf{K}_{i}+i\mathsf{J}_{i}).\end{split} $$

This means that if $\mathfrak{j}_{i}$ and $\widetilde{\mathfrak{j}}_{i}$ generate the $j$ and $\widetilde{j}$ representations of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ , then the states can also be understood as transforming in the $(j,\widetilde{j})$ representation of the Lorentz group, which has dimension $(2j+1)\times(2\widetilde{j}+1)$ . Clearly, to make contact with the $(\ell+1)\times(\ell+1)$ dimensional space of $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C})$ descendants, we must set

$$ j=\tilde{j}=\frac{\ell}{2}. $$

Under this correspondence, the north and south pole primaries are the states

$$ \begin{split}\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N}\;&\leftrightarrow\;\ket{\tfrac{\ell}{2}, \tfrac{\ell}{2}}\otimes\ket{-\tfrac{\ell}{2}, \tfrac{\ell}{2}}\,,\\
\psi^{+}_{-\ell,S}\;&\leftrightarrow\;\ket{-\tfrac{\ell}{2}, \tfrac{\ell}{2}}\otimes\ket{\tfrac{\ell}{2}, \tfrac{\ell}{2}}\,.\\
\end{split} $$

If we define the “descendants” of our tensored spin- $\ell/2$ Hilbert spaces via

$$ \ket{n; \bar{n}}\vcentcolon=(\mathfrak{j}_{-})^{n}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{j}}_{+})^{\bar{n}}\ket{\tfrac{\ell}{2}, \tfrac{\ell}{2}}\otimes\ket{-\tfrac{\ell}{2},\tfrac{\ell}{2}}\,, $$

then these correspond directly to our $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C})$ descendants via

$$ \mathsf{L}_{-1}^{n}\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}^{\bar{n}}\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N}\;\leftrightarrow\;\ket{n; \bar{n}}. $$

In fact, from equations (4.7), (4.9), and (A.4), we can see that the $\mathsf{RSW}$ inner product is equal to the standard inner product of our $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ representations with the operator $(-1)^{\mathfrak{j}_{3}+\mathfrak{j}_{3}}$ inserted in between:

$$ \begin{split}\big(\mathsf{L}_{-1}^{n_{1}}\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}^{\bar{n}_{1}}\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N},\mathsf{L}_{-1}^{n_{2}}\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}^{\bar{n}_{2}}\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N}\big)_{\mathsf{RSW}}=(-4\pi^{2})\bra{n_1, \bar{n}_1}(-1)^{\mathfrak{j}_{3}+\widetilde{\mathfrak{j}}_{3}}\ket{n_2, \bar{n}_2}.\end{split} $$

Because the tensored $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ representation decomposes as

$$ \tfrac{\ell}{2}\otimes\tfrac{\ell}{2}=\ell\oplus(\ell-1)\oplus\ldots\oplus 1\oplus 0\,, $$

our states are in correspondence with the set of spherical harmonics with $j\leq\ell$ , namely

$$ \left\{Y_{jm}(\theta,\phi)\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\!\!\!j=0,\ldots,\ell\\
m=j,\ldots,-j\end{subarray}}. $$

Interestingly, this is the exact same construction one encounters in the BFSS matrix model for matrices of size $(\ell+1)$ via matrix regularization of functions on the sphere [36, 37].

### A.2 Discrete irreducible representations of the Poincaré group

The role of the momentum operators in the Poincaré algebra is to interlace the $(\tfrac{\ell}{2},\tfrac{\ell}{2})$ representations of the Lorentz group for different $\ell$ . Interestingly, the Poincaré representations formed from the shadowed and unshadowed primaries are quite different. While one could replace $\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N}\to\widetilde{\psi^{-}_{2+\ell,S}}$ in the previous Subsection and the essential representation theory of the Lorentz group would not change, this is not true when translations are brought into the mix.

Using the south pole pointing null vector $S^{\mu}=(1,0,0,-1)$ , it is straightforward to compute

$$ \displaystyle(S^{\mu}\mathsf{P}_{\mu})\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N} \displaystyle=-2\ell\,\psi^{+}_{-(\ell-1),N} \displaystyle(S^{\mu}\mathsf{P}_{\mu})\widetilde{\psi^{-}_{2+\ell,S}} \displaystyle=2(\ell+1)\widetilde{\psi^{-}_{2+(\ell+1),S}}\,. $$

Therefore, while the momentum operator sends $\ell\to\ell-1$ for the primary basis, it sends $\ell\to\ell+1$ for the shadow basis. Schematically, this can be represented as

$$ \begin{split}&\mathcal{C}:\hskip 28.45274pt\emptyset\overset{\mathsf{P}_{\mu}}{\longleftarrow}(0,0)\overset{\mathsf{P}_{\mu}}{\longleftarrow}(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2})\overset{\mathsf{P}_{\mu}}{\longleftarrow}(1,1)\overset{\mathsf{P}_{\mu}}{\longleftarrow}(\tfrac{3}{2},\tfrac{3}{2})\overset{\mathsf{P}_{\mu}}{\longleftarrow}(2,2)\overset{\mathsf{P}_{\mu}}{\longleftarrow}\cdots\\
&\widehat{\mathcal{C}}:\hskip 58.04343pt(0,0)\overset{\mathsf{P}_{\mu}}{\longrightarrow}(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2})\overset{\mathsf{P}_{\mu}}{\longrightarrow}(1,1)\overset{\mathsf{P}_{\mu}}{\longrightarrow}(\tfrac{3}{2},\tfrac{3}{2})\overset{\mathsf{P}_{\mu}}{\longrightarrow}(2,2)\overset{\mathsf{P}_{\mu}}{\longrightarrow}\cdots\end{split} $$

At a conceptual level, we can imagine $\mathcal{C}$ as being generated by acting the Poincaré algebra on a wavefunction with $\ell=\infty$ (or perhaps more precisely, we can generate more of $\mathcal{C}$ by acting the Poincaré algebra on wave functions with progressively large $\ell$ ), whereas $\widehat{\mathcal{C}}$ can be generated by instead using the wavefunction with $\ell=0$ .

## Appendix B Wightman function review

For pedagogical purposes, in this Appendix we review fundamental properties of the Wightman function. We begin with a purely classical approach, and then comment on its manifestation in quantum field theory with modified inner products.

### B.1 Classical perspective

Suppose we are given initial conditions $\phi(X^{0},\vec{X})$ , $\partial_{0}\phi(X^{0},\vec{X})$ to the massless Klein-Gordon equation on a time slice with fixed $X^{0}$ and would like to evolve to some other time slice $Y^{0}$ . Then the kernel

$$ K(X,Y)\vcentcolon=\frac{i}{4\pi}\frac{1}{|\vec{X}-\vec{Y}|}\Big(\delta(|\vec{X}-\vec{Y}|-(X^{0}-Y^{0}))-\delta(|\vec{X}-\vec{Y}|+(X^{0}-Y^{0}))\Big) $$

allows us to evolve our initial conditions by

$$ \phi(Y)=\big(K(X,Y)\,,\phi(X)\big)_{\mathrm{KG},\,X} $$

where the $X$ subscript on the Klein-Gordon inner product indicates an integration over $\vec{X}$ on a surface of constant $X^{0}$ . As such, if we can reproduce the kernel $K(X,Y)$ with our desired mode expansion, then we can fully solve the massless Klein-Gordon equation as a classical PDE.

The kernel $K(X,Y)$ can also be split up into its positive and negative frequency parts, as the so-called Wightman Green’s functions $G^{+}(X,Y)$ and $G^{-}(X,Y)$ ,

$$ G^{\pm}(X,Y)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{2}}\frac{1}{-(X^{0}-Y^{0}\mp i\epsilon)^{2}+(\vec{X}-\vec{Y})^{2}}=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{2}}\frac{1}{(X-Y)^{2}\pm i\epsilon\,\mathrm{sgn}(X^{0}-Y^{0})}. $$

It can be readily checked that

$$ K(X,Y)=G^{+}(X,Y)-G^{-}(X,Y). $$

### B.2 Quantum perspective

While $K(X,Y)$ and $G^{\pm}(X,Y)$ can be understood as purely classical objects, it is also worthwhile to understand how they are instantiated within quantum field theory.

Recall that the quantum creation and annihilation operators are defined via

$$ \displaystyle\hat{a}(f) \displaystyle\vcentcolon=(f,\hat{\phi})_{\mathrm{KG}} \displaystyle\hat{a}^{\dagger}(f) \displaystyle=-(f^{*},\hat{\phi})_{\mathrm{KG}} \displaystyle[\hat{a}(f),\hat{a}^{\dagger}(g)] \displaystyle=(f,g)_{\mathrm{KG}}\,. $$

If $f$ is a positive frequency wave function, meaning it is a linear combination of plane waves like $e^{ik\cdot X}$ for $k^{0}>0$ , then $\hat{a}(f)\ket{0}=0$ and we say $\hat{a}^{\dagger}(f)\ket{0}$ is a single particle state with wave function $f$ . If one has two such positive frequency wave functions, then the Klein-Gordon inner product coincides with the standard QFT inner product because $\bra{0}a(f_{1})\hat{a}^{\dagger}(f_{2})\ket{0}=(f_{1},f_{2})_{\rm KG}$ . Furthermore, it is straightforward to check that the Klein-Gordon inner product of a postive frequency wave function with a negative frequency wave function is always $0$ .

In some contexts (such as this paper), it is advantageous to make use of other norms besides the Klein-Gordon norm. Say one uses an invertible linear operator $\mathcal{O}$ to define the inner product

$$ \left(f,g\right)_{\mathcal{O}}\vcentcolon=(f,\mathcal{O}g)_{\rm KG} $$

and suppose a basis of positive frequency wave functions $f_{i}$ diagonalizes this inner product via

$$ \begin{split}(f_{i},f_{j})_{\mathcal{O}}&=\delta_{ij}M_{i},\\
(f_{i}^{*},f_{j}^{*})_{\mathcal{O}}&=-\delta_{ij}(M_{i})^{*},\\
(f_{i},f_{j}^{*})_{\mathcal{O}}&=0,\end{split} $$

for some constants $M_{i}$ . (Of course, in this particular paper, $\mathcal{O}=\mathsf{RSW}$ and the $f_{i}$ are given by the $\mathsf{L}_{-1}^{n}\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}^{\bar{n}}\psi^{+}_{\Delta,N}\in\mathcal{C}$ , but let us keep our discussion more general here.)

If $f_{i}$ is a complete basis of positive frequency wave functions, and $(\mathcal{O}f_{i})^{*}$ is a complete basis of negative frequency wave functions, then using (B.5) and (B.6) we can decompose the field operator $\hat{\phi}(X)$ as

$$ \hat{\phi}(X)=\sum_{i}\frac{1}{M_{i}^{*}}\left(f_{i}(X)\hat{a}(\mathcal{O}f_{i})+(\mathcal{O}f_{i})^{*}(X)\hat{a}^{\dagger}(f_{i})\right). $$

Returning to the Green’s functions, one can show via explicit computation that they are given by the non-time-ordered two point functions

$$ \begin{split}K(X,Y)&=\bra{0}[\;\hat{\phi}(X),\,\hat{\phi}(Y)\;]\ket{0},\\
G^{+}(X,Y)&=\bra{0}\hat{\phi}(X)\hat{\phi}(Y)\ket{0},\\
G^{-}(X,Y)&=\bra{0}\hat{\phi}(Y)\hat{\phi}(X)\ket{0}.\end{split} $$

In particular, we can now expand the two point function $\bra{0}\hat{\phi}(X)\hat{\phi}(Y)\ket{0}$ using the mode expansion (B.10). The result is

$$ G^{+}(X,Y)=\sum_{i}\frac{f_{i}(X)(\mathcal{O}f_{i})^{*}(Y)}{M_{i}^{*}}\,. $$

(Note that (5.2) in the main text is exactly this equation.) Equation (B.12) is useful for the following reason: if one is not sure whether or not the bases $f_{i}$ and $(\mathcal{O}f_{i})^{*}$ are complete bases of positive and negative frequency wave functions respectively, one can simply evaluate the right-hand side of the above equation and see if it matches the left-hand side given in (B.3). If they match, the proposed bases are indeed complete.

It turns out that the Wightman function $G^{+}(X,Y)$ can also be thought of as a decomposition of the identity operator for positive frequency wave functions, analogous to the expression $I=\sum_{i}\frac{\ket{i}\bra{i}}{\innerproduct{i}{i}}$ . To see this, one must simply take the Klein-Gordon inner product of $G^{+}(X,Y)$ and the initial data by integrating $X$ over a time slice and treating $Y$ as a constant. This is easiest to see by acting it on the function $\mathcal{O}f_{j}(X)$ and getting $\mathcal{O}f_{j}(Y)$ back out:

$$ \begin{split}\left(G^{+}(X,Y),\mathcal{O}f_{j}(X)\right)_{\mathrm{KG},X}&=\sum_{i}\frac{\mathcal{O}f_{i}(Y)}{M_{i}}\left(f_{i}(X),\mathcal{O}f_{j}(X)\right)_{\mathrm{KG},X}\\
&=\mathcal{O}f_{j}(Y).\end{split} $$

Viewing a full positive frequency solution in spacetime as a single state in our Hilbert space, we see that $G^{+}(X,Y)$ is precisely the identity operator on positive frequency wave functions when it is convolved in the Klein-Gordon inner product.

## Appendix C Proving Poincaré invariance of Wightman function decomposition

In this Appendix we will prove that the sum on the right-hand side of (5.2) is Poincaré invariant. The proof is essentially symbol pushing. We say a function $F(X,Y)$ is Poincaré invariant if

$$ F(\Lambda X+v,\Lambda Y+v)=F(X,Y) $$

for all Lorentz transformations $\Lambda$ and four-vectors $v$ . If we define an arbitrary element $\mathsf{A}$ of the Poincaré algebra in terms of basis elements (2.1) as

$$ \mathsf{A}=\theta^{i}\mathsf{J}_{i}+\phi^{i}\mathsf{K}_{i}+v^{\mu}\mathsf{P}_{\mu}\,, $$

then the infinitesimal version of (C.1) is

$$ \mathsf{A}_{X}F(X,Y)+\mathsf{A}_{Y}F(X,Y)=0\,, $$

where the subscripts in $\mathsf{A}_{X}$ and $\mathsf{A}_{Y}$ denote the differential operator $\mathsf{A}$ acting on the variable $X$ and $Y$ respectively.

Say we have a function $F$ which is defined by

$$ F(X,Y)\vcentcolon=\sum_{i}\frac{f_{i}(X)g_{i}^{*}(Y)}{M_{i}^{*}}\,, $$

where $g_{i}=(\mathsf{RSW})f_{i}$ and $(f_{i},g_{j})_{\rm KG}=\delta_{ij}M_{i}$ . We further define the matrices $a_{i}^{\;i^{\prime}}$ and $b^{j^{\prime}}_{\;j}$ via the equations

$$ \mathsf{A}f_{i}=\sum_{k}a_{i}^{\;k}f_{k},\hskip 28.45274pt\mathsf{A}g_{j}=\sum_{k}g_{k}b^{k}_{\;j}. $$

Here we require that $\mathsf{A}f_{i}$ and $\mathsf{A}g_{j}$ can both be written as linear combinations of $f_{i}$ ’s and $g_{j}$ ’s respectively, (i.e., that the sets $f_{i}$ and $g_{j}$ are closed under the Poincaré algebra) but crucially we do not need to assume that the combined set of $f_{i}$ ’s and $g_{j}$ ’s are complete.

The Poincaré invariance of the Klein-Gordon inner product can be written as

$$ (\mathsf{A}f_{i},g_{j})_{\rm KG}+(f_{i},\mathsf{A}g_{j})_{\rm KG}=0 $$

where we have used $\mathsf{A}^{\dagger}=-\mathsf{A}$ . The above equation is equivalent to

$$ (a_{i}^{\;j})^{*}M_{j}+M_{i}b^{i}_{\;j}=0. $$

Complex conjugating the above equation and dividing by $M_{i}^{*}M_{j}^{*}$ gives

$$ \frac{1}{M_{i}^{*}}a_{i}^{\;j}+\frac{1}{M_{j}^{*}}(b^{i}_{\;j})^{*}=0. $$

Finally, we compute

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{A}_{X}F(X,Y)+\mathsf{A}_{Y}F(X,Y) \displaystyle=\sum_{i}\frac{1}{M_{i}^{*}}\left((\mathsf{A}f_{i})(X)g^{*}_{i}(X)+f_{i}(X)(\mathsf{A}g_{i})^{*}(Y)\right) \displaystyle=\sum_{i,j}\frac{1}{M_{i}^{*}}(a_{i}^{\;j}f_{j}(X)g^{*}_{i}(Y)+f_{i}(X)g^{*}_{j}(Y)(b^{j}_{\;i})^{*}) \displaystyle=\sum_{i,j}\left(\frac{1}{M_{i}^{*}}a_{i}^{\;j}+\frac{1}{M_{j}^{*}}(b^{i}_{\;j})^{*}\right)f_{j}(X)g_{i}^{*}(Y) \displaystyle=0 $$

which concludes the proof that $F(X,Y)$ is Poincaré invariant.

## Appendix D Computing $M_{\ell,n,\bar{n}}$ from Poincaré symmetry

We will now show how the $M_{\ell,n,\bar{n}}$ coefficients of (4.9) can be determined from Poincaré symmetry up to an overall multiplicative constant.

Before doing so, it is worth explaining why the the $\mathsf{RSW}$ inner product between $\mathsf{L}^{n}_{-1}\bar{\mathsf{L}}^{\bar{n}}_{-1}\psi^{\pm}_{-\ell,N}$ and $\mathsf{L}^{n^{\prime}}_{-1}\bar{\mathsf{L}}^{\bar{n}^{\prime}}_{-1}\psi^{\pm}_{-\ell^{\prime},N}$ is only non-zero if $n=n^{\prime}$ , $\bar{n}=\bar{n}^{\prime}$ , and $\ell=\ell^{\prime}$ , as indicated in (4.7). First, note that $\mathsf{L}_{\pm 1}$ and $\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{\pm 1}$ are raising and lowering operators with respect to $\mathsf{L}_{0}$ and $\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{0}$ . This implies that $\mathsf{L}^{n}_{-1}\bar{\mathsf{L}}^{\bar{n}}_{-1}\psi^{\pm}_{-\ell,N}$ is an eigenstate of $\mathsf{L}_{0}$ and $\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{0}$ with eigenvalues $-\ell/2+n$ and $-\ell/2+\bar{n}$ , respectively. Because $\mathsf{L}_{0}^{{\dagger_{\mathsf{RSW}}}}=\mathsf{L}_{0}$ and $\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{0}^{{\dagger_{\mathsf{RSW}}}}=\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{0}$ , we have that $\mathsf{L}_{0}$ and $\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{0}$ are self-adjoint with respect to the $\mathsf{RSW}$ inner product. By basic linear algebra, this means that wave functions which are eigenstates of $\mathsf{L}_{0}$ and $\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{0}$ with different eigenvalues must have an inner product of 0.

Let us now compute the recursion relation between $M_{\ell,n,\bar{n}}$ and $M_{\ell,n-1,\bar{n}}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle M_{\ell,n,\bar{n}} \displaystyle=\left(\mathsf{L}_{-1}^{n}\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}^{\bar{n}}\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N},\mathsf{L}_{-1}^{n}\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}^{\bar{n}}\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N}\right)_{\mathsf{RSW}} \displaystyle=\left(\mathsf{L}_{-1}^{n-1}\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}^{\bar{n}}\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N},\mathsf{L}_{1}\mathsf{L}_{-1}^{n}\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}^{\bar{n}}\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N}\right)_{\mathsf{RSW}} \displaystyle=2\big((-\ell/2+n-1)+(-\ell/2+n-2)+\ldots+(-\ell/2)\big)\left(\mathsf{L}_{-1}^{n-1}\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}^{\bar{n}}\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N},\mathsf{L}_{-1}^{n-1}\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}^{\bar{n}}\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N}\right)_{\mathsf{RSW}} \displaystyle=n(n-\ell-1)M_{\ell,n-1,\bar{n}}\,, $$

where in the second line we used $\mathsf{L}_{-1}^{{\dagger_{\mathsf{RSW}}}}=\mathsf{L}_{1}$ , in the third line we commuted $\mathsf{L}_{1}$ past each instance of $\mathsf{L}_{-1}$ using $[\mathsf{L}_{1},\mathsf{L}_{-1}]=2\mathsf{L}_{0}$ until $\mathsf{L}_{1}$ annihilated $\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}^{\bar{n}}\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N}$ at the end, and along the way used that $\mathsf{L}_{-1}^{n}\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}^{\bar{n}}\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N}$ is an eigenstate of $\mathsf{L}_{0}$ with eigenvalue $-\ell/2+n$ .

Likewise, we also have the recursion relation

$$ M_{\ell,n,\bar{n}}=\bar{n}(\bar{n}-\ell-1)M_{\ell,n,\bar{n}-1}. $$

Solving the recursion relations (D.1) and (D.2), we have

$$ M_{\ell,n,\bar{n}}=(-1)^{n+\bar{n}}\frac{n!\,\ell!}{(\ell-n)!}\frac{\bar{n}!\,\ell!}{(\ell-\bar{n})!}M_{\ell,0,0}. $$

Having made full use of Lorentz symmetry, we must use the momentum operators $\mathsf{P}^{\mu}$ to create a recursion relation between $M_{\ell,0,0}$ and $M_{\ell-1,0,0}$ . (Actually, one can compute $M_{\ell,0,0}$ for all $\ell$ directly from (3.6) (just set $z_{1}=z_{2}=0$ ) finding $M_{\ell,0,0}=-(2\pi)^{2}$ , but it is nice give a symmetry argument as well.)

We need to use a translation operator which changes $\ell$ . For simplicity, we use the specific translation operator $S^{\mu}\mathsf{P}_{\mu}$ , where $S^{\mu}=(1,0,0,-1)$ is the south pointing null vector

On the primary states, we can directly compute

$$ (S^{\mu}\mathsf{P}_{\mu})\psi^{\pm}_{-\ell,N}=-2\ell\,\psi^{\pm}_{-\ell+1,N}. $$

On the shadowed states $(\mathsf{RSW})\psi^{\pm}_{-\ell+1,N}=\widetilde{\psi^{\pm}_{\ell+1,S}}$ , we can also directly compute

$$ (S^{\mu}\mathsf{P}_{\mu})(\mathsf{RSW})\psi^{\pm}_{-\ell+1,N}=2\ell\,(\mathsf{RSW})\psi^{\pm}_{-\ell,N}. $$

Using $(S^{\mu}\mathsf{P}_{\mu})^{\dagger}=-S^{\mu}\mathsf{P}_{\mu}$ , we find

$$ \displaystyle((S^{\mu}\mathsf{P}_{\mu})\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N},(\mathsf{RSW})\psi^{+}_{-\ell+1,N})_{\mathrm{KG}} \displaystyle=-(\psi^{+}_{-\ell,N},(S^{\mu}\mathsf{P}_{\mu})(\mathsf{RSW})\psi^{+}_{-\ell+1,N})_{\mathrm{KG}} $$

which upon using (D.4) and (D.5) becomes44 4 More precisely, the recursion relation is $\ell M_{\ell+1,0,0}=\ell M_{\ell,0,0}$ . In order to divide by $\ell$ in the $\ell=0$ case, we must take the limit $\ell\to 0$ and not plug in $\ell=0$ directly.

$$ M_{(\ell+1),0,0}=M_{\ell,0,0}\,. $$

This is our new recursion relation. Combining (D.3) and (D.7), we have

$$ M_{\ell,n,\bar{n}}=(-1)^{n+\bar{n}}\frac{n!\,\ell!}{(\ell-n)!}\frac{\bar{n}!\,\ell!}{(\ell-\bar{n})!}M_{0,0,0} $$

which determines $M_{\ell,n,\bar{n}}$ up to a multiplicative constant which turns out to be $M_{0,0,0}=-(2\pi)^{2}$ .

## Appendix E Expression for descendants on the $X^{1}=X^{2}=0$ plane

We set $\Delta=-\ell$ where $\ell\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ . We begin by considering which wave functions $\mathsf{L}^{n}_{-1}\bar{\mathsf{L}}^{\bar{n}}_{-1}\psi_{-\ell,N}(X)$ are nonzero when $X^{1}=X^{2}=0$ . Noting that $\psi_{-\ell,N}(X)=(X^{0}-X^{3})^{\ell}$ , all we must do is study the repeated action of $\mathsf{L}_{-1}$ and $\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}$ on $(X^{0}-X^{3})$ . It is straightforward to compute

$$ \begin{split}\mathsf{L}_{-1}(X^{0}-X^{3})&=-X^{1}+iX^{2},\\
\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}(X^{0}-X^{3})&=-X^{1}-iX^{2},\end{split}\quad\quad\quad\begin{split}(\mathsf{L}_{-1})^{2}(X^{0}-X^{3})&=0,\\
(\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1})^{2}(X^{0}-X^{3})&=0,\end{split} $$

$$ \mathsf{L}_{-1}\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}(X^{0}-X^{3})=X^{0}+X^{3}. $$

The above equations imply that, if one is to compute $\mathsf{L}^{n}_{-1}\bar{\mathsf{L}}^{\bar{n}}_{-1}(X^{0}-X^{3})^{\ell}$ using the product rule of differentiation, the only terms which will be non-zero when $X^{1}=X^{2}=0$ will be terms where each factor of $(X^{0}-X^{3})$ which was acted on by one $\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{-1}$ was then subsequently acted on by one $\mathsf{L}_{-1}$ . (Note that this can only hold when $n=\bar{n}$ .) By a combinatorial argument, the number of such terms will be $n!\,\ell!/(\ell-n)!$ , so we have

$$ (\mathsf{L}^{n}_{-1}\bar{\mathsf{L}}^{\bar{n}}_{-1}\psi_{-\ell,N})(X^{0},0,0,X^{3})=\begin{cases}\frac{n!\,\ell!}{(\ell-n)!}(X^{0}-X^{3})^{\ell-n}(X^{0}+X^{3})^{n}&n=\bar{n}\\
0&n\neq\bar{n}\end{cases}. $$

Let us now do the analogous computation for the shadowed modes. We can once again compute

$$ \begin{split}\mathsf{L}_{1}(X^{0}+X^{3})&=X^{1}+iX^{2},\\
\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{1}(X^{0}+X^{3})&=X^{1}-iX^{2},\end{split}\quad\quad\quad\begin{split}(\mathsf{L}_{1})^{2}(X^{0}+X^{3})&=0,\\
(\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{1})^{2}(X^{0}+X^{3})&=0,\end{split} $$

$$ \mathsf{L}_{1}\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{1}(X^{0}+X^{3})=X^{0}-X^{3}. $$

Using the equation $\widetilde{\psi_{2+\ell,S}}=(-X^{\mu}X_{\mu})^{-\ell-1}(X^{0}+X^{3})^{\ell}$ and noting that $\mathsf{L}_{1}(X^{\mu}X_{\mu})=\bar{\mathsf{L}}_{1}(X^{\mu}X_{\mu})=0$ , we can repeat our previous analysis to obtain

$$ (\mathsf{L}^{n}_{1}\,\bar{\mathsf{L}}^{\bar{n}}_{1}\,\widetilde{\psi_{2+\ell,S}})(X^{0},0,0,X^{3})=\begin{cases}\frac{n!\,\ell!}{(\ell-n)!}(X^{0}+X^{3})^{-n-1}(X^{0}-X^{3})^{n-\ell-1}&n=\bar{n}\\
0&n\neq\bar{n}\end{cases}. $$

We conclude with the interesting observation that if we take $n=\bar{n}=\ell$ , our north pole primaries are sent to the south pole and vice versa:

$$ \mathsf{L}^{\ell}_{-1}\bar{\mathsf{L}}^{\ell}_{-1}\psi_{-\ell,N}=(\ell!)^{2}\psi_{-\ell,S}\hskip 28.45274pt\mathsf{L}^{\ell}_{1}\,\bar{\mathsf{L}}^{\ell}_{1}\,\widetilde{\psi_{2+\ell,S}}=(\ell!)^{2}\widetilde{\psi_{2+\ell,N}}. $$

## Appendix F Inner product integrals

### F.1 Klein-Gordon inner product of primaries

In this Appendix we will derive the formula for the Klein-Gordon inner product of two conformal primary modes

$$ \displaystyle\left(\psi^{\pm}_{-n,q(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})},\psi^{\pm}_{-m,q(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2})}\right)_{\mathrm{KG}} \displaystyle=\mp\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{|n-m|}\delta^{2}(z_{1}-z_{2})\delta_{n+m,-2} \displaystyle\left(\psi^{\pm}_{-n,q(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})},\psi^{\mp}_{-m,q(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2})}\right)_{\mathrm{KG}} \displaystyle=0 $$

for $n\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ , $m\in\{-2,-3,-4,\ldots\}$ or $m\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ , $n\in\{-2,-3,-4,\ldots\}$ . Strictly speaking, these inner products involve integrals that must be computed using a regularization which shall be given, and whichever of $n$ or $m$ is in the set $\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ must be evaluated in the limit that it approaches said integer.

#### F.1.1 $\pm\pm$ case

We start with the $++$ case. The Klein-Gordon inner product can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\left(\psi_{-n,q(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})}^{+},\psi_{-m,q(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2})}^{+}\right)_{\mathrm{KG}}=i\,m\,q^{0}(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2})\;\mathcal{I}^{++}(n,m-1)-i\,n\,q^{0}(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})\;\mathcal{I}^{++}(n-1,m) $$

where the integrals $\mathcal{I^{\pm\pm}}(n,m)$ are defined on the $X^{0}=0$ slice via

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{I}^{++}(n,m) \displaystyle=\int d^{3}X(-\vec{q}(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})\cdot\vec{X}+i\epsilon)^{n}(-\vec{q}(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2})\cdot\vec{X}-i\epsilon)^{m} \displaystyle\mathcal{I}^{--}(n,m) \displaystyle=\int d^{3}X(-\vec{q}(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})\cdot\vec{X}-i\epsilon)^{n}(-\vec{q}(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2})\cdot\vec{X}+i\epsilon)^{m} \displaystyle\mathcal{I}^{+-}(n,m) \displaystyle=\int d^{3}X(-\vec{q}(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})\cdot\vec{X}+i\epsilon)^{n}(-\vec{q}(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2})\cdot\vec{X}+i\epsilon)^{m} \displaystyle\mathcal{I}^{-+}(n,m) \displaystyle=\int d^{3}X(-\vec{q}(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})\cdot\vec{X}-i\epsilon)^{n}(-\vec{q}(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2})\cdot\vec{X}-i\epsilon)^{m} $$

where the four integrals have different combinations of signs of the $i\epsilon$ ’s.

In order to compute these integrals, we will employ the use of the Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative

$$ {}_{\lambda}D^{p}_{\alpha}f(\alpha)=\begin{cases}\left(\frac{d}{d\alpha}\right)^{k}\frac{1}{\Gamma(k-p)}\int_{\lambda}^{\alpha}(\alpha-\alpha^{\prime})^{k-p-1}f(\alpha^{\prime})d\alpha^{\prime}&\hskip 28.45274pt\text{ if }p>0,p\notin\mathbb{Z}\\
\frac{1}{\Gamma(|p|)}\int_{\lambda}^{\alpha}(\alpha-\alpha^{\prime})^{|p|-1}f(\alpha^{\prime})d\alpha^{\prime}&\hskip 28.45274pt\text{ if }p<0\end{cases} $$

where $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ . This operator mimics both differentiation and integration depending on the sign of $p$ . The reader should be aware that ${}_{\lambda}D^{p}_{\alpha}$ is ill-defined when $p$ is a non-negative integer $p=0,1,2,\ldots$ . If we ever wish to calculate ${}_{\lambda}D^{p}_{\alpha}f(\alpha)$ when $p$ is one of these integers, we must do so with a limit $\lim_{p^{\prime}\to p}({}_{\lambda}D^{p^{\prime}}_{\alpha}f(\alpha))$ . This observation will become important later on.

An important property the operator ${}_{\lambda}D^{p}_{\alpha}$ satisfies is

$$ \begin{split}\lim_{\alpha\to 0^{+}}\big[{}_{+\infty}D^{p}_{\alpha}(e^{iA\alpha})\big]=(iA)^{p}&\hskip 14.22636pt\text{ if }\Im{A}>0\text{ for all }{p}\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\\
\lim_{\beta\to 0^{-}}\big[{}_{-\infty}D^{p}_{\beta}(e^{iA\beta})\big]=(iA)^{p}&\hskip 14.22636pt\text{ if }\Im{A}<0\text{ for all }{p}\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.\end{split} $$

The prescribed direction of the limits $\alpha\to 0^{+}$ and $\beta\to 0^{-}$ in the above equations, which depend on the sign of $\Im{A}$ , is needed in the forthcoming steps so that ${}_{+\infty}D^{p}_{\alpha}$ and ${}_{-\infty}D^{p}_{\beta}$ reproduce expected derivative properties when the real part of $A$ is integrated over.55 5 Here we elaborate on the direction of the limit of $\alpha\to 0$ . Without loss of generality, take $\Im{A}=\epsilon>0$ where $\epsilon$ is small. Consider the integral $I(\alpha)=\int_{-\infty+i\epsilon}^{+\infty+i\epsilon}\frac{dA}{2\pi}e^{iA\alpha}=\delta(\alpha)$ . We want ${}_{+\infty}D^{p}_{\alpha}I(\alpha)$ to mimic the expected behavior of $\partial_{\alpha}^{p}\delta(\alpha)$ for $p>0$ , in particular that $\lim_{\alpha\to 0}\partial_{\alpha}^{p}\delta(\alpha)=0$ . So, which direction for the limit of $\alpha\to 0$ should we take for ${}_{+\infty}D^{p}_{\alpha}I(\alpha)$ to be guaranteed to be zero, for $p\notin\mathbb{Z}$ ? Inspecting ${}_{+\infty}D^{p}_{\alpha}I(\alpha)=\int_{-\infty+i\epsilon}^{+\infty+i\epsilon}\frac{dA}{2\pi}(iA)^{p}e^{iA\alpha}$ , we have a branch cut from the fractional exponent $A^{p}$ for $A$ on the negative real axis. This branch cut is avoided by the contour of integration which runs from $-\infty+i\epsilon$ to $+\infty+i\epsilon$ . In order to close the contour of the $A$ integral in the upper half plane and show the integral is zero, we need for $\alpha>0$ . Therefore, the correct direction of the $\alpha\to 0$ limit is $\alpha\to 0^{+}$ for $\Im{A}>0$ . Likewise, we require $\alpha\to 0^{-}$ for $\Im{A}<0$ .

We now use the Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative and (F.9) to express $\mathcal{I}^{++}(n,m)$ via

$$ \mathcal{I}^{++}(n,m)=(-i)^{n+m}\lim_{\alpha\to 0^{+}}({}_{+\infty}D^{n}_{\alpha})\lim_{\beta\to 0^{-}}({}_{-\infty}D^{m}_{\beta})\int d^{3}Xe^{i\alpha(-\vec{q}(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})\cdot\vec{X}+i\epsilon)}e^{i\beta(-\vec{q}(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2})\cdot\vec{X}-i\epsilon)} $$

where the integral on the right-hand side of the above equation evaluates to

$$ \displaystyle\ \int d^{3}Xe^{i\alpha(-\vec{q}(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})\cdot\vec{X}+i\epsilon)}e^{i\beta(-\vec{q}(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2})\cdot\vec{X}-i\epsilon)} \displaystyle=(2\pi)^{3}\delta^{3}(\alpha\vec{q}(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})+\beta\vec{q}(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2}))e^{\epsilon(\beta-\alpha)} \displaystyle=-\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{4\alpha\beta}\frac{\delta^{2}(z_{1}-z_{2})}{q^{0}(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})}\delta(\alpha+\beta)e^{\epsilon(\beta-\alpha)}. $$

Plugging (F.12) into (F.10) gives

$$ \mathcal{I}^{++}(n,m)=-(-i)^{n+m}\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{4}\frac{\delta^{2}(z_{1}-z_{2})}{q^{0}(z_{1},{\bar{z}}_{1})}\lim_{\alpha\to 0^{+}}({}_{+\infty}D^{n}_{\alpha})\lim_{\beta\to 0^{-}}({}_{-\infty}D^{m}_{\beta})\frac{e^{\epsilon(\beta-\alpha)}}{\alpha\beta}\delta(\alpha+\beta). $$

One may then compute

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\alpha\to 0^{+}}({}_{+\infty}D^{n}_{\alpha})\;\lim_{\beta\to 0^{-}}({}_{-\infty}D^{m}_{\beta})\;\frac{e^{\epsilon(\beta-\alpha)}}{\alpha\beta}\delta(\alpha+\beta) \displaystyle=\lim_{\alpha\to 0^{+}}({}_{+\infty}D^{n}_{\alpha})\;\frac{-1}{\Gamma(-m)}\alpha^{-m-3}e^{-2\epsilon\alpha}\Theta(\alpha) \displaystyle=\frac{\Gamma(-3-n-m)}{\Gamma(-n)\Gamma(-m)}(-1)^{n+1}(2\epsilon)^{3+n+m}. $$

Plugging (F.15) into (F.13) gives

$$ \mathcal{I}^{++}(n,m)=i^{n-m}\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{4}\frac{\delta^{2}(z_{1}-z_{2})}{q^{0}(z_{1},{\bar{z}}_{1})}\frac{\Gamma(-3-n-m)}{\Gamma(-n)\Gamma(-m)}(2\epsilon)^{3+n+m} $$

and plugging (F.16) this into (F.3) we get

$$ \left(\psi_{-n,q(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})}^{+},\psi_{-m,q(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2})}^{+}\right)_{\mathrm{KG}}=\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{2}\delta^{2}(z_{1}-z_{2})i^{n-m}\frac{\Gamma(-2-n-m)}{\Gamma(-n)\Gamma(-m)}(2\epsilon)^{2+n+m}. $$

In this final step, we must recall that the Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative is not defined at positive integer values, and a limit must be taken. Let us first assume that $n\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ and $m\in\{-2,-3,-4,\ldots\}$ . While we can plug $m$ directly into the above formula, $n$ must be taken as a limit approaching an integer. If we then take the $\epsilon\to 0^{+}$ limit afterwards, we get

$$ \begin{split}\lim_{\epsilon\to 0^{+}}\lim_{n^{\prime}\to n}i^{n^{\prime}-m}\frac{\Gamma(-2-n^{\prime}-m)}{\Gamma(-n^{\prime})\Gamma(-m)}(2\epsilon)^{2+n^{\prime}+m}=\frac{-1}{n+1}\delta_{n+m,-2}\hskip 14.22636pt\text{ for }\hskip 14.22636pt\begin{subarray}{c}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!n\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\\
m\in\{-2,-3,-4,\ldots\}\end{subarray}.\end{split} $$

Likewise, if we instead take $n\in\{-2,-3,-4,\ldots\}$ and $m\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ , we get

$$ \lim_{\epsilon\to 0^{+}}\lim_{m^{\prime}\to m}i^{n-m^{\prime}}\frac{\Gamma(-2-n-m^{\prime})}{\Gamma(-n)\Gamma(-m^{\prime})}(2\epsilon)^{2+n+m^{\prime}}=\frac{-1}{m+1}\delta_{n+m,-2}\hskip 14.22636pt\text{ for }\hskip 14.22636pt\begin{subarray}{c}n\in\{-2,-3,-4,\ldots\}\\
\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!m\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\end{subarray}. $$

Plugging the above two equations into (F.17), we can write the combined result as

$$ \left(\psi_{-n,q(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})}^{+},\psi_{-m,q(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2})}^{+}\right)_{\mathrm{KG}}=-\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{|n-m|}\delta^{2}(z_{1}-z_{2})\delta_{n+m,-2} $$

as desired, which holds for both the case $n\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ , $m\in\{-2,-3,-4,\ldots\}$ as well as the case $n\in\{-2,-3,-4,\ldots\}$ , $m\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ . This completes the computation of the $++$ case of (F.1).

Note that from the identity $(f^{*},g^{*})_{\rm KG}=-(f,g)_{\rm KG}^{*}$ we obtain the $-$ $-$ case of (F.1) as well.

#### F.1.2 $\pm\mp$ case

We start with the $+-$ case of (F.2). The Klein-Gordon inner product can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\left(\psi_{-n,q(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})}^{+},\psi_{-m,q(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2})}^{-}\right)_{\mathrm{KG}}=i\,m\,q^{0}(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2})\;\mathcal{I}^{+-}(n,m-1)-i\,n\,q^{0}(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})\;\mathcal{I}^{+-}(n-1,m) $$

and following a similar logic as the last section, the integral $\mathcal{I}^{+-}(n,m)$ is given by

$$ \mathcal{I}^{+-}(n,m)=-(-i)^{n+m}\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{4}\frac{\delta^{2}(z_{1}-z_{2})}{q^{0}(z_{1},{\bar{z}}_{1})}\lim_{\alpha\to 0^{+}}({}_{+\infty}D^{n}_{\alpha})\lim_{\beta\to 0^{+}}({}_{+\infty}D^{m}_{\beta})\frac{e^{\epsilon(-\alpha-\beta)}}{\alpha\beta}\delta(\alpha+\beta). $$

One may then compute

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{\alpha\to 0^{+}}({}_{+\infty}D^{n}_{\alpha})\lim_{\beta\to 0^{+}}({}_{+\infty}D^{m}_{\beta})\;\frac{e^{\epsilon(-\alpha-\beta)}}{\alpha\beta}\delta(\alpha+\beta) \displaystyle=\lim_{\alpha\to 0^{+}}({}_{+\infty}D^{n}_{\alpha})\;\frac{1}{\Gamma(-m)}\alpha^{-m-3}\Theta(-\alpha)=0\,. $$

which implies

$$ \mathcal{I}^{+-}(n,m)=0. $$

Accordingly, we have

$$ \displaystyle\left(\psi_{-n,q(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})}^{+},\psi_{-m,q(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2})}^{-}\right)_{\mathrm{KG}}=0\,. $$

which completes the proof of the $+-$ case of (F.2). Once again, from the identity $(f^{*},g^{*})_{\rm KG}=-(f,g)_{\rm KG}^{*}$ we obtain the $-$ $+$ case of (F.2) as well.

### F.2 $\mathsf{RSW}$ inner product

In this Appendix we will compute the $\mathsf{RSW}$ inner products of the conformal primary wave functions using the previously calculated Klein-Gordon inner products (F.1) and (F.2). For $n,m\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ , we will find that the $\mathsf{RSW}$ inner products are

$$ \displaystyle\left(\psi^{\pm}_{-n,q(z_{1},{\bar{z}}_{1})},(\mathsf{RSW})\psi^{\pm}_{-m,q(z_{2},{\bar{z}}_{2})}\right)_{\mathrm{KG}} \displaystyle=\mp(2\pi)^{2}|1-z_{1}{\bar{z}}_{2}|^{2n}\delta_{n,m} \displaystyle\left(\psi^{\pm}_{-n,q(z_{1},{\bar{z}}_{1})},(\mathsf{RSW})\psi^{\mp}_{-m,q(z_{2},{\bar{z}}_{2})}\right)_{\mathrm{KG}} \displaystyle=0\,. $$

Equation (F.27) follows directly from (F.2). We now carry out the computation of (F.26) by acting $\mathsf{W}$ , $\mathsf{S}$ , and $\mathsf{R}$ successively on the second term in the Klein-Gordon inner product, using (F.1) as our starting point. Applying $\mathsf{W}$ to (F.1) just sends $m\to-2-m$ and we get

$$ \left(\psi^{\pm}_{-n,q(z_{1},{\bar{z}}_{1})},(\mathsf{W})\psi^{\pm}_{-m,q(z_{2},{\bar{z}}_{2})}\right)_{\mathrm{KG}}=\mp\frac{(2\pi)^{3}}{2(n+1)}\delta^{2}(z_{1}-z_{2})\delta_{n,m}. $$

We then insert the shadow operator $\mathsf{S}$ into the above equation. Using the definition of $\mathsf{S}$ given in (3.1), it is straightforward to compute

$$ \left(\psi^{\pm}_{-n,q(z_{1},\bar{z}_{1})},(\mathsf{SW})\psi^{\pm}_{-m,q(z_{2},\bar{z}_{2})}\right)_{\mathrm{KG}}=\mp(2\pi)^{2}|z_{1}-z_{2}|^{2n}\delta_{n,m}. $$

Now we must finally act with $\mathsf{R}$ . Here we note the identity

$$ \mathsf{R}q(z,{\bar{z}})=|z|^{2}\,q(1/{\bar{z}},1/z) $$

from which we compute

$$ (\mathsf{R})\widetilde{\psi}_{2+m,q(z,{\bar{z}})}=\frac{(-(\mathsf{R}q(z,{\bar{z}}))\cdot X)^{m}}{(-X^{\mu}X_{\mu})^{1+m}}=|z|^{2m}\widetilde{\psi^{\pm}}_{2+m,q(1/{\bar{z}},1/z)}. $$

If we insert $\mathsf{R}$ into (F.29) and use (F.31), we then get

$$ \begin{split}\left(\psi^{\pm}_{-n,q(z_{1},{\bar{z}}_{1})},(\mathsf{RSW})\psi^{\pm}_{-m,q(z_{2},{\bar{z}}_{2})}\right)_{\mathrm{KG}}&=\mp(2\pi)^{2}|z_{2}|^{2m}|z_{1}-1/{\bar{z}}_{2}|^{2n}\delta_{n,m}\\
&=\mp(2\pi)^{2}|1-z_{1}{\bar{z}}_{2}|^{2n}\delta_{n,m}\end{split} $$

which completes the proof of (F.26).

### F.3 Relation to previous literature

Previous literature [3] has used another normalization convention for the conformal primary states $\psi^{\pm}_{\Delta,q}$ defined in (2.5), differing by a factor of $(\mp i)^{\Delta}\Gamma(\Delta)$ . The Klein-Gordon inner product of such states is proportional to the Dirac delta distribution $\delta(i(2-\Delta_{1}^{*}-\Delta_{2}))$ .

We stripped the $(\mp i)^{\Delta}\Gamma(\Delta)$ prefactor off of our definition because we are studying integer modes and $\Gamma(\Delta)$ diverges at $\Delta\in\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}$ . This is why we had to re-compute the Klein-Gordon inner products from scratch using different integration techniques. However, if we naïvely divide the Klein-Gordon inner product in [3] by these divergent $\Gamma(\Delta)$ factors, we can reproduce our KG equations (F.1) and (F.2) if we use the ad-hoc replacement rules $\delta(i(2+n+m))\mapsto\delta(0)\delta_{n+m,-2}$ and $\frac{\delta(0)}{\Gamma(0)}\mapsto\frac{1}{2\pi}$ .

## Appendix G $\mathsf{SW}$ as a spacetime integral transform

The shadow operator $\mathsf{S}$ is defined as an integral over the momentum coordinate $q(z,\bar{z})$ in (3.1). However, the combined operator $\mathsf{SW}$ is actually a well-known integral transform over the spacetime coordinate $X$ on the null cone. This integral transform is known among mathematicians and is used to construct the inner product for the discrete series representation of the Lorentz group, see for instance Vol. 2, Sections 9.2.7 and 9.2.8 of [38].

We define $\widetilde{\mathsf{S}}$ via the position integral over a 2D slice of the null cone (denoted $\int d^{2}Y$ , see [35] for a review of these kinds of embedding space integrals) via

$$ \widetilde{\mathsf{S}}(-q\cdot X)^{-\Delta}\vcentcolon=\frac{1-\Delta}{\pi}\int d^{2}Y(-2X\cdot Y)^{\Delta-2}\frac{1}{(-q\cdot Y)^{\Delta}} $$

Using the Feynman parameterization trick and the fundamental integral $\int d^{2}Y(-2Y\cdot Z)^{-2}=\pi/(-Z^{\mu}Z_{\mu})$ , one can compute

$$ \widetilde{\mathsf{S}}(-q\cdot X)^{-\Delta}=\frac{(-X^{\mu}X_{\mu})^{\Delta-1}}{(-q\cdot X)^{\Delta}} $$

which demonstrates that $\widetilde{\mathsf{S}}=\mathsf{SW}$ . It should also be noted that $\widetilde{\mathsf{S}}$ is also equal to the so-called “Kelvin transform” $\mathcal{K}$ , which acts on functions $f_{\Delta}(X)$ of scaling dimension $\Delta$ as

$$ (\mathcal{K}f_{\Delta})(X)=(-X^{\mu}X_{\mu})^{(\Delta-2)/2}f_{\Delta}\left(\frac{X}{(-X^{\mu}X_{\mu})^{1/2}}\right). $$

Soft Gravitons in the BFSS Matrix Model

Noah Miller, Andrew Strominger, Adam Tropper and Tianli Wang

Center for the Fundamental Laws of Nature, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA

## Abstract

BFSS proposed that asymptotically flat M-theory is dual to a large $N$ limit of the matrix quantum mechanics describing $N$ nonrelativistic D0-branes. Recent insights on the soft symmetries of any quantum theory of gravity in asymptotically flat space are applied to the BFSS matrix model. It is shown that soft gravitons are realized by submatrices whose rank is held fixed in the large $N$ M-theory limit, rather than the usual linear scaling with $N$ for hard gravitons. The soft expansion is identified with the large $N$ expansion and the soft theorem becomes a universal formula for the quantum mechanical scattering of such submatrix excitations. This formula is shown to be the Ward identity of large type IIA $U(1)_{RR}$ asymptotic gauge symmetry in the matrix model, whose asymptotic boundaries are at future and past timelike infinity.

## 1 Introduction

The holographic principle has a concrete and well-understood realization in anti-deSitter space (AdS) [1]. One hopes that the principle extends in some form to (nearly) flat spacetimes like the one we inhabit. The basic fact that the ratio of the boundary to bulk volume goes to a constant at large radius in AdS and to zero in flat space suggests that flat space holography may differ qualitatively from its AdS counterpart. But exactly how is an outstanding open question.

Two seemingly different approaches to flat space holography are the Banks-Fischler-Shenker-Susskind (BFSS) matrix model [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10] and celestial holography [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. BFSS is a top-down construction equating the momentum- $N$ sector of discrete lightcone quantized (DLCQ) M-theory with a quantum mechanics of $N\times N$ hermitian matrices representing open strings stretching between $N$ D0-branes. Celestial holography is a bottom-up approach applicable to any quantum theory of gravity in flat space, including M-theory, in which the proposed dual field theory lives on the celestial sphere at null infinity. Since the two approaches are applicable to the same theory it is natural to explore their connection.

The starting point of celestial holography (as well as AdS holography) is that both sides of a dual pair must have the same symmetries. Given the bulk description, soft theorems provide an efficient route to finding these symmetries [14]. So the first question we ask in this paper is ‘Is the soft graviton theorem realized in BFSS?’ We answer this by showing that soft gravitons are matrix subblocks whose rank is held fixed (rather than scaling with $N$ like the hard gravitons) in the large- $N$ limit which recovers the full uncompactified M-theory.11 1 This is reminiscent of the large- $N$ limit of QCD, where baryons have masses of order $N$ and mesons of order $1$ . It would be interesting to see how far this analogy can be pushed. The soft limit is then nontrivially identified with the M-theory limit. It would be illuminating to derive the soft theorem directly from the matrix model, and would provide a novel test of the latter.

Soft theorems are in general expected to be Ward identities of symmetries. Hence one asks if this expectation holds for the soft theorem in the matrix model. Using the known expression for the BFSS matrix model in a background $U(1)_{RR}$ gauge field [17] we show that the soft theorem is the Ward identity of ‘large’ $U(1)_{RR}$ gauge transformations [18] which do not die off at past or future timelike infinity.22 2 This is in accord with the fact that 11D supertranslations with non-zero momentum on the M-theory circle KK reduce to $U(1)_{RR}$ gauge transformations [19, 20].

We hope the answers to these basic questions provide a jumping off point for relating these two approaches to flat holography. Many further questions remain unanswered.

We will begin by reviewing the BFSS matrix model in Section 2. In Section 3, we leverage the soft graviton theorem in M-theory into an analogous one in the matrix model dual. We demonstrate that the soft expansion in the matrix model is a $1/N$ expansion. In Section 4, we discuss the interplay between soft theorems and supertranslation symmetry in M-theory arguing that the analog of supertranslation symmetry in the matrix model is a large gauge symmetry of the RR 1-form.

## 2 Matrix Model Review

In this section we briefly review the relevant features of the BFSS matrix theory [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10], which conjectures that the compactification of M-theory on a lightlike circle $X^{-}\sim X^{-}+2\pi R$ with momentum $P^{+}=N/R$ is dual to the low-energy dynamics of $N$ D0-branes in 10 dimensions or, equivalently, a certain supersymmetric quantum mechanical theory of $N\times N$ Hermitian matrices. Readers familiar with BFSS may safely skip this section.

### 2.1 BFSS Duality

Compactification of 11-dimensional M-theory on a spacelike circle gives type IIA string theory [21, 22]. The massless degrees of freedom in M-theory are the 11-dimensional supergraviton multiplet. The D0-branes in type IIA string theory are identified as the KK-modes of this supergraviton multiplet. The number of units $N$ of momentum around the circle corresponds to the number of D0-branes. The BFSS matrix model concerns a lightlike compactification of M-theory which can be defined as an infinitely large boost of a spacelike one [5].

Let us define the lightcone coordinates $X^{\pm},$ and lightcone momenta $P^{\pm}$ by

$$ X^{\pm}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(X^{0}\pm X^{10}),\hskip 30.0ptP^{\pm}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(P^{0}\pm P^{10}). $$

Lightcone quantization is performed on surfaces of constant $X^{+}$ which plays the role of time, with $P^{-}$ the Hamiltonian. The lightlike compactification of M-theory is

$$ (X^{+},X^{-})\sim(X^{+},X^{-}+2\pi R). $$

$P^{+}$ is quantized according to

$$ P^{+}=N/R. $$

BFSS argued that the sector of M-theory with total momentum $P^{+}=N/R$ can be described by a rescaled version of the Hamiltonian encoding the low-energy dynamics of $N$ $D0$ -branes in type IIA string theory [2, 3, 4]

$$ H=\frac{R}{2}\text{Tr}\Bigg[P^{I}P^{I}-\frac{1}{2(2\pi l_{p}^{3})^{2}}[X^{I},X^{J}][X^{I},X^{J}]-\frac{1}{2\pi l_{p}^{3}}\Psi^{T}\Gamma^{I}[X^{I},\Psi]\bigg] $$

subject to the constraint on physical states

$$ f_{ABC}(X^{I}_{B}P^{I}_{C}-\frac{i}{2}\Psi^{\alpha}_{B}\Psi^{\alpha}_{C})|\psi_{\text{phys}}\rangle=0 $$

which forces states to be invariant under $U(N)$ transformations. Here $X^{I}$ are $N\times N$ Hermitian matrices with the index $I=1,...,9$ running over the directions transverse to the lightlike compactification. $P^{I}$ are their conjugate momenta. $\Psi^{\alpha}$ is an $N\times N$ Hermitian matrix-valued spinor of $Spin(9)$ with $\alpha=1,...,16$ and gamma matrices $\Gamma^{I}_{\alpha\beta}$ . One can decompose these matrices as

$$ X^{I}=X^{I}_{A}T^{A},\hskip 30.0ptP^{I}=P^{I}_{A}T^{A},\hskip 30.0pt\Psi^{\alpha}=\Psi^{\alpha}_{A}T^{A} $$

where $T^{A}$ are generators of the Lie algebra of $U(N)$ in the adjoint representation normalized so that $\text{Tr}(T^{A}T^{B})=\delta^{AB}$ .

We now review some basic properties of this theory [23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28]. The bosonic potential $V\sim\Tr([X^I, X^J]^2)$ is classically at a minimum $V=0$ when $[X^{I},X^{J}]=0$ for all $I$ and $J$ , which implies all matrices can be simultaneously diagonalized. The $N$ eigenvalues are then positions of the $N$ D0-branes. For example, $N$ non-interacting D0-branes travelling along trajectories $x_{i}^{I}(t)$ with $i=1,...,N$ are described by the diagonal matrices

$$ X^{I}(t)=\begin{pmatrix}x^{I}_{1}(t)&0&\ldots&0\\
0&x^{I}_{2}(t)&\ldots&0\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
0&0&\ldots&x^{I}_{N}(t)\end{pmatrix}. $$

The off-diagonal elements are open strings stretching between the D0-branes.

A clump of $m<N$ coincident D0-branes corresponds to an $m\times m$ sub-block of this matrix for which all of the eigenvalues $x_{i}^{I}$ in the sub-block are equal. Quantum mechanically, these clumps are marginally bound states with complicated wave functions. They are dual to the higher KK-momentum supergraviton modes in the M-theory picture. Widely separated clumps are noninteracting because the strings stretched between them are very massive and forced into their ground states.

### 2.2 Scattering

Consider a set of $n$ gravitons in M-theory with individual momenta $k_{j}^{+}=N_{j}/R,$ with $j=1,...,n$ and total momentum $P^{+}_{\text{tot}}=(N_{1}+\cdots+N_{n})/R=N/R.$ Each graviton is dual to a marginally bound clump labeled by the number of D0-branes $N_{j}$ , the transverse momentum $k^{I}_{j}$ , and the polarization information of the 11D supergraviton multiplet $\epsilon_{j}$ which in the D0-brane description is encoded by the trace ‘center of mass’ fermions, with the explicit map given in [29, 30, 31, 32]. The dictionary [3, 4, 5, 33] between clumps of D0-branes and a collection of M-theory gravitons is:

| M-Theory |  | BFSS |
|---|---|---|
| $k_{j}^{+}$ | $\Longleftrightarrow$ | $N_{j}/R$ |
| $k_{j}^{I}$ | $\Longleftrightarrow$ | $k_{j}^{I}$ |
| $k_{j}^{-}$ | $\Longleftrightarrow$ | $R(k_{j}^{I})^{2}/2N_{j}$ |

*Table 1: Dictionary between momenta of gravitons in M-theory and momenta of D0-brane clumps in the BFSS matrix model. The final relation is determined using the mass-shell condition for M-theory gravitons $0=-2k_{j}^{+}k_{j}^{-}+k_{j}^{I}k_{j}^{I}$*

Widely separated multi-graviton ‘scattering states’ in M-theory with quantum numbers $k_{1}^{\mu},\epsilon_{1},...,k_{n}^{\mu},\epsilon_{n}$ correspond to widely-separated multi-clump states in the matrix model with D0-brane quantum numbers $N_{1},k_{1}^{I},\epsilon_{1},...,N_{n},k_{n}^{I},\epsilon_{n}$ . In order to formulate the scattering problem in BFSS, one should consider initial and final scattering states corresponding to widely separated wavepacket clumps of D0-branes, evolving past into future using the BFSS Hamiltonian (2.4) [34, 35]. The BFSS duality conjecture states that this scattering amplitude matches with the one that one would compute in (lightlike compactified) M-theory, namely

$$ \mathcal{A}_{\text{M}}(k_{1}^{\mu},...,k_{n}^{\mu})=\mathcal{A}_{\text{BFSS}}(N_{1},k_{1}^{I},...,N_{n},k_{n}^{I}). $$

### 2.3 The M-theory Limit

The scattering amplitudes of uncompactified 11-dimensional $M$ -theory are obtained by taking the radius large with external momenta held fixed

$$ R\to\infty,~~~~~~~k^{\mu}_{j}~~{\rm fixed}. $$

From the expression for the momenta this is easily seen to be equivalent to

$$ N\sim N_{j}\sim R\to\infty,~~~~~~~k^{I}_{j}~~{\rm fixed}, $$

and hence is a variety of large- $N$ limit. In this limit, the discretuum of allowed values of external momentum approach a continuum and any scattering proccess can be studied.

## 3 Soft Graviton Theorem in the Matrix Model

In this section we show that the soft theorem is realized within BFSS duality and, moreover, that the soft limit is the same as the M-theory limit with external momenta/D0-charges suitably scaled.

### 3.1 The Soft Theorem in M-Theory

Weinberg’s soft graviton theorem [36] applies to essentially any gravitational theory in an asymptotically flat spacetime.33 3 Of course Weinberg considered only four dimensions, but the extension to higher dimensions is straightforward [37, 38, 39, 40, 19] In particular it must hold in 11-dimensional M-theory which contains gravitons as part of the low energy effective action.

Consider a generic scattering amplitude $\mathcal{A}_{\text{M}}(k_{1}^{\mu},...,k_{n}^{\mu})$ involving external particles with future-directed momenta $k^{\mu}_{j}$ . These external particles may be ingoing or outgoing gravitons or some other particles. Momenta are parameterized by a vector $v^{I}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and a scale $\omega\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ according to

$$ k^{\mu}_{j}=\omega_{j}\hat{k}^{\mu}_{j}=\frac{\omega_{j}}{2}(1+v_{j}^{2},2v_{j}^{I},1-v_{j}^{2}),\hskip 30.0ptq^{\mu}_{s}=\omega_{s}\hat{q}^{\mu}_{s}=\frac{\omega_{s}}{2}(1+v_{s}^{2},2v_{s}^{I},1-v_{s}^{2}). $$

where we denote the momentum of the soft graviton by $q^{\mu}_{s}$ . The soft graviton theorem states:

$$ \mathcal{A}_{\text{M}}(q^{\mu}_{s},\epsilon_{s}^{\mu\nu};k_{1}^{\mu},...,k_{n}^{\mu})=\Bigg[\frac{\kappa}{2}\epsilon^{s}_{\mu\nu}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\eta_{j}\frac{k^{\mu}_{j}k^{\nu}_{j}}{q_{s}\cdot k_{j}}+\mathcal{O}\left(\Big(\frac{\omega_{s}}{\omega_{j}}\Big)^{0}\right)~\bigg]\mathcal{A}_{\text{M}}(k_{1}^{\mu},...,k_{n}^{\mu}) $$

where $\eta_{j}=+1~(-1)$ if the $j^{\rm th}$ particle is outgoing (incoming), $\epsilon_{s}^{\mu\nu}$ is the polarization tensor of the soft graviton, and $\kappa=\sqrt{32\pi G_{N}}$ [36].

In the soft limit, the ratios $\omega_{s}/\omega_{j}\rightarrow 0$ . The coefficient of the leading soft divergence $(\omega_{s}/\omega_{j})^{-1}$ is universal. This leading soft term has corrections which are a power series in $(\omega_{s}/\omega_{j})$ .

### 3.2 Soft Limit in the Matrix Model

In this subsection we show the soft limit in the BFSS matrix model is the M-theory limit with hard gravitons represented by subblocks whose size grows like $N$ and soft gravitons by subblocks of fixed finite size.

Both soft and hard gravitons are parameterized as in Equation (3.1) with $q_{s}^{+}=\sqrt{2}\omega_{s}$ and $k_{j}^{+}=\sqrt{2}\omega_{j}$ . This expression implies

$$ \frac{n_{s}}{R}=\sqrt{2}\omega_{s}~~,~~q_{s}^{I}=\omega_{s}v_{s}^{I}\sim\omega_{s}\hskip 20.0pt\text{and}\hskip 20.0pt\frac{N_{j}}{R}=\sqrt{2}\omega_{j}~~,~~k^{I}_{j}=\omega_{j}v_{j}^{I}\sim\omega_{j} $$

where we have used the dictionary provided in Table 1 with $N_{j}$ , the block sizes, corresponding to the hard M-theory gravitons, and $n_{s}$ to the soft ones. Thus, the momentum $k_{j}^{+}$ for a particular graviton dictates the size of the corresponding block in the matrix model. In the matrix model, the soft limit then reads

$$ \textbf{Soft Limit:}~~~~~~~\frac{n_{s}}{N_{j}}=\frac{\omega_{s}}{\omega_{j}}\rightarrow 0. $$

Scattering amplitudes with a soft external particle in the BFSS matrix model, thus, correspond to situations where a block of size $n_{s}$ is dwarfed by the other blocks of size $N_{j}$ . This happens automatically in the M-theory limit (2.10) as long as we keep $n_{s}$ fixed! Hence the soft limit is the same as the M-theory limit, but with a new type of external state constructed from a finite number $n_{s}$ of D0-branes.

In the M-theory limit, the difference between scattering a graviton with $(N_{j},k^{I}_{j})$ versus $(N_{j}-1,k^{I}_{j})$ with one fewer D0-branes vanishes. This might have led to the naive conclusion that submatrices with sizes or order one don’t matter and that the scattering of a single D0-brane $(1,k^{I}_{s})$ vanishes altogether. This is not the case because of the soft pole. Note also the leading term in the scattering amplitude for a bound state with a fixed finite number $n_{s}$ of D0s differs only by the multiplicative factor $1/n_{s}$ .

We illustrate a $2\rightarrow 3$ scattering process with soft emission diagrammatically from the M-theory perspective, the D0-brane perspective, and the block diagonal matrix perspective explicitly in Figure 1.

We now write the leading soft graviton theorem of M-theory (3.2) in terms of BFSS variables. If we define a convenient basis for graviton polarization tensors

$$ \epsilon^{\mu\nu}_{IJ}(v)\equiv\frac{1}{2}\big(\epsilon^{\mu}_{I}\epsilon^{\nu}_{J}+\epsilon^{\nu}_{I}\epsilon^{\mu}_{J}\big)-\frac{1}{d}\delta_{IJ}\epsilon^{\mu}_{K}\epsilon^{K\nu}\hskip 20.0pt\text{with}\hskip 20.0pt\epsilon^{\mu}_{J}(v)\equiv\partial_{J}\hat{q}^{\mu}_{s}=(v_{J},\delta^{I}_{J},-v_{J}) $$

and write the soft graviton polarization as

$$ \epsilon_{s}^{\mu\nu}=e^{IJ}\epsilon_{IJ}^{\mu\nu}, $$

then after some algebra and using the dictionary 1, the soft theorem becomes 44 4 There is a small technical subtlety in Equation (3.7). The BFSS matrix model describes M-theory in a sector with momentum $P^{+}=N/R$ , so all amplitudes must be manifestly momentum conserving in $P^{+}$ and cannot be off-shell in $P^{+}$ . Equivalently, the number of D0-branes $N$ is always conserved. Therefore, we cannot simply append a small block of size $n_{s}$ to the matrix, but we must shrink the size of the other blocks slightly. Assuming that the amplitudes are analytic in $N_{j}$ (in the large $N$ limit, this follows from the analyticity of the M-theory S-matrix) one may perform a first order Taylor expansion to see that the expression will only be corrected at subleading terms.

$$ \mathcal{A}_{\text{BFSS}}(n_{s},q^{I}_{s},\epsilon_{s},\text{out; in})=\bigg[-2\kappa\sum_{j=1}^{n}\eta_{j}\frac{N_{j}}{n_{s}}\frac{e_{IJ}(v_{s}-v_{j})^{I}(v_{s}-v_{j})^{J}}{(v_{s}-v_{j})^{2}}+\cdots~\bigg]\mathcal{A}_{\text{BFSS}}(\text{out; in}). $$

Finally, we define the inversion tensor in 9 spatial dimensions as55 5 This is the same inversion tensor familiar from conformal field theory.

$$ \mathcal{I}^{IJ}(v)=\delta^{IJ}-2\frac{v^{I}v^{J}}{v^{2}}. $$

In terms of this inversion tensor, the leading soft graviton theorem in the BFSS matrix model reads

$$ \mathcal{A}_{\text{BFSS}}(n_{s},q^{I}_{s},\epsilon_{s},\text{out; in})=\bigg[\kappa\sum_{j=1}^{n}\eta_{j}\frac{N_{j}}{n_{s}}e_{IJ}\mathcal{I}^{IJ}(v_{s}-v_{j})+\cdots~\bigg]\mathcal{A}_{\text{BFSS}}(\text{out; in}). $$

Note that the soft pole $\omega_{j}/\omega_{s}$ gets recast into the ratio of block sizes $N_{j}/n_{s}$ , which diverges in the soft limit according to Equation (3.4).

Sub-leading corrections to this expression are given by an expansion in $n_{s}/N_{j}$ . Because $n_{s}\sim\mathcal{O}(1)$ and $N_{j}\sim\mathcal{O}(N),$ we can identify the subleading terms in the soft expansion on the gravity side with a $1/N$ expansion on the gauge theory side.

It would be illuminating to derive the soft theorem directly from the matrix model. It is not obvious to us even how the factor of $N_{j}/n_{s}$ would emerge.

## 4 Asymptotic Symmetries in the Matrix Model

In this section, we use the soft graviton theorem in 11D to show that the insertion of a single D0-brane in a 10D BFSS scattering amplitude generates a large gauge transformation on the background RR 1-form gauge potential $C_{\mu}$ in the matrix model.66 6 The result easily generates to finite bound clumps of D0-branes by dividing by $n_{s}$ . Since this is a quantum-mechanical model the relevant asymptotic regions are at $t=\pm\infty$ . The RR 1-form is of the form $C_{\mu}=\partial_{\mu}\theta_{e,v_{s}}$ , for some particular gauge parameter $\theta_{e,v_{s}}$ given in (4.9) depending on the polarization $e_{IJ}$ and velocity $v_{s}$ of the soft D0-brane. This is summarized in Equation (4.10), which is the main result of this section. This large $U(1)$ gauge symmetry arises in the KK reduction of the 11D supertranslation symmetry.77 7 Symmetries associated to 10D supertranslations would have to come from modes independent of the $X^{+}$ circle and hence involve $n_{s}=0$ . It is not clear to us how to describe these in the matrix model.

### 4.1 Background RR Gauge Potentials

The standard BFSS matrix model, with the Hamiltonian given by Equation (2.4), describes a system of D0-branes living in world where all background fields are turned off. The effect of coupling the D0-branes to external background fields can be incorporated by adding terms to the Lagrangian. In particular the interaction term coupling the D0-branes to the $U(1)_{RR}$ gauge field $C_{\mu}$ generalizes the usual electromagnetic interaction $Q\int dt\;\dot{x}^{\mu}C_{\mu}(x)$ between a charge $Q$ particle and the gauge field, where $x^{\mu}$ is the worldline of the particle.

In the matrix model, the precise interaction term was found in [17] to be

$$ S_{RR}[C_{\mu}]=\int dt\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\big(\partial_{I_{1}}\cdots\partial_{I_{n}}C_{\mu}(t,\vec{0})\big)I^{\mu(I_{1}\cdots I_{n})} $$

where $\mu=0,\ldots,9$ and $x^{\mu}=(t,x^{I})=(t,\vec{x})$ . The ‘multipole moments’ of the current $I^{\mu}$ are defined by

$$ \displaystyle I^{\mu(I_{1}\cdots I_{n})} \displaystyle=\Tr(\mathrm{Sym}(I^\mu, X^{I_1}, \cdots, X^{I_n} ))+I^{\mu(I_{1}\cdots I_{n})}_{\text{F}} $$

where

$$ I^{\mu}=(\mathbb{1}/R,\dot{X}^{I}/R). $$

Here, $\mathrm{Sym}$ is a symmetrized average over all orderings of the input matrices. $I^{\mu(I_{1}\cdots I_{n})}_{\text{F}}$ are terms involving at least two fermionic matrices, $\Psi$ , which will not be relevant to this paper for reasons discussed in section 4.2. If one takes the matrices $X^{I}$ to be diagonal, as in Equation (2.7), then the action reduces to the electromagnetic form, as expected.

### 4.2 Large $U(1)_{RR}$ Gauge Transformations

If the RR 1-form is pure gauge, then the interaction term (4.1) becomes a total derivative. Plugging $C_{\mu}=\partial_{\mu}\theta$ into Equation (4.1), one can show that88 8 To demonstrate this, one must use that the multipole moments satisfy the conservation law $\partial_{t}I^{0(I_{1}\cdots I_{n})}=I^{I_{1}(I_{2}\cdots I_{n})}+\cdots+I^{I_{n}(I_{1}\cdots I_{n-1})}$ .

$$ \begin{split}S_{RR}[\partial_{\mu}\theta]&=\frac{1}{R}\int dt~\partial_{t}\left[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}(\partial_{I_{1}}\cdots\partial_{I_{n}}\theta(t,\vec{0}))I^{0(I_{1}\cdots I_{n})}\right]\\
&=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}(\partial_{I_{1}}\cdots\partial_{I_{n}}\theta(t,\vec{0}))I^{0(I_{1}\cdots I_{n})}\bigg|_{t=-\infty}^{t=+\infty}.\end{split} $$

Therefore, a pure gauge background field affects amplitudes by a position-dependent phase acting on the initial and final states.

The asymptotic symmetry group of gauge theories is typically defined as the set of ‘large’ gauge transformations which satisfy some set of boundary conditions modulo ‘small’ gauge transformations which vanish at the boundary. For the remainder of this section, we will consider the case where $C_{\mu}=\partial_{\mu}\theta$ is pure gauge and given by such a large gauge transformation $\theta$ which is non-vanishing as $t\rightarrow\pm\infty.$ The boundary conditions which $\theta$ must satisfy near past and future timelike infinity [41, 42, 43, 44, 14] specify that as $t\rightarrow\pm\infty$ , the gauge parameter $\theta(t,\vec{x})$ can only depend on the ratio $\vec{x}/t$

$$ \theta(t,\vec{x})\xrightarrow{t\rightarrow\pm\infty}\theta(t,\vec{x})=\theta(\vec{x}/t) $$

implying that these large gauge transformations are parameterized by a single function on $\mathbb{R}^{9}$ .99 9 This is the limit relevant for nonrelativistic charged massive scattering states of the more general formula for large $U(1)$ gauge transformations. Outside of the above specification, the gauge parameter is arbitrary.

Now we show that the boundary term (4.4) reduces to a very simple expression on asymptotic scattering states. As functions of $X^{I}$ , asymptotic scattering wavefunctions are sharply peaked in momentum space and non-trivially supported only on matrices of the form

$$ X^{I}=\begin{pmatrix}x^{I}_{1}(t)&&\\
&\ddots&\\
&&x^{I}_{N}(t)\end{pmatrix}+\Delta X^{I},\hskip 21.33955pt\Delta X^{I}\sim\mathcal{O}(t^{0}) $$

where $\vec{x}_{i}(t)=\vec{v}_{i}t+\vec{x}_{i,0}$ tracks the position of the $i^{th}$ D0-brane. Note that $\vec{x}_{i}(t)=\vec{x}_{j}(t)$ when the $i^{th}$ and $j^{th}$ D0-branes share a bound state. $\Delta X^{I}$ is a matrix whose values do not grow with time as $t\to\pm\infty$ . The entries within the blocks on the diagonal of $\Delta X^{I}$ correspond to the degrees of freedom of the bound states modulo their center of mass motion. As such, these entries can take values on the order of the spatial size of these bound states.

The off block-diagonal components of $\Delta X^{I}$ describe strings stretched between distant D0-brane bound states. The mass of the string is proportional to its length, so these strings have mass scaling like $t$ . When the string excitations become heavy, the wavefunction for these components gets frozen to the ground state of a quantum (super)harmonic oscillator with frequency $\omega\sim t$ . The width of such a wavefunction shrinks as $\sim t^{-1/2}.$ This situation is summarized in Figure 4.

We find that the only terms that survive at $t=\pm\infty$ are 1010 10 In this footnote we demonstrate why the fermionic term $I_{\text{F}}^{0(I_{1}\ldots I_{n})}$ in Equation (4.2) doesn’t contribute to our analysis. First, we notice that the couplings $\partial_{I_{1}}\cdots\partial_{I_{n}}\theta(\vec{x}/t)$ contains $n$ spatial derivatives, each pulling down a factor of $1/t$ . So, for the term $(\partial_{I_{1}}\cdots\partial_{I_{n}}\theta)I^{0(I_{1}\cdots I_{n})}$ to be non-vanishing at $t=\pm\infty$ , $I^{0(I_{1}\cdots I_{n})}\sim t^{n}$ at asymptotic times. The bosonic moments, $I^{0(I_{1}\cdots I_{n})}_{\text{B}}=\text{Tr}(\text{Sym}(X^{I_{1}}\cdots X^{I_{n}})),$ scale as $t^{n}$ , since every bosonic matrix has entries growing as $t$ . In fact, only the entries linear in $t$ , which are $v^{I}t$ , survive in this limit. Next, we use the fact that the BFSS action is invariant under $R\mapsto\lambda R,X\mapsto\lambda^{1/3}X,\Psi\mapsto\lambda^{1/2}\Psi,t\mapsto\lambda^{-1/3}t$ [45]. This invariance must persist when coupled to a background field if we map $\theta\mapsto\lambda\theta$ , which implies that each multipole term $I^{\mu(I_{1}\ldots I_{n})}$ must have a constant scaling dimension in $\lambda$ for the action to be invariant. Therefore, if two $\Psi$ ’s are added, three $X$ ’s must be removed, making the whole term scale three lower powers of $t$ and vanish at the boundary.

$$ \displaystyle S_{RR}[\partial_{\mu}\theta] \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\eta_{j}\frac{N_{j}}{R}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\big(\partial_{I_{1}}\cdots\partial_{I_{n}}\theta(t,0)\big)x_{j}^{I_{1}}\cdots x_{j}^{I_{n}}\bigg|_{t=-\infty}^{t=+\infty}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\eta_{j}\frac{N_{j}}{R}\theta(\vec{v}_{j}) $$

where we noticed that middle expression is just a Taylor expansion of $\theta(t,\vec{x})$ and used $\theta(t,\vec{x}_{j})=\theta(\vec{x}_{j}/t)$ according to our earlier considerations.

In a quantum amplitude, this addition to the action becomes an overall phase. Therefore, placing BFSS in such a background gauge field modifies the amplitude via

$$ \evaluated{\mathcal{A}_{\text{BFSS}}(\text{out; in})}_{C_\mu= \partial_\mu\theta}=\exp( i \sum_{j = 1}^n \eta_j \frac{N_j}{R} \theta(\vec{v_j}) )\evaluated{\mathcal{A}_{\text{BFSS}}(\text{out; in})}_{C_\mu= 0}. $$

From the soft graviton theorem (3.9), if we define the gauge parameter $\theta_{e,v_{s}}$ by

$$ \theta_{e,v_{s}}(\vec{x}/t)\equiv\frac{e_{IJ}(v_{s}-x/t)^{I}(v_{s}-x/t)^{J}}{|\vec{v}_{s}-\vec{x}/t|^{2}} $$

which depends on the velocity $\vec{v}_{s}$ and polarization structure $e_{IJ}$ of the soft D0-brane, then by combining (4.8) and (3.7), we see that

$$ \lim_{n_{s}/R\to 0}~\frac{n_{s}}{R}\evaluated{\mathcal{A}_{\text{BFSS}}(n_s, k^I_s, \epsilon_s, \text{out; in})}_{C_\mu= 0}=-i\evaluated{\frac{d}{d \varepsilon}}_{\varepsilon= 0}\evaluated{\mathcal{A}_{\text{BFSS}}(\text{out; in}) }_{C_\mu= \varepsilon\partial_\mu\theta_{e,v_s}}. $$

Therefore, the insertion of a single D0-brane in a momentum eigenstate in the amplitude generates the action of a large $U(1)_{RR}$ gauge transformation (4.9) on the asymptotic scattering state. A general gauge transformation can be generated by an appropriate coherent superposition of a momentum-eigenstate D0-brane.
